# Ber Wilson Platform — Build Log

Session-by-session history. **`CLAUDE.md` in the repo root is the canonical reference** — architecture, conventions, the deploy runbook and the DO NOT rules live there, along with the hard-won rules distilled out of this log (§12).

This file is **not** auto-loaded into a Claude Code session. It is the archive: grep it when a session needs the reasoning behind a decision — *"why is the digest at 7:00am and not 6:30?"*, *"what did the Drive filing pass actually measure?"*, *"have we hit this bug before?"*

Split out of `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-09-23, when that file reached 606k characters against a 150k limit above which it is silently truncated — meaning the project's own operating instructions had begun to risk not reaching the sessions that need them. The entries below are **verbatim and unedited**.

Workstream 3, the last of the four planned on 10-29. Richard: *"ok finish that

`notify/policy.ts` held `pepper_note` on 2026-10-21 with the reason *"The

## Reading the last note she actually sent

Three of its fourteen bullets said *"this is the fifth morning I've raised
them"*, two more said third or fourth, and two sections ended *"Another 30
behind these."* Against **199 open commitments** the note samples about ten and
counts the rest. Nothing in it marked what had changed, so one morning read
exactly like the last — §12's rule that a line identical for every reader
cannot justify sending them the message, in its other form: identical every DAY
fails the same test.

## ⚠ What the plan said to do, and why half of it was wrong

The plan was to lead with what changed AND to use `pepper_note_items.times_named`
to DROP an item after N mornings. `memory.ts`'s own header refuses the second
half, with a reason:

> The mention count … ANNOTATES … and it applies a small, expiring,
> within-band penalty … **Demoting at all would be the platform silently
> overruling a reader IF they had no way to say "not today"**; `snoozed_until`
> is that way, it is one tap in the note, and the penalty is bounded at 125
> against 5,000 between bands — so it can reorder a morning and **can never
> hide anything**.

That is the third module header in one day to overrule the plan on its own
recorded evidence (after `fold.ts` on `estimated_value` and `task-reminder.ts`
on dated tasks). Dropping was not built. What was built is purely ADDITIVE and
hides nothing.

## What it is

`arrivedSince()` / `arrivedClause()` in `memory.ts` mark a commitment that
arrived since the last note, and the prompt (now **1.4**) gains a
`## New since I last wrote` section placed directly after the summary, with the
rule that an item named there appears NOWHERE else.

Measured before building: **4 to 16 commitments arrive per day, median ~9**,
against the standing 199. So the section has real, bounded content every
morning rather than being a heading that is usually empty.

⚠ **PARSED, NOT STRING-COMPARED.** `sinceIso` is `Date.toISOString()` (`…Z`)
and `created_at` comes from PostgREST with `+00:00`. Lexicographically `+`
sorts BEFORE `Z`, so two representations of the SAME instant compare the wrong
way round under `>=`. A test asserts the naive comparison really does disagree,
so nobody "simplifies" it back.

⚠ **MARKING WAS NOT ENOUGH — THE CAP WAS EATING THE NEW ONES.** First run: 13
commitments arrived in 24 hours and exactly **2** reached the rendered note.
`rank()` orders by `commitmentWeight` (due date, overdue days), so a brand-new
UNDATED obligation sorts near the bottom and `MAX_PER_SECTION = 12` cuts it —
the one genuinely new thing in a daily note was the thing most likely to be
dropped from it. `withArrivals()` now admits arrivals ON TOP of the ranked
twelve (bounded at 6) rather than making them compete: the existing order is
untouched, and the overflow count is derived from what was actually shown
rather than `length - MAX_PER_SECTION`, which would have overstated by up to
six. 13 of 13 now reach the note.

## ⚠ THE PROMPT WAS PUTTING AN INVENTED SENTENCE IN FRONT OF THE READER

Generating a note to check the new section surfaced something worse than the
thing being fixed. The records-line rule read:

> "WHAT I CHANGED IN THE RECORDS MYSELF" is yours to own in one short line near
> the end — **"I filled in three contact titles and set Weirton's location from
> Tuesday's thread."**

The model printed that sentence **verbatim, as a statement of what it had
done** — naming a real project and a real weekday. The actual changes were
three company names, two email addresses and one phone number across six
different people. §12 has this exactly: *a prompt example is training data, and
a stale one is a lie the model repeats with confidence.* What makes it
expensive here rather than merely untidy is WHICH line it is: §11's 10-12 trade
is that Pepper may write to records unattended **because every change is
reported each morning**, so a fabricated report is the safeguard failing
silently. Looking back at the last note actually sent, *"I corrected one
company name on Seth Lloyd's record from Tuesday's thread"* is the same shape.

Every illustrative example in the prompt is now a placeholder shape
(`"<record>'s <field>: the record says <A>, the mail says <B>. Which?"`), with
a general rule that every example is a shape and never a fact. A test asserts
the prompt names none of six live records and that the general rule is still
there; planting a violation confirmed it fails.

Two more defects found the same way and fixed in 1.4:
- **The input's internal markers were being pasted into the reader's note** —
  `[sitting in mailbox]` appeared verbatim, which reads as a leaked debug line.
- **Items were duplicated** between the new section and "You owe".

## ⚠ And the model was counting rows it had been handed

With the example removed, the line came back as *"2 phone numbers, 2 email
addresses, and 3 company names"* against a real 1 / 2 / 3. Right kinds, wrong
number, in the line that reports unattended writes. §12: **never make the model
count rows — print the count.** The section heading now carries the tally,
computed over ALL changes rather than the capped display list:
`WHAT I CHANGED IN THE RECORDS MYSELF (6 in total — 3 × Company, 2 × Email,
1 × Phone; USE THESE NUMBERS, do not count the rows below)`. The regenerated
note reads *"I updated 3 company fields, 2 email fields, and 1 phone field"* —
exact.

## It is STILL HELD, deliberately

The approved plan said to flip `pepper_note` to live only after a week of
reading the unsent output, and it has not been flipped. Sending a daily 06:50
email to both executives on the strength of one afternoon's reading is not a
call to make unilaterally, and the hold costs nothing: the note assembles and
renders every morning either way. The `held:` string now says what changed and
what to read before flipping the one word.

## What it turned out NOT to be

The plan was to port `PepperNote.liveTasks` into the live task reminder, on the
grounds that 89 of 146 open tasks were undated and therefore invisible to the
only outbound channel Pepper still has.

Both halves of that were wrong, and in opposite directions.

**1. The reminder is correct as specified, and its specification is Richard's
own.** `task-reminder.ts` opens with his 10-21 instruction verbatim: *"The only
messaging I want to go out are reminder of important tasks that have a due date
that week."* The header then records the decision explicitly — *a due date IS
the importance signal, and that is a decision, not a shortcut* — because `tasks`
has no priority column and inventing a second notion of importance would be a
field nobody maintains. Widening the message to undated work would have
overridden a recorded instruction, exactly as Workstream 1 would have earlier
the same day. It was not done.

Checked rather than assumed: the Monday message already names unowned DATED
tasks, and of the 13 open tasks with no assignee **exactly one carries a date** —
and that one is already in the message. The reminder covers its whole scope.

**2. ⚠ THE BACKLOG FIGURES WERE WRONG, AND THE WAY THEY WERE CAUGHT IS THE
POINT.** The measurement used `status <> 'completed'` and reported **146 open,
89 undated, 45 overdue, 22 unassigned**. The column holds **`open` and `done`**;
there is no `completed`, so the predicate was true for every row in the table and
swept in all 105 finished tasks.

The truth is **41 open, of which 37 carry no due date — 90% — 13 unassigned and
2 overdue.**

It surfaced because the rendered board disagreed with the query: the page's own
header says *41 open across the team, 2 past their date* while the query claimed
146 and 45. §12 twice over — check what a column's values ARE before filtering
on one, and when a check disagrees with the screen, suspect the check. The
alarming half evaporated (2 overdue, not 45) and the half that mattered got
worse: 90% undated rather than 61%. Both figures are corrected in the earlier
entry for this date, which had already shipped with the wrong ones.

## What it is

**A due-date slice, in the URL.** `all | overdue | week | undated`. The board
had an `unassigned` option on its assignee filter and no date filter at all, so
nine rows in ten were reachable only by scrolling past the handful that were
dated. A backlog you cannot select is one nobody drains. Live counts match the
database exactly: 41 / 2 / 1 / 37.

**Bulk editing.** Checkbox per row, a sticky bar offering Set due date, Assign
and Mark done over the selection. Every action loops the existing
`PATCH /api/tasks/[id]` rather than gaining a bulk route of its own — a bulk
route would have to re-implement `guardTask`, the non-executive retag check,
`settleCommitmentForTask` (ticking a promoted task settles its obligation on the
counterparty's thread) and `queueTaskSheetRefresh`. §12: never fork a shared
pass. One request per row is the price of not owning a second copy of all four,
and the rows number tens.

⚠ **COMPLETE, NEVER DELETE, IN BULK.** The single-row control pair is
deliberate and documented: ticking stamps `completed_at`, writes to
`activity_log` and settles a commitment; deleting destroys the row and its notes
with only `to_jsonb(old)` to recover it. One of those is safe to do fifty at a
time and one is not, so only one is in the bar.

⚠ **ONE `router.refresh()`, ON THE TRAILING EDGE** — §12: an optimistic client
mutation with no refresh leaves every server-rendered count lying until the tab
is reloaded.

## ⚠ The React Compiler refused three versions of the filter, and the lint
baseline is why that mattered

Adding the due slice INSIDE the `filtered` memo makes the React Compiler abandon
that memo — *"existing memoization could not be preserved"* — which is a lint
**error**, and §9 freezes the baseline at 22 problems deliberately. §12: a
legitimate exemption gets NAMED with its reason, never absorbed by raising the
baseline. So it was fixed rather than accepted, across four attempts:

1. Inline in the memo, with `Date.now()` → also tripped `react-hooks/purity`.
2. The clock hoisted to a mount-captured `useState`, predicate still inline → the
   compiler still bailed on `filtered`.
3. Predicate lifted to a module-scope `matchesDue` → still bailed.
4. Its own `useMemo` over `filtered` → the error simply moved onto the new memo,
   including after removing the `dueFilter === 'all' ? filtered : …` branch
   (returning a dependency unchanged from one arm is its own refusal case).

What works is a plain derived value with no hand-memoization for the compiler to
fail to preserve — which is what the compiler wants anyway. `filter` preserves
relative order, so the tier-then-date sort `filtered` ends on still holds, and
everything downstream reads `visible`: the bar's count, "select all shown", the
drag list and the empty state. Baseline back to exactly 22.

`matchesDue`, `DUE_FILTERS` and `dueWindowFrom` live in
`src/lib/tasks/due-filter.ts`, not in the board — §12: a helper shared between
server and client code must not be exported from a `'use client'` file, and it
is also the only way the predicate is testable at all.

## Workstream 1 was planned, then WITHDRAWN after re-testing its recorded reason

The plan was to widen `foldDealFields` to the `estimated_value` the thread
summary already carries. It was approved and then abandoned, because the module
header at `src/lib/curator/fold.ts:22-37` lists `estimated_value` and
`stage_signal` under *"WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT FOLDED, each for a recorded
reason"* — which I had not read when planning. §12 says a workaround's recorded
reason must be re-tested before it is inherited. It was. It holds, three ways:

1. **The clearing was deliberate and is in the audit log.** On 2026-10-05 an
   actor named `estimated-value-cutover@berwilson.com` nulled `estimated_value`
   on 8 projects. The figures removed were **$48,000,000,000**, $3B, $2B, $1.8B,
   $1B, $1B, $750M and $1.5M. A $48B contract value for a two-person firm was
   not a contract value.
2. **The corpus cannot answer the question the column asks.** Reading the
   evidence behind the 6 candidate deals: **GridEdge carries five figures across
   five threads** — $8.5M (acquisition proposal), $1.5M (counter-proposal
   floor), $5M (a SAFE Ber Wilson *rejected*), $500k (a pitch), $8.5M. Those are
   the positions in a live negotiation, and `pick()`'s newest-wins would stamp
   whichever landed last as *the* value. **IAN carries $3.6M and $350M on the
   same record** — 36 acres at $100k/acre of land, versus an LOI to acquire the
   company. §12: a money figure must carry its SHAPE; one column cannot hold
   both, and nothing in the thread says which one it wants.
3. **Richard has already ruled on where deal economics live** — the calculator
   was removed 10-23 with *build it in Excel first, then bring it back*.

So the fold was not built. The downstream consequences are real and stay as a
finding: `pipelineValue()` has no figure, the composer's gate has no platform
figures to authorise, and the pursuit profile has no size bounds. If it is ever
automated, the honest source is an **executed** document, never a thread summary.

## The queue reads four ways

One fixed order — `decideWeight` descending — answers "what is most
consequential" and nothing else. Sifting ~130 rows across six kinds also needs
"what landed since I last looked" and "what can I clear without reading".

Four orders now (`consequence`, `recent`, `confident`, `quick`), as views of ONE
population: the chip counts above the list are deliberately unaffected by which
is chosen, because a sort that changed the numbers would be a filter wearing a
sort's clothes.

⚠ **THE SORT KEY DID NOT EXIST.** `DecideItem` carried `occurredAt` (filled only
by a staged meeting) and `deadline` (filled by nothing at all since leads left
on 10-22) and no arrival time. "Most recent" needed one honest `arrivedAt` on
all six producers — seven fill sites, since the meeting branch is separate, and
there it is the STAGING and not the call: a conversation from last Tuesday
staged this morning is new to the reader this morning.

⚠ **AND THE DOCUMENT TABLES HAVE NO `created_at`.** Both `documents` and
`opportunity_documents` depart from §4's convention and carry `uploaded_at`.
Reaching for the conventional name would have been `42703` — which fails the
WHOLE query, not the column, and on this page would have rendered as "no
documents are waiting".

⚠ **`decideWeight` IS NOT A TOTAL ORDER AND COULD NOT BE THE TIEBREAK.** Its
value is exactly 0 for every row with no deadline, verdict or value — on the
live queue that is every document row, the largest kind present. A comparator
returning 0 for two distinct rows lets them swap places between renders of
identical data: the flat-`MEETING_BOOST` bug one level up, which made all five
staged meetings tie. Every order now ends on the row id, and a test sorts three
weightless rows from both input orders to prove it.

`score` is deliberately NOT offered as an order. §12: `fit_score` carries ±20
points of sampling noise, and `decideWeight`'s own note records removing it as a
TIEBREAKER — offering it as the PRIMARY key would be strictly worse than the bug
that was fixed. A test asserts no order names a score.

The view is in the URL (§12 — a filter kept only in component state is not a
view), seeded server-side so the first paint is right, and synced back with
`history.replaceState` rather than `router.replace`. `LeadsClient` took that
decision first and wrote down why: this page runs three corpus-wide document
passes and a portfolio match per staged session, so a Next navigation per
keystroke would make the search unusable.

`SortControls` on the dashboard carried *"Same track-and-pill idiom as
`Segmented` … if a third of these appears, merge them."* This was the third, so
it moved onto `Segmented` rather than being copied again. What stays different
is deliberate: the dashboard sorts on the SERVER and keeps `router.push`.

Also corrected the page description, which still promised *"Ranked so the most
consequential is first"* after the order became choosable — §12's rule about a
comment claiming a control that is not there, applied to reader-facing copy.

## Why the queue was not auto-filing the obvious — and now does

The answer to Richard's second question is that `matchDocument` **does** find
them. `bestMatch` accepts a record's whole name, two distinctive shared words,
or a human-asserted alias. `/decide` simply never acted on the result: it
offered the filing and waited for a click. The rows that genuinely do not match
are the ambiguous ones (`Englert` names two Alaska records and was withdrawn for
exactly that reason) and one-word names, which need a shared contact.

Richard's direction: a whole-name match should file itself. It now does, as a
sweep phase straight after `unparented` — which is what creates most of these, so
a file that arrived this run and says "GridEdge" in its own name is on GridEdge
before anybody opens the queue.

⚠ **§11 IS UNTOUCHED.** Nothing is created; every row already exists as a
`documents` row and only its parent changes. That is the 10-12 amendment's
"Pepper UPDATES records" case, so the write goes through
`createAdminClient(PEPPER_ACTOR)` after `assertPepper()`. `documents` carries
`log_documents`, and verified live: all 13 filings are credited to
`info@berwilson.com` (9 DELETE where the row crossed into
`opportunity_documents`, 4 UPDATE where it stayed), not to "system".

The bar is `identifiesRecord` — the record's whole name, contiguously, once
punctuation is flattened. Threshold-free, already measured on this corpus, and
already the bar for the one other unattended write that turns on a name. NOT the
matcher's bar: two distinctive shared words was measured at 9 wrong records out
of 9.

Measured before building: 60 documents carry a proposal, 13 name their record
outright. Every one of the 13 was read by hand before writes were enabled —
GridEdge ×5, Alaska Strategic Materials JV ×2, West Wendover ×2, Dino Plumbing
×2, Elite Solutions, Synetra. All 13 filed; the second run filed 0, as §12's
pairing rule requires. The queue went 139 → 126.

### ⚠ THE ALIAS THAT SILENTLY BECAME THE COUNTERPARTY'S NAME

36 of the 48 candidates were alias-grade, and the plan was to file those too. The
live register will not bear it.

`tokenize()` drops any token of two characters or fewer. So the alias
**`"Tensor CM"`** — written by a human to NARROW to the construction-management
engagement — is stored as the single token **`tensor`**, the counterparty's own
name. It then matches `Tensor MNDA (with Non-Circumvention).docx`, `Tensor IQ
LLC - Bio Jonathan Houk.pdf` and every other Tensor IQ document, and files them
onto that one engagement with `certainty: 'linked'` — a FACT outranking every
similarity score.

This is §12's recorded Tensor failure — *one `Tensor MNDA` "proving" four
unrelated sites on the counterparty word alone* — arriving through the alias
door, which is the door §12 recommends as the REMEDY for weak matching.

Measured across the whole register: **13 of 86 aliases lose at least one word,
and 8 collapse to a single token.** Most are harmless, because the dropped word
is a deliberate stopword — `"Project Riverdale"` → `riverdale` is correct. Two
are not: `"Tensor CM"` → `tensor`, and `"Forge 42"` → `forge`. Also
`"3 Mag"` → `mag` and `"HD-5534-A-1"` → `5534`.

A second alias case found the same way: `Doc2_Myton_Quantum_Campus_MOU_Updated.docx`
is proposed for **Box Elder** Quantum Campus on its alias `"Quantum Campus"`,
while the document's own name says **Myton**. This is the cause of the open item
raised 10-18, where a *Helper, Utah* recording landed on Box Elder the same way.

The collapse is NOT fixed here, deliberately: alias tokens also drive THREAD
routing across the whole corpus, so changing what one alias means has a far
larger blast radius than this pass. It is an open item for Richard, because
which record should own the bare word `tensor` is his call, not a code decision.

Both refusals are now tests, with the real file names in them.

**Done 2026-10-29 (a job can read the mail — and the premise behind the ask was mostly wrong):**

Richard: *"The idea is that I can cut down on having to decide where things go. Can the jobs section do a job of scrubbing back through that data? For example, once a project called Whiskey is created, it should definitely be able to match any mention of the word Whiskey and know to append those items to the project. Not to mention the contacts on the email also being on the project. So I would like it to have the ability to scrub through data to clean it up and also scrub through data to create a project."*

── THE PREMISE, MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BUILT ────────────────────────

§12 says measure the data's SHAPE rather than its size, and that the premise has repeatedly turned out to be wrong. It did again, in four steps, each of which changed the design.

**1. The backlog is real.** 1,823 of 2,080 deal threads (88%) are linked to no record at all.

**2. Re-running the existing matcher over them places 20.** `bestMatch` against today's 41 targets: 1.1%. The hits are exactly the records created AFTER routing last ran — Eagle Mountain (8), Tensor Site CM (8), Synetra, Dino, Elite Solutions. `routed_at` spans 09-18 → 10-29 while records were created 10-08, 10-21 and 10-28, and a routed thread is never revisited. So the "stale router" theory is true and worth 20 threads.

**3. The Whiskey example already works.** `whiskey` appears as a whole word in **4** threads and **3 are already filed** on the project. It works because `whiskey` is genuinely rare — document frequency 4 of 2,080, 0.2%.

**4. And that is exactly why the rule cannot be generalised.** Measuring every record's distinguishing tokens against the corpus:

| record | reduces to | df | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eagle Mountain Data Center & Land Acquisition | `mountain` | 281 | 13.5% |
| American Energy Rail Corridor - Community Development | **`american`** | 99 | 4.8% |
| Tensor Site Construction Management | `management` | 87 | 4.2% |
| Elite Solutions | **`elite`** | 65 | 3.1% |
| Myton Development / Myton Rail | **`myton`** — both | 34 | 1.6% |
| Whiskey (TX) | `whiskey` | 4 | 0.2% |

§12 already says it: *"Every word must match" is the same test as "one shared word" once the stopwords are gone.* Three records reduce to ONE ordinary word, and two different records reduce to the SAME word, which makes both unmatchable rather than mis-matched.

**So I swept the rule §12 actually prescribes** — the whole name, with at least one token rare in the corpus and owned by one record — across maxDf 1 → 50 and read the output:

```
maxDf   placed  ambiguous
    8        7          2
   20       28         11
   50       68         23
```

At maxDf=20, reading the 28: `[heber] Business in Utah — June 25, 2026` (a **newsletter**, five issues of it), `[geologic] 49 commitments outstanding` and `[weirton] 84 commitments outstanding` (**Pepper's own morning notes**, read back as evidence about a deal), `[garage] 11 new leads — 1 closing soon` (a digest this platform sent itself), `[wendover] California Housing Plan For Remesh`. Perhaps 3 of 28 are right. This is the 10-19 precedent exactly, where any-word matching created 9 records and all nine were wrong.

**The conclusion that decided the build: the matcher must not get looser. The JOB gets the verbs.** What separates a newsletter from a PSA is READING the thread — which a model can do and a similarity score cannot — and the human press is what makes acting on that reading safe. That is what /jobs is for.

**5. The second half of the ask was the cheapest real win.** Contacts already in the directory, writing on a thread already linked to a record, and not a player on it: **62 person-record pairs across 20 records**. The link is a fact and the contact is a fact, so this is a join rather than a guess. (⚠ The first version of that script reported **0** — `.in()` with 900 uuids is a 33KB GET and Kong answers `URI too long`. §12, read that same morning, and still walked into. A refusal read as an absence.)

── WHAT WAS BUILT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

**One capability added to the tool that already existed** — `search_email_threads` gains `only_unfiled` and returns `filed_on` for every result (which records the thread is already on; empty meaning none). That is the one thing neither existing correspondence tool did.

⚠ **AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS BUILT TWO NEW TOOLS INSTEAD, WHICH SHIPPED A REGRESSION. See the section at the end.**

⚠ **CONTAINMENT IS APPLIED IN THE TOOL, NOT LEFT TO THE GENERIC SCRUB.** `executeToolCall` scrubs results by walking them for `project_id`; a thread names its record only through `thread_links`, so a conversation on a protected project would have come back whole — subject, participants, summary — with nothing downstream able to see it needed removing. That is §12's *a nullable pointer added to a table filtered by a DIFFERENT pointer breaks an existing security filter without touching it*, arriving from the other side. The withheld COUNT goes back with the answer.

**Three verbs**, each reading its target back before writing, each idempotent, none able to delete:

| verb | what it does | refusals proven live |
|---|---|---|
| `link_thread` | files a conversation onto a deal, `certainty='linked'`, `applied_message_count=0` so the record receives the whole of it | re-filing the same thread → `skipped`; a dangling record id → `failed` |
| `add_player` | puts a directory contact on a deal | already in that role → `skipped`; a merged contact → `skipped` |
| `create_record` | opens a project or an opportunity | a name the register already answers to → `skipped`, naming the record to file onto instead |

`evidence` is REQUIRED on `link_thread` and `create_record` where it is optional on `update_field`: the reviewer presses on one line, and a conversation on the wrong deal answers for it until somebody notices.

⚠ **`create_record` IS LEGAL UNDER §11 AND THE REASON IS THE SAME ONE /decide's ACCEPT RESTS ON.** The invariant is that mail must not become a record WITHOUT human review; a job proposes and a person presses apply, which IS the review. Deliberately not given to the curator or to any cron.

**`src/lib/records/players.ts`.** The player insert carries three non-obvious obligations — role prose on `role` with the category from the registry, the exactly-one shared-children check, and a unique constraint whose opportunity half is a PARTIAL index so it can be neither a naive insert nor an upsert — and all three lived inside `applySession` where a second caller was about to copy them. One path now, with the roll read once and passed down.

── LIVE, AND IT REFUSED THE RIGHT THING ───────────────────────────────────

Richard's own job, verbatim, against the real corpus: *"Find every piece of correspondence about the Whiskey (TX) project that is not yet filed onto it…"* — 10 rounds, 220s.

It read the five threads the matcher flagged, rejected all five by name (*"PA Brown Field Data Center, Steelton/Weirton/Riverdale, asset-based commercial loans, generic cold outreach, an Army Reserve Center in Texas"*), and — the test that matters — **declined the Zorro teaser**, which mentions Whiskey in passing: *"It is about Zorro. Filing it on Whiskey would violate the rule against filing threads about one deal just because they mention another."* That is the §12 rule being applied to a case it was not shown.

Its two proposals verified against the database: Merlin Corbin on the *Whiskey - Texas Site* thread, Timothy Seibert on *Whiskey - Zorro*, both filed on Whiskey, neither already a player, neither merged. ⚠ **And it picked the right Merlin** — `merlin@zenthium.ai` rather than `Merlin Corbin (via Google Drive)` / `drive-shares-dm-noreply@google.com`, the junk contact Pepper's old refusal-reads-as-absence loop created (§13).

── ⚠ THREE THINGS CAUGHT BEFORE SHIPPING ──────────────────────────────────

**1. The review UI had two hand-written kind maps.** `KIND_TONE` and `KIND_LABEL` in `OperationReview.tsx`, keyed by a loose `string`, each falling back to the raw token — so a new verb got a count and a chip reading `link_thread`, which is §12's *never print a stored enum at a reader*, and nothing failed. This is the same drift §12 records being fixed in /decide's count map and then repeated one component over in its chip row, and again in the Documents tab. Now one `Record<JobOperationKind, {label, tone}>` in `operations.ts`; the build names a missing entry.

**2. The tone I first gave it does not exist.** `amber` is not one of the thirteen declared tones, and `Chip` passes an unknown string through as CLASS NAMES — its documented bridge for the legacy `*_BADGE` triples. So the chip would have rendered unstyled, green through typecheck and build: §12's *a Tailwind class string stored in the database is never generated*, arriving through the one escape hatch left open on purpose. The field is typed `Tone`; a planted `amber` now fails the build, proven.

**3. One query, two haystacks.** The keyword search I wrote narrowed in SQL on `words[0]` against the BODY and then required the remaining words in the subject and summary only — a far smaller text. `steelton cleveland` returned **1** thread out of the ~84 whose bodies carry both, and the caller would read that as "there is nothing". Fixed to test every word against the same text (1 → 10), and then the whole tool was deleted as a duplicate — but the trap is general and is why the rule is recorded.

⚠ **AND THE `OPERATION_KINDS.length === 5` CANARY WAS TESTING THE COPY.** It could only ever say "the number changed", and the way to make it pass was to edit the number — so adding a verb with no describe branch and no fixture was one keystroke from green. It now derives from the fixture list and fails by NAME; a planted `planted_violation` kind proved it.

── VERIFICATION ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

828 tests (up from 817), lint at the frozen 23, typecheck clean, build 0. All three executors exercised end to end against the live database on a throwaway record — created, linked, playered, each repeat skipped, a dangling id failed — then deleted, leaving 0 rows. **Deployed.**

── ⚠ AND THEN I SHIPPED A DUPLICATE TOOL NAME AND HAD TO UNDO IT ──────────

The first version of this work added `search_correspondence` and `get_thread_content` to `agent-tools.ts`. **`agent-tools-modules.ts` has had a `search_correspondence` since it was written** — a SEMANTIC search over message bodies AND attachment text, which the agent prompt explicitly directs the model to for *"what was actually said, agreed, quoted, required, or scheduled in email"*, and which `get_record_brief` is built around. `get_thread_content` was the same mistake against `get_email_thread`.

`agentTools` spreads both files, so the model was handed **two function declarations under one name**, and my `case` sat earlier in the dispatch than the `MODULE_TOOL_NAMES.has(toolName)` check — so a keyword search silently replaced the semantic one on **every agent turn, every Ask Ber AI question and every job**, for the ~3 hours it was deployed. Typecheck, build and 824 tests were green throughout: nothing in TypeScript objects to two entries in an array sharing a `name`.

**How I missed it:** I grepped `from('email_threads')` across `src/lib` and read every thread helper I found, and concluded nothing existed. I never grepped the TOOL NAMES. §12 says it exactly — *a fork is hardest to see as two SIBLING MODULES written days apart, because neither looks like a copy; the tell is a second module answering the same question.* `agent-tools-modules.ts` is described in its own import comment as "same shape, kept separate only to stop this file from doubling in length", which is precisely the sibling the rule names.

**The fix:** both duplicates deleted — 250 lines, `agent-tools.ts` byte-identical to its state before this session — and the one genuinely new capability (`only_unfiled` + `filed_on`) added to `search_email_threads`, which is the §12-correct move: add a parameter to the shared tool rather than fork it. **`agent-tools.test.ts`** now asserts no two tools share a name, that every module tool is actually in the roster, and that every tool has a usable description and a snake_case name; a planted duplicate fails it by name, proven and reverted.

Verified after the fix: **43 tools, no duplicate names**; `search_correspondence` returns `passages` and `referenced_documents_not_held` again; `search_email_threads` with `only_unfiled` returns the backlog in 155ms; and `"whiskey"` comes back with `filed_on` showing *Whiskey - Zorro* correctly on **both** records.

── ⚠ THE MODEL ROUTED AROUND ITS OWN VOCABULARY, AND THE PROMPT FIX WORKED ──

The first create-oriented run found two real candidates and proposed them as **`create_task`**: *"Create project record for The Door Church Murray construction"* and *"Promote WinCo #182 lead to project record"* — a note asking somebody else to do what the verb it had just been given does. A reviewer presses apply on that and nothing happens.

⚠ **THE SECOND ONE WAS ACTUALLY THE RIGHT CALL**, which is why the prompt now says so rather than banning the shape: a LEAD that should become a project is promoted on `/leads`, and that flow carries its files, notes and fit assessment across — a bare `create_record` beside it loses all three. The prompt gained both halves: *if you mean to open the record, propose create_record; a task is for work only a PERSON can do*, with the lead-promotion exception named.

**Re-run after the fix, through the REAL queue** (`status='queued'`, claimed by `/api/cron/job-runner` within the minute, run in the app rather than in a script): 206s, **two `link_thread` proposals and zero `create_record`** — correctly, because it found no work the platform has no record for.

⚠ **AND THE STRONGEST CASE FOR THIS WHOLE APPROACH IS IN THAT OUTPUT.** One of the two threads is subject-lined **`HGH edits`** — a typo, naming nothing, carrying no record name a matcher could ever reach. Its 2,918-character body discusses the HTH Master Partner Agreement and names both Zenthium and Harvest Time Holdings, and the job placed it on *Zenthium Partnership* with that as its stated evidence. Verified: both threads exist, both had **0 existing links**, and the body of that one does carry both names. The second thread (`Master Partner Agreement w/ HTH Tim Seibert`, 306 chars) names HTH but NOT Zenthium, and the model said so — justifying it as the forwarding of the same agreement, which is a chain-of-reasoning link rather than a name match, and exactly the kind of judgement the review row exists to let a human check.

⚠ **A HARNESS NOTE WORTH MORE THAN IT LOOKS.** Two of my own test runs went wrong in ways the feature was not responsible for, both the same mistake in different clothes. (1) Inserting a row with `status='working'` and no heartbeat makes it **indistinguishable from a job a deploy abandoned** — `claimNextJob` matches `heartbeat_at.is.null` — so the real runner reclaimed it, ran it in parallel with my script against a single-threaded model, and a kickstart then killed it to `failed`. The reclaim was correct; the harness was lying to it. (2) My watcher polled for `done|failed` and the terminal state for a job WITH proposals is **`review`** ("Needs you") — so a successful run read as a hang. Enumerate every terminal state, not the happy path; and to test a queue, use the queue.

⚠ **WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: a re-route pass for the 20 threads.** It is real and free, but it is a change to the SWEEP rather than to /jobs, and the measurement says it is 20 threads against a backlog of 1,823 — the job is the lever. Recorded in `OPEN-ITEMS.md` rather than half-built.

**Done 2026-10-28 (the queue could only ever offer the matcher's answer — and 120 rows whose Accept button 404'd):**

Richard: *"The decide button is only giving me 'create project' when I should be able to associate it to current project or opportunity. Make sure I have all the appropriate actions. I should also have a search button at the top to filter through all the decides… Perhaps also in the job to be done I can ask the AI to rescrub the Decide items and see if it can direct them where they need to go. Most seem so obvious where they belong."*

── THE PREMISE, MEASURED FIRST ────────────────────────────────────────────

He was right, and the queue of four said why in one line each. `email_intake_sessions` where `status='pending'`, with their stored candidate lists:

| Session | Disposition | Its candidates | What it obviously is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GridEdgeDC** | `create` | Heber Development 0.38, Myton Development 0.38 | the opportunity **GridEdge** |
| **Firm Power IPP Partnership** | `create` | *none* | Deseret / Bonanza Power Generation |
| **Fairbanks Antimony Mine** | `create` | Gold mine 0.55, Myton Development 0.38 | an Alaska record |
| True North Carabank Steel JV | *(meeting)* | 1 | — |

Not one of the four had the right answer in its own list. The cause is structural and has two halves:

1. **`match_candidates` is frozen at staging time.** It is written once by `findMatchingRecords` when the correspondence is first read, and never recomputed. Every record created afterwards is invisible to it.
2. **The pre-decide model may only choose from that list.** `resolveMergeTarget` resolves `merge_target_name` against `match_candidates` and nothing else — deliberately, because the model chose from a closed list and anything else it returns was invented. So a stale or weak list guarantees `create`.

And the matcher was not wrong to produce it. `resolveRecordByName(['GridEdgeDC'])` needs the whole name or one rare shared token; `gridedgedc` is a single token that is neither. Trigram over `projects` cannot reach an opportunity at all. §12 is explicit that ambiguity must mean no match — the matcher behaved correctly and the QUEUE was wrong to have no other answer.

── WHAT WAS BUILT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

**1. Choose a deal — a person's pick, which outranks the resolver.**

A third control on every row that can be filed, opening a two-step dialog: pick the record, then say what to do with it. Two steps rather than two dialogs because on a staged conversation those are genuinely different decisions over the same record — *file the whole conversation onto Steelton* and *put its three follow-ups on Steelton's board* — and a row with five controls at 64px had stopped being readable.

The verbs available are computed **server-side**, like `accept` already was: the browser is never handed enough of the portfolio or of the session to know which writes are legal. An email package offers `merge` and `task`; a document offers `file`; **a recorded meeting offers `task` and never `merge`**, and that omission is the point — a meeting's confirm route wants the meeting's metadata, a target per deal it covered, a decision per attendee and per follow-up, all built by the review screen. A thinner second version assembled from a list row would be a sibling-module fork (§12) that silently created no attendees and no minutes.

Routes: `/api/email-ingestion/merge` and `/api/email-ingestion/tasks` now take an optional `target: {kind, id}` which is **read back before anything moves**, exactly as the refile route already did. `/api/documents/[id]/refile` needed no change — it has always taken an arbitrary target; only the UI never offered one.

**2. A search box.** Any word, any order, over the title, subtitle, the model's note and **the deal each button would file onto** — so "steelton" finds the conversation whose only mention of Steelton is the name on its Accept button, which is exactly the row somebody searching for Steelton wants. §12: a keyword search matching only the whole phrase answers "nothing" where it means "not adjacent"; `cleveland steelton` must find *Steelton — Cleveland-Cliffs (PA)*. Applied BEFORE the kind chips, so their counts are the list rather than a second quantity above it.

⚠ It is an AND where §12's retrieval rule is an OR, and that is deliberate: the retrieval rule governs a corpus search, where the alternative to a loose match is claiming nothing exists. Here the reader can SEE the list and is narrowing it — a filter that widens as you type more never converges. One shared helper (`src/lib/utils/search.ts`) now serves this and the record picker.

**3. Re-check where these belong** — `/api/decide/rescrub`, human-pressed.

Shows the model the session and **all 33 record names at once**, which is the one thing neither the trigram nor the name ladder can do. That is recognition over a closed list small enough to read, not search. The reply is resolved back against the register, WHOLE and case-folded — the single safety property of handing a model a list — and on a hit the record is written into `match_candidates` AND the predecision, because `resolveMergeTarget` reads only the first and a recommendation with no id behind it is the "label with nothing behind it" the merge route's own header records.

It changes a recommendation and nothing else: no record created, nothing filed, no session confirmed or dismissed. §11 untouched.

Live, twice:

```
run 1: examined 3, placed 2, unplaced 1   (GridEdgeDC refused — see below)
run 2: examined 3, placed 1, unchanged 2
run 3: examined 3, placed 0, unchanged 3   ← idempotent
```

⚠ **THE FIRST RUN LOST THE HEADLINE MATCH TO THE PROMPT'S OWN DECORATION.** Shown `GridEdge (opportunity)`, the model answered `"GridEdge (opportunity)"` at **0.95**, over a thread whose body executes a mutual NDA with GridEdgeDC. The resolver refused it correctly — no record answers to that name — and the right match was thrown away by the formatting of the list, not by the judgement. Fixed at both ends: the type tag now LEADS in square brackets (`[opportunity] GridEdge`, which matters because several record names END in parentheses — *Whiskey (TX)*, *Steelton — Cleveland-Cliffs (PA)* — so a trailing tag reads as part of the name), and the resolver strips the tag in either position and looks the remainder up as a WHOLE key again. Not a fuzzy match and it must not become one: `Alaska` still does not resolve to *Alaska Strategic Materials JV*, which matters because the two Alaska records already have their documents split across each other (§13).

⚠ **A PLACEMENT HAD TO BE MADE TO SURVIVE THE MORNING.** `predecidePendingSessions` selects on `predecision is null OR prompt_version != current`. Writing this pass's version into that column would make the session permanently eligible and the nightly run would undo every placement; leaving it ABSENT does the same for a session the pre-decide phase had not reached yet. So the rescrub keeps the version the row had and stamps the current one when it had none — the row genuinely IS judged now, by a later pass against a bigger list, and the selector's own words are "undecided, or decided by a prompt that no longer exists", of which neither is true. Proven by deleting the key from a live row and re-running.

── ⚠ 120 ROWS HAD A BROKEN ACCEPT BUTTON ──────────────────────────────────

`performAccept` was an `if/else if` chain inside the client component:

```ts
if (action === 'task') { … }
else if (item.kind === 'intake' && action === 'merge') { … }
else if (item.kind === 'intake') { … }
else if (item.kind === 'document' || item.kind === 'misfiled') { … }
else { await patch(`/api/review/${item.id}`, …) }     // ← the trailing arm
```

`unparented` — the "No deal yet" class, a THIRD document-shaped kind added on 10-25 — matches none of those tests and fell into the final `else`, which PATCHes the review route with a **document's** uuid. Measured: `findUnparentedDocuments()` returns **120 offered rows** (55 with a proposed target, 65 set-aside), and every one of their Accept buttons answered `404 Review item not found`. Typecheck, build and 802 tests all green, because every arm of that chain takes a string.

§12 names the shape — when a function branches on where something came from, every source that can reach it needs an arm — and names the remedy: assert the members against each other rather than fixing them one failure at a time. So the routing became `planAccept()`, a pure function returning the request as data, and `accept-request.test.ts` walks every kind × every action and asserts the URL belongs to a table that kind's rows live in.

⚠ **IT FOUND A SECOND INSTANCE ON ITS FIRST RUN.** `task` was tested BEFORE any kind, so a `review` row pressed with `task` would have posted a `review_queue` uuid as a `session_id`. Nothing offers that combination today — which is exactly what let the first instance survive to 120 live rows.

Also: `unparented` had no entry in the `DISMISS` map and therefore no Set-aside button at all — the one row in the queue with no way to say "nothing to do here". It now records `filing_confirmed_at`, which is a real answer ("it belongs to no deal, leave it") and not merely a hiding, so the queue can still reach zero.

── ⚠ THREE LAYOUT BUGS, ALL FOUND BY DRIVING THE DIALOG ───────────────────

None was visible in a typecheck, a build, or a static screenshot of the page. All three came out of a CDP script that clicks "Choose a deal", types, and picks.

1. **The options list was clipped by the dialog.** `DialogContent` carries `max-h-[calc(100dvh-2rem)] overflow-y-auto` — correctly, so a long dialog scrolls — and §12 records that an overflow container is a clipping container. The absolute dropdown rendered in exactly the right place and was cut off at the dialog's edge. `RecordPicker` gained `layout="inline"`; `overlay` stays the default for the lead sheet, where the picker sits among other content and must not push it around.
2. **The longest record name made the dialog overflow its own padding** and took the dialog's heading off the right edge with it. A grid item's default `min-width: auto` is its content, so `truncate` on the option did nothing until the ROOT had `min-w-0`.
3. **The search icon drew itself under the field.** `absolute … top-1/2` was anchored to the root, which is correct only while the root holds nothing but the input; with the list inline, "half way down" became half way down input + list. A wrapper per positioning context, rather than a second set of offsets to keep in step with whatever the list does next.

And at **820px** a row offering *File onto Deseret / Bonanza Power Generation*, *Task on Deseret / Bonanza Power Generation* and *Choose a deal* ran straight out of the panel and printed **on top of its own title** — the action group was `shrink-0`, so nothing in the row could give. The row wraps now (`basis-[18rem]` on the content decides when) and the labels cap at 15rem.

── ⚠ TAILWIND READ ITS OWN BUILD OUTPUT AS SOURCE ─────────────────────────

Running a dev server on `BW_DIST_DIR=.next-dev` to take the screenshots made **every page 500**:

```
Parsing CSS source code failed — Unexpected token Delim('!')
./src/app/globals.css:1210:16
  .h-\[2\.7\!\3 R\] { height: 2.7!R; }
```

Pointing at a line in a file nobody had edited. Tailwind v4 scans the repo for class-name candidates and skips what **git ignores** — `.gitignore` covered `/.next/` and `/.next-verify*/` but not an arbitrary `BW_DIST_DIR`, so the dev build's own compiled output became source and a mangled string became a class. The glob is now `/.next-*/`, wide enough for the next person's suffix. Worth knowing because `BW_DIST_DIR=.next-verify npm run build` is CLAUDE.md's own sanctioned way to compile without shipping.

── ALSO ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

- **One `RecordPicker`, where there were two and a third was about to be written.** `LeadDetailSheet` carried a local copy whose own docblock said it was "the same shape as the meeting review's record picker" — two components answering one question, already drifting (one filtered on focus, the other only once you typed). §12: grep for a renderer before building one, and wire every surface that should call it afterwards. The lead sheet now imports the shared one; the meeting review's inline version is a different shape (it filters out what is already added) and was left alone deliberately.
- **`DecideKind` and `AcceptAction` moved to `src/lib/decide/types.ts`.** `planAccept` has to name every member to assert it covers them, and §12 forbids a shared helper exported from a `'use client'` file — the verification loader cannot resolve a `.tsx` at all. The component re-exports them so existing importers are unaffected.
- **The picker is filtered for the reader's confidential projects** (`viewerHiddenProjectIds`). Zero are confidential today, which is exactly when the filter is cheap to add and impossible to remember later: a picker is a cross-portfolio surface and offering the name leaks the project's existence before access is even asked about (§8).

⚠ **THE AUDIT ONLY EVER LOOKED AT LIST AND BOARD PAGES, AND THE BYPASS COUNTS POINT STRAIGHT AT WHAT IT MISSED.** The worst remaining colour files are `DocumentsTab` 30, `DiligenceTab` 18, `EntitiesTab` 18, `VendorDocuments` 18, `InvestorRequirements` 12 — the record *detail tabs*. The `dark:` map tracks the same files almost 1:1, and so does the hand-rolled-button map. The codemods of 10-26/10-27 drained `slate-*` from 365 to **0** and took `<Panel>` to 39 files, because they reached what was on screen. Whatever nobody rendered kept its old classes. `/projects/[id]` and its twelve tabs, `/opportunities/[id]` and its nine, all twelve `new`/`edit` forms, `/contacts/[id]`, `/investors/[id]`, `/steel/[id]`, `/company/structure` and every settings page had **never been looked at, in either theme**.

So: 76 new screenshots, both themes where it mattered, at 1512×950 and at 390×844. Richard chose "shoot the unseen screens first" over going straight to the primitives, which was right — four of the fixes below are things no amount of reading the source would have surfaced, and two of the things that *looked* wrong turned out to be recorded decisions.

── THE CHECK THAT SAW NOTHING ─────────────────────────────────────────────

⚠ **`conventions.test.ts` REPORTED 0 NAMELESS ICON-ONLY BUTTONS AGAINST A REAL 21, IN NINE FILES, FOR AS LONG AS IT HAS EXISTED.** The regex was `/<button\b([^>]*?)>([\s\S]*?)<\/button>/g`. `[^>]` cannot cross a `>` — and `onClick={() => setOpen(false)}` contains one. So on virtually every real button in the app the "attribute span" ended inside the arrow function and the "children" began mid-attribute; the children then failed the icon-only shape test and the button was silently skipped. Its own docblock argued at length that the pattern was *"deliberately narrow… with no false positives"*, and that was true. It was also blind.

This is §12's rule inverted, and the inversion is why it cost so much: *when a check fails, suspect the check* — but a check that PASSES is never suspected at all.

Rewritten as a brace-aware walk (`buttonTags`), tracking quote and brace depth and closing the open tag on the first `>` at depth zero. Then proved, which is the part that matters:

- planted a violation of exactly the shape that defeated the old regex → **new scan: 1 hit, at the right line. Old regex, run against the same file: 0.**
- that proof is now a permanent test, so the next rewrite cannot repeat the silent failure
- widened from `src/components` to all of `src` — **0 violations either way**, so it was free
- the one real false positive, `DragHandle`'s `{...handleProps(…)}` spread (which supplies a per-card `aria-label`), is **named with its reason** rather than absorbed

⚠ **AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THE FIX REPORTED `board.tsx:392`, WHICH IS THE MIDDLE OF A KEYDOWN HANDLER.** `stripComments` deletes a block comment newlines and all, so any line number derived from its output is wrong by however much documentation sits above. Every other assertion in that file is a COUNT and never cared; this is the only one reporting a LOCATION. Added `blankComments`, which preserves lines. ⚠ **Then the one-shot replace hit the WRONG one of two identical call sites** — there were two `const src = stripComments(…)` lines and `replace(…, 1)` took the first, which belongs to a different test. The symptom was identical to the first bug, which is exactly how it wasted a second cycle.

⚠ **THE RATCHET BASELINES HAD NOT BEEN RE-MEASURED SINCE 10-17, WHICH IS THAT BLOCK'S OWN STATED RULE.** `slate-*` baseline **365** against a real **0**; raw colour pairs **149** against **48**; `text-[11px]` **256** against **192**; `shadow-*` **15** against **13**. A ratchet carrying 300 of headroom is not a ratchet, it is a comment. All lowered. The card shell was **raised** 226 → 231 and said so out loud: 226 was measured with a narrowed scan that no longer matches what the script reports, and writing a number the tree disagrees with is how a test gets muted on the next unrelated touch.

── DEFECTS NO SCREENSHOT WAS NEEDED FOR (but nobody had read the source either) ──

⚠ **A GRID ITEM STRETCHES; A `<Link>` WRAPPED AROUND ONE MOVES THE STRETCH TO THE LINK.** `StatTile`'s `href` branch renders `<Link className="block">` around a `<Panel>` with no `h-full`, so **any tile with a link rendered shorter than its siblings** — and `/dashboard`'s KPI band has had a ragged bottom edge for as long as it has existed. Every class correct, typecheck green, build green, visible only in a screenshot.

⚠ **FIVE LOCAL `Stat` COPIES SURVIVED THE AUDIT'S `/investors` CONVERSION** — steel's board, earnings, commissions and marketing, plus `investors/raises/[id]`. All printed the figure at `text-lg` where the shared tile prints 30px, so `/steel` and `/dashboard` disagreed about what a KPI looks like. Two took raw ramp NAMES (`tone="amber"`, `tone="emerald"`) instead of the status tokens. And `/steel` passed the string `'—'` as a **value**, which is precisely the failure `stat.tsx`'s own docblock cites §12 for: a bare em dash at a value's own weight reads as a failed render. It now says *"No deal has been decided yet"* at body weight. Each grid became `StatGrid`, because `StatTile` renders `dt`/`dd` and those are only valid inside a `dl`.

⚠ **"Just in" PRINTED `2026-10-27` AT A READER** — on the dashboard's most prominent band. All three producers write a bare `YYYY-MM-DD`, so it is formatted at the single READER and the fourth producer is right for free. `formatDate` already existed and already handles the UTC-midnight trap. Its sibling two lines away in `DriveFolderLink` was already doing it correctly at line 347 and wrong at line 262.

⚠ **`px-3.5.5` IS NOT A TAILWIND CLASS.** `/tasks`' "New task" button — the primary action on the app's landing screen — has had no horizontal padding at all.

── WHAT THE SCREENSHOTS FOUND ─────────────────────────────────────────────

⚠ **`/` REDIRECTS TO `/tasks`, AND `/tasks` WAS THE ONLY PAGE IN THE APP WITH NO MASTHEAD.** It opened on "45 open across the team" in 14px grey while every list page opens on a 28px title. The first thing anyone sees was the least-dressed thing here. The recorded reason was real — `AppHeader` already prints "Team Tasks" a line above — but it is equally true of the dozen pages that carry both, and the 14px locator and the masthead do different jobs. `/intel` and `/steel` had the same hole, opening straight onto a tab row, so a whole division of the business was named only by a locator. All three now use `PageHeader`, the only `text-display` in the repo.

⚠ **A CREATE FORM MUST NOT DISPLACE THE THING IT CREATES.** `ComposeDocument` stood **450px** tall above the document list, so Steelton — 188 live documents, the most in the portfolio — opened its Documents tab showing the kind picker, the instruction box and the counsel notice, and **not one document**. It collapses to a row now, and forces itself open whenever `busy`, a result or an error means there is something to report. §12's inverse rule is why it collapses rather than moving below the list: it is still the first thing on the tab.

⚠ **THREE NUMBERS FOR ONE QUANTITY, VISIBLE WITHOUT SCROLLING.** The tab badge said "Documents 191", the heading said "Documents (191)", and the filter chip directly under it said "All 188". The badge and heading counted the graveyard; everything that can actually be shown excludes it. §12 names this exactly — read `documents` with `superseded_at is null` or the graveyard reads as a gap. Fixed on **both** record types, because `projects/[id]` and `opportunities/[id]` are the same screen twice and that pair has drifted before (12 `error.tsx` on one side, **0** on the other).

⚠ **A CHIP IS FOR A TOKEN AND `project_players.role` HOLDS A SENTENCE.** §4 keeps that column as prose on purpose, so the Players tab wrapped *"Counterparty; provided attachments for the Steelton Power Story pursuit"* onto two lines inside a pill. The registry key — the thing that IS a token, and the reason `contact_roles` exists — is now the chip, with the prose beside it. Which also puts the 53-role registry built on 10-21 on screen on that tab for the first time.

⚠ **TEN FILTER CHIPS OVER AN EMPTY LIST.** A record with no diligence rendered "All (0)" plus nine category chips that could only ever return nothing, above the sentence saying there was nothing to control. Gated on `items.length`, and the bare italic string became an `EmptyState` so the way to act is where the eye lands.

Also: the agent's four suggested prompts wrapped into three ragged centred lines (2+1+1), which reads as a layout that failed rather than one that was chosen — they are a list of equal offers and are laid out as one, which fixes the dock too, where the wrap was worse.

── THE TWO FEATURES, BOTH OF WHICH HAD BEEN REFUSED ───────────────────────

Richard asked for both.

**Saved views.** Refused once with a reason that still stands: `ProjectFilters` used to mirror its filters into `localStorage` and replay them on arrival, so a bare `/projects` rendered differently for each executive **with no way for the sender of a link to tell**, and the list re-rendered under the reader after hydration. `url-facets.tsx` still carries the prohibition.

⚠ **THAT OBJECTION IS ABOUT THE STORAGE, NOT THE FEATURE.** `saved_views` is a shared table, and choosing a view NAVIGATES to a URL carrying the whole query. The address bar still describes the screen; a pasted link still means one thing to everybody; a bare `/projects` is still the unfiltered list; nothing is ever replayed. That is strictly better than the remedy the refusal left behind — *bookmark the filtered URL* — because the name is shared too. `?view=` is a LABEL and nothing resolves it into filters, so a link works for a reader who cannot see the view and a deleted view degrades to a working link rather than a broken page. The highlight therefore compares the FILTERS, not the label.

Verified against the real database: create → ok; duplicate name → **refused with its own sentence** (§12: a refusal reported as an absence is how the caller creates the duplicate that guarantees the next refusal); no filters → refused; no name → refused; delete → true; delete again → false. ⚠ **An empty slug would have read as a duplicate name** — a name of pure punctuation or a non-Latin script reduces to nothing, collides on `(path, slug)`, and the route would report "already exists", naming a cause that is not the cause. Random fallback, with a test.

**Trend deltas.** `StatTile` has shipped a `trend` prop and an inline `Sparkline` since 10-27 and has never drawn one, because nothing here remembers what a figure was last week — every number on `/dashboard` is computed live. The audit recorded it as "not built" for exactly that reason: it is a schema question. So `portfolio_snapshots`, one row a week from a new launchd agent at Monday 05:30, no model call.

⚠ **COMPUTED THROUGH THE DASHBOARD'S OWN HELPERS** — `portfolioTotal`, `leafRecords`, `pipelineValue`, `weightedValue`, `readOpenCommitments`. A second derivation would be a fork, and a delta between a figure and a DIFFERENTLY-derived figure is noise that argues with the number printed above it. Proved by seeding today's row and reading it back: **$12B pipeline, $11.9B weighted, 19 active projects, 2 overdue tasks** — the four figures on the dashboard at that moment.

⚠ **CONFIDENTIAL PROJECTS ARE EXCLUDED AT WRITE TIME, ABSOLUTELY, and the comment says why: a stored total cannot be filtered afterwards.** Once a protected project's value is inside `pipeline_value` there is no taking it back out. `hiddenProjectIds()` with no user returns every confidential project and fails closed — the shape §8 and §12 both ask for.

⚠ **NO HISTORY MEANS NO LINE, NEVER A ZERO.** `deltaFrom` returns null for a missing prior, a prior of 0 (Infinity), and any non-finite input. Eight tests cover the cases that would otherwise put `NaN` or `Infinity` into the markup, **none of which is reachable from the UI until next Monday** — a fixture that builds the field directly cannot catch a producer that never fills it. The colour follows the SUBJECT, not the sign (`deltaGood`), because overdue tasks rising is bad and would otherwise paint a growing backlog green. And *"vs last week"* is derived from the real gap, so a missed Monday reads "vs 14 days ago" rather than quietly claiming a week.

── THINGS THAT LOOKED WRONG AND WERE NOT ──────────────────────────────────

⚠ The plan said to demote `AppHeader`'s `<h1>` to a `<p>`, because 53 pages ship two `<h1>` elements. **Re-tested the recorded reason and it still holds:** 49 of 97 pages have no heading of their own, so for them that locator is the document's ONLY `<h1>`, and demoting it would silently strip a heading from half the application. §12 says a workaround's recorded reason must be re-tested before it is inherited — this one survives. The right order is to give those pages mastheads first, which is what three of them just got.

⚠ The collapsed board columns with vertical labels on `/steel` and `/opportunities` look unfinished and are a **measured 10-27 decision** (steel went from 1,200 of 1,451px wasted on empty columns to 2 populated lanes plus 5 legible rails). Not touched.

── VERIFICATION ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

**787 tests pass** (745 → 787: 8 delta, 7 saved-view, 1 planted-violation, plus the day's others), **lint frozen at 23** throughout, typecheck clean at every step, and every change above re-shot in the theme it was made in. Two migrations applied by piping to `docker exec supabase-db psql` as `postgres`; `gen-types` run twice (101 → 103 table types).

⚠ **A TYPE ERROR SHIPPED IN THE FIRST COMMIT.** After the 21 `aria-label` additions the suite and lint were re-run and `tsc` was not; two of them referenced `doc.name`, which does not exist on that row type. Caught on the next unrelated typecheck and fixed in the following commit. The lesson is the obvious one and it is already in §12 in another form: the three checks answer different questions and passing two of them is not passing.

⚠ **`pkill -f "next-server"` WOULD HAVE KILLED PRODUCTION.** The dev server for screenshots runs on :3001; the launchd job runs `next start` on :3000 and its command line matches that pattern. The guard refused it. Killing by `lsof -ti:3001` is the correct form, and production was confirmed still answering afterwards.

⚠ **AND THE DEV SERVER WAS KILLED MID-SESSION BY MEMORY PRESSURE.** `vm_stat` showed ~95MB free with swap at **23.8 of 24.5GB**, LM Studio holding 22.07GB plus a 639MB embedder. That is this box's steady state (§2 says as much); `next dev` plus headless Chrome is simply what tips it. Screenshot work on the Studio has to be done in short bursts, and the memory is the reason — not a harness fault.

── NOT DONE, AND WHY ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Two phases of the approved plan were not built, and both are named here rather than quietly dropped:

- **A shared `<Table>` primitive.** 25 tables in 21 files, 20+ `<th>` spellings, exactly one sticky header and one `table-fixed` (both `ProjectsTable`, the one the audit touched), plus 6 CSS-grid pseudo-tables. It is the biggest single lever left for how this app reads. It is also the biggest diff, and §12 is explicit that a shared renderer wired to one surface is worse than none — so it needs the conversions done in one go, with screenshots, on a box that can hold a dev server.
- **Tooltips.** `ui/tooltip.tsx` has 2 consumers against **289 `title=` attributes in 115 files**. This app explains itself constantly and delivers all of it through a ~1s browser tooltip that never appears on touch and cannot be styled. Converting the high-traffic ones is a direct visible upgrade; every conversion must leave an `aria-label` behind or the icon-button assertion regresses.
