Offering "add as a contact" for each of 96 would have manufactured exactly the rolodex the 10-21 and 10-22 sessions spent two days cleaning up — where `matchParty` reporting a refusal as an absence turned one archived row into two fresh ones inside a day. **So the queue is a CLASSIFIER, and the classification decides which buttons exist at all.** Five classes — `internal` | `organization` | `label` | `fragment` | `candidate` — and `create` is withheld from three of the five. First measured run: **candidate 27, fragment 33, internal 5, organization 28, label 3**. After the corrections below: **candidate 21, fragment 25, organization 37, internal 8, label 5**.

"Brad" is heard twice — once with the company "Ber Wilson" and once with nothing — so whichever arrived first decided the row, and one of our own people was being offered as an external candidate **on a line whose company column read "Ber Wilson"**. Now the sightings merge first (fill-never-overwrite, and `is_organization` additive so a `true` cannot be silenced by a later absence) and the verdict reads the merged record. The test for it is named after the row that caught it.

Davidson" / "DA Davidson", "JP Morgan" / "JP Morgan Chase" — six live pairs that would have become six duplicates on a reader's first pass. **WHAT WAS BUILT**

- **`party_notes`** — shaped *exactly* like `opportunity_notes` (itself shaped like `updates`), so `ExtractedItems`, `ConfidenceBadge` and the card idiom read one shape rather than a fourth. `note_date` is the CONVERSATION's clock and not the row's: a recording swept at 02:00 is yesterday's call, and sorting a relationship history by `created_at` puts a backfilled August call above this morning's coffee.
- ⚠ **THE LATCH IS A PARTIAL UNIQUE INDEX AND IT HAD TO BE.** `unique (party_id, meeting_id)` is satisfied by every NULL pair (§4's own convention manufactures that shape), and `unique nulls not distinct` would have capped a contact at ONE hand-typed note forever. Hence `where meeting_id is not null` — which also means it can never be an `ON CONFLICT` target (§12), so `logMeetingOnContacts` reads before it writes. Proven with planted violations before any code used it: two typed notes land, the same meeting twice is refused, a contact-scoped meeting carrying a project is refused, and both pointers NULL is accepted.
- **`logEntry` gained a `contact` target** rather than a second composer — §12's own rule, which that module's header was written to make. `PasteInput` and `/api/updates/save` follow it, so a typed note on a person gets the extraction, the risks, the decisions and the follow-up tasks a typed note on a deal gets. Its five inline `kind === 'project' ? 'Update' : 'Note'` ternaries collapsed to one `noun`.
- **`meetings.scope` gained `'contact'`** — a human saying a call belongs to no deal. Terminal, because `reconcile-unfiled` selects on `'unfiled'` and so never revisits it. ⚠ **NO `party_id` COLUMN, DELIBERATELY:** a networking breakfast with three new people has no primary one, and a single pointer would force the writer to invent one. The attendees array already carries them all.
- **`meeting_attendee_skips`** — the tombstone that lets the queue reach zero, keyed on a STORED GENERATED `name_key` so the conflict is on the key and never on `name`, and so `ON CONFLICT` works where an expression index would not.
- **The recap now reaches the PEOPLE**, at the same choke point `syncAttendeeActivity` runs from. That projection carries the title, the date and the scope and **not one word of what was said** — 38 such rows against 11 contacts, and a reader opening any of those profiles learned that a conversation had happened and nothing about it.

**THREE BUGS FOUND BY RUNNING IT, NOT BY READING IT**

1. ⚠ **`.contains('attendees', [{ party_id }])` WAS A SILENT NO-OP.** `supabase-js` renders an Array argument as a POSTGRES array literal — `` `{${value.join(',')}}` `` — so an array of objects becomes the literal `{[object Object]}` and Postgres answers `invalid input syntax for type json`. The caller logged it and returned `{written: 0}`, which is indistinguishable from "this contact has been on no calls". A live round trip reported a contact **linked to three calls with an EMPTY feed**, green at every layer above it: `tsc` clean, build clean, 639 tests passing. It is a JSON string now, and the test for it asserts the CALL SHAPE against a stub client — planted back, it fails; restored, it passes.
2. ⚠ **`embedPartyEnrichment`'s DELETE WOULD HAVE EATEN EVERY CONTACT NOTE.** It read "every chunk for this party with no `document_id` and no `update_id`", which was exactly right while enrichment was the only thing with a `party_id` and nothing else — and silently widened the moment `party_note` chunks existed. §12 names this shape ("a nullable pointer added to a table filtered by a DIFFERENT pointer breaks an existing filter without touching it") and here the breakage is a **DELETE**: pressing *Enrich Profile* would have removed a contact's whole indexed conversation history with nothing reporting it. ⚠ **The first proof of the fix passed VACUOUSLY over a party with zero chunks** — §12's own warning, caught by printing the population — so it was re-run against a party that had one, with a `party_note` chunk planted to prove the predicate no longer reaches it.
3. ⚠ **A MEETING NOTE PRINTED ITS OWN RECAP TWICE.** The card rendered `summary` above `body` guarded by `summary !== body`, and a meeting note's body is `"Recorded call — <title>"` followed by the recap, which IS the summary. The heading made them unequal. All 33 backfilled notes showed the same paragraph twice — and `tsc`, 644 tests and the verification script were all green over it. **Found by rendering the page in a browser, which is the only thing that could have found it.**

**THE BACKFILL, AND WHY IT WAS NEEDED** — §12: fixing a generator changes nothing the reader sees. `upsertMeetingFromImport` now writes a contact note when it registers a recording, which covers every recording from today onward and **none** of the 18 already in `meetings`. `verify-contact-capture.mts` said so in the first run it was ever given: **33 of 33 distinct (contact, call) pairs with no note**. ⚠ **The verify script and the backfill disagreed by one — 34 against 33 — and reconciling them was the right amount of work**: one live meeting lists the same person twice ("Richard White" and "Richard", both stamped by the owner override), so one counted SLOTS and the other counted PAIRS. The latch is per pair, so the pair is the unit; §12's one quantity, one definition. 33 conversations now sit on 11 contacts' feeds, and the backfill runs the pass TWICE and refuses to report success if the second run writes anything.

**CONTAINMENT** — the queue is a cross-portfolio surface, so the hidden-project exclusion runs in SQL before the limit and the WITHHELD COUNT is carried rather than derived (once the rows are gone, `rows.length - visible.length` is structurally zero). ⚠ **And a recording is registered `unfiled` and its recap reaches the attendees' feeds minutes before the thread router files it** — which may be onto a project marked `confidential`. §8 is absolute about what follows, so `attachMeetingToRecord` WITHDRAWS the contact notes when the destination is protected. The recap cannot be un-read; it can be un-published, and the register entry keeps it behind the step-up. ⚠ **`readAttendeeQueue` takes the hidden set as a REQUIRED PARAMETER rather than resolving it itself**, which is the one place this work departs from §12's "a security filter belongs at the choke point as a default" — resolving the viewer there would import `next/headers`, which §12 records does not resolve under `deploy/register.mjs` AT ALL and poisons the whole module including its pure functions. A required argument cannot be forgotten silently; a default can.

**ONE HOME FOR A PREDICATE** — `OWN_COMPANY` was a private regex in `meet-import.ts` keeping Ber Wilson off the list of deals a title could name. The findings queue needs the identical answer for a different reason, so it moved to `src/lib/utils/own-company.ts` with both readers selecting from it (§12: a predicate transcribed into its readers has a home per reader, and the one that lies to you is found last). Also fixed in passing: the contact profile printed **"Board meeting meeting"** and **"Recorded call — not filed on a deal yet meeting"**, because every branch of `scopeLabel` already ended in its own noun.

**VERIFIED** — 644 tests (+27: 22 classifier, 5 feed), lint 22 (the documented baseline, not an increase), tsc 0, 98 tables, 181 routes. `scripts/verify-contact-capture.mts` green on all six invariants, each printing what it examined so a vacuous pass is distinguishable from a real one. A full round trip on live rows — create "Jonathan Houk", link 3 mentions across 3 calls, write 3 feed notes, re-run as a no-op, skip a name, refuse "Mike", refuse a recap-less meeting, then reverse all of it back to the 96-finding baseline. Both pages rendered in a browser, which is what found bug 3. **DEPLOYED.**

The threshold is right (it was measured against the 73s median, not picked) and the near-miss is a coincidence, but it is worth writing down that a feature can be correct, deployed, configured and unexercised, and that the only way to know which is to read the log table rather than the code.

The gap is a factor of eight at the median. Texts leave this box as mail to `<10 digits>@tmomail.net` and the carrier decides where to fragment and where to truncate — so sending a 3,000-character answer would hand the most important sentence in it to T-Mobile's segmentation. Richard was asked, with the numbers and a rendered mock of each option, and chose: **TLDR plus a link over text, the full answer by email, only over the 90-second bar.**

The text is `<bottom line>\n\n<conversation link>`; the email is unchanged. `plainText()` strips the markdown a carrier renders as literal hashes and asterisks (headings, bold, bullets, links, tables, fenced blocks), `clip()` cuts on a sentence boundary where one is worth taking and a word boundary otherwise — never mid-token, because *"the PSA closes 17 Oct for $13"* is a figure that reads as finished and is not (§12). A `document_ready` text already carried exactly what Richard asked for on the document half — `driveFileUrl ?? <platform documents tab>` — so nothing was built there; it is reported here because it had never been seen to run.

⚠ **THE CONTAINMENT MESSAGE WAS LEAKING THE THING IT CONTAINED.** `guardOutboundText` returns *"it names a protected project (\"X\")"* — the project's name, which is correct for a server log and is the one string that must never go outbound. The existing code put `escapeHtml(withheldBecause)` straight into the email body, so a question whose answer brushed a `confidential` project produced an email that withheld the answer and then named the project in its own explanation. §8 says a protected project leaves every outbound channel; this was the explanation of that rule breaking it. Split into two strings: `withheldBecause` (specific, for the log and the return value) and `withheldPublic` = *"it touches a protected project"* (generic, for anything that leaves). Never fired in production — no project currently carries `confidential` — which is precisely why nothing had caught it.

⚠ **`maxTokens: 300` WOULD HAVE SILENTLY DISABLED THE FEATURE I JUST BUILT.** The TLDR is 240 characters — about 60 tokens — so I budgeted 300 and moved on. `qwen3.6` reasons before it answers and the think block comes out of the same allowance: a cap sized to the output spends the whole budget thinking and emits nothing, which my own code reads as a failed call and downgrades to the trimmed answer **forever, with no error anywhere**. Every other prose call in this repo budgets 1,500–8,000; 300 was the outlier and that is what gave it away. Raised to 2,048, and the live `ai_queries` row then settled it beyond argument: **1,561 tokens out for a 209-character answer** — the model spent roughly 1,500 tokens reasoning to produce about 50 of prose, so the original cap would have been exhausted five times over before a single visible character was emitted. The general shape: **a budget sized to what you want OUT is wrong for a model that thinks first**, and the failure is a permanent silent downgrade rather than a crash.

**Registration, which is where this kind of change goes missing.** A new TEXT kind has four homes and the symptom of forgetting one is a channel that is silently off: the CHECK on `pepper_outbound_texts.kind` (migration `20261023000001`), the mirroring union in `src/lib/provenance/db.ts`, `defaultTextKind()` in `src/lib/notify/index.ts`, and the policy row. The document was refused and the figure named: *"Refused: a figure in the draft ($20.0M) is in none of the records this was built from."* ⚠ **The human's own instruction is part of the input set, and that is what makes the refusal recoverable rather than a dead end** — the way to get a number into a document is to say it. ⚠ Scoped to **money and percentages only**: dates, acreages, megawatts and "three parties" are numbers too, and gating them would refuse honest documents constantly (§12 — narrow a static check until it has no false positives).

Here there are two readers, and §12's in-progress-status rule bites hard: a kickstart kills the pass before it can write either verdict, so a DB-enforced latch would be **immortal** and a deal could never be composed on again. Concurrency is refused in the pass against `requested_at` and a 900s staleness horizon — a check that cannot wedge. **TWO FALSE POSITIVES FORCED THE KIND-DRIFT TEST TO MATCH SHAPE RATHER THAN WORDS.** v1 flagged any quoted key and caught `src/lib/utils/investors.ts`, where `'term_sheet'` is an **InvestmentStage** — a negotiation stage on a capital-raise commitment. v2 required two or more and caught `src/lib/drive/classify.ts`, whose `'offer'`, `'proposal'` and `'agenda'` are **filename-matching tokens** for sorting an incoming file into a Drive subfolder. Both are honest English nouns in unrelated code, and that is the lesson: **these keys are ordinary words and a word search can never tell a taxonomy from a sentence.** v3 matches a TypeScript union member or an object key, still requires two, and was **proved to still fail on a planted union** before being trusted.

**Other things the build taught, each one §12 already warning about it:**
- ⚠ **`as never` — I wrote two and §4 forbids them.** Measured: a naive `grep "as never"` returns **79 hits repo-wide**, every one of them the words "as never" in prose (*"reported as never indexed"*). Matching a real cast (`as never` followed by `)`, `;`, `,`) returns **zero** outside my file. CLAUDE.md was exactly right; my grep was measuring documentation. Both casts removed properly — the parent columns written out explicitly so the exactly-one CHECK is type-checked, and the two documents tables branched rather than cast, since every column used exists on both.

- ⚠ **A name collision caught before it became a trap.** `src/lib/ai/document-kinds.ts` already exports `documentKind()` for FILE FORMATS (pdf/docx/pptx). Mine was about document SHAPE. Two unrelated concepts one import away from each other, renamed to `composeKind` / `COMPOSE_KINDS` / `compose-kinds.ts` before anything depended on either.
- ⚠ **My own verification test passed vacuously and I nearly kept it.** Section 6 asserted that a record with nothing on it refuses rather than inventing — against *Eagle Mountain*, which carries **11 threads**. `ready` was the CORRECT answer and the check proved nothing. Re-pointed at *Tonga Development Project* (0 threads, 0 meetings, 0 documents, measured) and it now asserts a real refusal, with the thread count printed so the population is visible. §12: an empty population passes behind the same tick — print what was examined.
- ⚠ **The undo was half an undo.** `--clean` deleted the `documents` row and left the storage object: **2 orphans, 144,441 bytes.** Now it reads `storage_path` BEFORE deleting the row (deleting first orphans the file with nothing pointing at it) and trashes the Drive copy too.
- ⚠ **`status: 'failed'` needs a reason or the column is decoration**, so the table carries CHECKs: a `ready` row must name its document and table, a `failed` row must carry an error.

**VERIFIED END TO END ON LIVE DATA.** A *Myton Rail* briefing memo: **111.1s**, title *"Myton Rail & Campus Initiative: Briefing Memo"*, **23 sources** recorded, 5,965 characters stored, `embedding_status='skipped'`, sha256 written, PDF on the record. The prose is specific and correct: *"Multi-phase development of a 5,000–50,000 acre site in Duchesne County, UT (Myton/Antelope)"*, *"Ber Wilson Position: Prime Developer and General Contractor"*, the CRISI predevelopment grant package. Deployed:** committed, pushed, built (exit captured unpiped, §12), kickstarted, `tailnet-setup.sh` green on all three endpoints, `lmstudio-check.sh` green. `/api/documents/compose` is in the build's route table and answers 401 unauthenticated. **THE MEASUREMENT CAME FIRST AND IT JUSTIFIED THE WORK.** Over the 68 answers `agent_messages` has ever stored: median **73s**, p90 **455s** (7.6 min), slowest **1,005s** (16.8 min), and **22 of 68 — 32% — over two minutes**. Business-hour AI traffic is ~560 calls a week at ~40s each, about 8% occupancy.

⚠ **THE FIRST ANSWER WAS THAT TWO-THIRDS OF IT ALREADY WORKED, AND NOBODY KNEW.** The SSE route never reads `request.signal`, the `ReadableStream` has no `cancel()` handler, and `runAgent` takes no abort signal — the `send()` helper's own catch has said so in a comment all along: *"client disconnected — agent run continues so the message still persists."* The answer has always landed in the database whether or not anyone was watching. And because the dock lives in the ROOT layout, which App Router reuses across soft navigations (the same fact the 10-20 badge session learned), asking from ⌘J on `/dashboard` and walking to `/tasks` already kept streaming. So the feature was not "make the run survive" — it was **"let a later mount find out that it did"**. Three gaps, one mechanism: the dock's `key={scope?.id ?? 'portfolio'}` remounts the chat on a record boundary, a reload shows nothing, and a second tab shows nothing. None of them ever stopped the run.

**The job row is the question itself.** `run_state` + `run_started_at` on the USER row of `agent_messages` — which the route already inserts before starting — so no new table, and the shape matches what the card batch and meeting transcription already do. ⚠ **LIVENESS IS A CLOCK, NOT THE COLUMN (§12):** a `launchctl kickstart` kills the process before either verdict can be written and a deploy IS a kickstart, so `run_state='running'` is immortal on its own; every reader pairs it with the clock. `settleRun()` is called from BOTH the SSE and JSON branches and from BOTH outcomes, because a verdict written only on the happy path leaves `running` behind on every error.

⚠ **THE RECOVERY POLLER WAS CAPPED AT 240s AGAINST A 30-MINUTE BUDGET** — so it gave up on precisely the long, well-evidenced turns worth waiting for, and then showed an error above an answer sitting in the database. Now the deadline is `run_started_at + AGENT_TIME_BUDGET_MS`, i.e. the server's own clock and not a fresh one: a turn that started twelve minutes ago has eighteen left. ⚠ And it was declared INSIDE `sendMessage`, reachable only from the dropped-stream catch; the reattach needed the identical loop, so it was lifted to one module-level `pollForAnswer` with two callers rather than becoming §12's hardest fork to see — two functions written days apart, neither looking like a copy.

**On "do questions build on each other" the honest answer was: yes, unevenly, and the uneven part is why it felt like they don't.** History IS loaded and passed. On a project page the dock resumes that record's last conversation. But the portfolio-wide ⌘J dock resumed **nothing** — `if (!scopeQuery) return` — so every global question after a reload started blank, and `/intel` has kept a conversation sidebar all along that the dock could not reach. ⚠ `scope=portfolio` had to become a real scope rather than the absence of one: listing with no filter returns every conversation the user owns, so "the most recent" would have been whichever deal chat was newest, opening on the dashboard. Portfolio resumes only within 24h (an old question under ⌘J reads as confusion, not history); a record scope resumes always; a live run beats both.

⚠ **A LATENT BUG, FOUND BY READING THE COMMENT AGAINST THE CODE.** History loaded `.order('created_at', { ascending: true }).limit(20)` under a comment saying *"last 20 messages"* — that returns the **first** twenty. It has never once bitten, because the longest conversation is 12 — which is also why **live data cannot distinguish the two readings** and the verification had to build a 24-message fixture to pull them apart (§12's rule about a worked example whose figures coincide). Fixed to `descending` + reverse.

**Notification: a toast and an email, over 90s, and no bell.** The threshold is set against the measured 73s median, so the third of answers that actually make somebody wait notify and the ones they watched arrive stay silent. ⚠ **AN IN-APP BELL WAS BUILT HERE AND DELETED ON 2026-09-24 — 52 rows written, ZERO ever read or dismissed** — so the surface is a `sonner` toast (already in the root layout) plus email, and nothing persistent. ⚠ The toast callback is fired OUTSIDE the `setMessages` updater, from text accumulated in a plain local, because React may call an updater twice and a callback fired from inside one is a toast that sometimes appears twice.

⚠ **THE EMAIL COLLIDED HEAD-ON WITH THE OTHER SESSION RUNNING THE SAME AFTERNOON.** Richard had just told it *"lets have pepper hold off on the emails and chats for now"*, and it was mid-build on `src/lib/notify/policy.ts`, which holds every kind by default and makes `notify()` refuse an unknown one. Two instructions from the same person on the same day, so he was asked rather than guessed at: *"Send it — I asked the question."* It is registered `trigger: 'human', live: true` alongside `lead_handoff`, under that file's own carve-out — a message you typed a question to get is not Pepper broadcasting at you, and it only sends when the turn ran past 90 seconds, which is exactly when you have given up watching. ⚠ Had it NOT been registered, the gate would have held it silently, which is the failure that file exists to prevent.

**Containment is decided before the body is built.** Two additive tests, because they catch different things: `isConfidentialProject` for a question asked ON a protected deal, and `guardOutboundText` for a portfolio-wide question whose ANSWER names one. Either sends a link-only email naming no record. Email is the most outbound channel there is — it goes through Gmail, off the box, and cannot be recalled — so there is no opt-out parameter for a caller to forget. The link uses `publicOrigin(request.headers)`, never `nextUrl.origin` (§12), and the origin is read in the handler because the streaming branch outlives it. Idempotency is `notification_log`'s existing `unique (kind, dedupe_key)` on the assistant message id, claimed before sending — so no `notified_at` column was needed.

**THE SHAPE: ONE REGISTRY, TWO PLACEMENTS.** §12 is explicit — *a CHECK is a list baked into the schema; an FK points at rows. - **`project_players.role_key`** — what somebody is **to this deal**. Already modelled; now categorised.

One vocabulary serves both, with **no per-row scope flag**: the placement IS the scope, and a flag would be complexity with no demonstrated need. Both FKs are `on update cascade` with **no delete rule**, so a rename carries its holders and a role somebody holds cannot be deleted — that is what `active=false` is for, exactly as with `leads.route`.

| string | must reach | would otherwise be |
|---|---|---|
| *"Owner of the 5,000-acre Myton site…"* | `land_owner` | `owner` |
| *"Seller / Portfolio Owner"* | `seller` | `owner` |
| *"Academic partner / Endorser organization"* | `academic_partner` | `endorser` |
| *"GridEdge Introducer/Liaison"* | `referral_source` | `agency_staff` |
| *"Contractor / Prefab steel manufacturer"* | `steel_fabricator` | `general_contractor` |
| *"Participant Royalty Owner"* | **nothing** | `owner` |

**AND ONLY ROLES THAT DESCRIBE A PERSON TRAVEL ONTO THE CONTACT.** §12: filling a blank and overwriting a value are different acts, and which is safe turns on whether the source DESCRIBES its subject or only MENTIONS it. A law firm is a law firm on every deal; **the seller on Steelton is not "a seller" in general**, and writing that onto their contact would be the directory asserting something nobody said. `DEAL_SCOPED_ROLES` holds the eight that do not travel (owner, owner's rep, seller, buyer, guarantor, land_owner, offtaker, client). **63 contacts seeded with 71 roles**, plus the 7 carrying the hand-typed `investor` tag.

**WHAT CLOSES THE LOOP IS THAT EVERY WRITER NOW GOES THROUGH ONE FUNCTION.** §12: *a shared renderer wired to one surface is worse than no shared renderer* — the reason the old 33-value list reached 1 row in 104 is that each writer decided for itself and none knew the list existed. `categorizePlayerRole()` is the single choke point: `resolveRoleKey` (the model answered with a key or exact label) then `mapRoleText` (the measured prose rules), null when neither is sure, and the registry has the final say so a rule naming a retired role cannot resurrect it. Wired into all five writers. **And the extraction prompt's vocabulary is GENERATED from the same rows the column references** (`roleVocabularyForPrompt`), not spelled out as a literal — a role added in settings is in the next call, a role retired disappears from it. `EXTRACTION_PROMPT_VERSION` 1.1 → 1.2.

**Done 2026-10-21 (the backup left the building, and the thing nobody had ever done to it):**

Richard: *"Would it be smarter to keep a backup of our Mac studio deployment in the Google cloud since we have a ton of free storage there? Also, my Mac mini is on all the time at my work desk is likely more of a security threat backing up to a computer that's always on."* Then, after the measurements: *"I trust the backup being in our GSuite Drive quota for now. Lets back everything up to the drive in a Folder labeled as backup (critical) or something of that nature so it doesn't get deleted."*

**⚠ THE SECURITY PREMISE WAS ALREADY HANDLED, AND SAYING SO IS WHAT MADE THE DECISION EASY.** The mini copy has been age-encrypted since 2026-07-07 to a recipient whose private key lives only on Richard's MacBook and in his password manager — verified: there is no `~/.config/age` on the Studio. So the always-on mini was holding opaque bytes it could not read, and an attacker who took it would get nothing. That cuts both ways, which is the useful half: **Google would hold the same opaque bytes**, so encryption turns "where does the backup live" from a security question into a logistics one. On logistics it was not close.

What the measurements said:

| | |
|---|---|
| Nightly volume | 127MB db + 1.5GB storage = ~1.7GB |
| 14-day local retention | 25GB, held twice (Studio plaintext, mini ciphertext) |
| **Mac mini** | 228GB disk, **37GB free** — the backups were 25GB of that, at 83% capacity |
| Studio | 926GB, 237GB free |
| **GSuite pooled quota** | 6,597GB limit, **17.6GB used** → ~6.58TB free. 25GB is **0.4%** |
| Upstream | `networkQuality` 57Mbps; a real timed resumable upload to Drive **5.5MB/s (44Mbps)** |
| Scope | `moose@` **already holds full `drive`** — no re-consent, no manual step |

⚠ **AND THE EXPOSURE WAS SOMEWHERE NEITHER OF US WAS LOOKING.** The *Studio's* local copies are **plaintext** — 25GB of unencrypted `pg_dumpall` output in `~/Backups/berwilson`. Encryption only ever happened on the way out the door. That is unchanged by this session and is recorded as an open item, because it is the one copy an attacker on the box can actually read.

**THE EXISTING UPLOADER COULD NOT BE REUSED, AND ITS OWN DOCBLOCK SAID WHY.** `uploadToFolder` in `src/lib/integrations/google-drive-write.ts` is **multipart** and `Buffer.concat`s metadata + file into one buffer, so a 1.6GB artifact peaks ~3.2GB RSS on a 36GB box where llama-server holds ~25GB and swap already runs full. Its comment reads *"Revisit if a >100MB drawing set ever shows up"* — a backup is 16× past that line. It is also a `src/lib` module, and the backup runs from `~/supabase-selfhost/backup.sh` under launchd, which is §12's five-load-time-failures trap. So `deploy/drive-backup-push.mjs` is standalone with zero `src/lib` imports, and the old docblock's prediction is now cited in the new file rather than left to be rediscovered.

⚠ **A SINGLE-REQUEST 1.6GB UPLOAD LANDS EXACTLY ON UNDICI'S 300s CEILING, WHICH IS A BUG §12 ALREADY RECORDS IN ANOTHER COSTUME.** At the measured 5.5MB/s, 1.6GB is ~291s, and a resumable `PUT` gets no response headers until the whole body is received — so `headersTimeout` fires at 300s on any night the link is slightly slow, and §12 says plainly that no option in this codebase reaches that timeout. The fix is **chunked** resumable upload: 128MiB per `PUT` (~23s each, 13 chunks for the storage artifact), which is clear of the ceiling and makes every completed chunk a resume point. ⚠ `redirect: 'manual'` is load-bearing there — an intermediate chunk answers **308 Resume Incomplete** and `fetch` treats 308 as a *redirect*, so without it the real status is never seen. On a failure the script asks the session how many bytes it actually holds (`Content-Range: bytes */TOTAL`) rather than trusting its own arithmetic.

**THE FOLDER RECREATES ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HONEST ANSWER TO RICHARD'S QUESTION.** He asked: *"Of course if it were to get deleted, you would just back it up again right?"* Half true, and the half that is false is the one that matters — the next night re-uploads the current state, but the **history** is gone, and a 30-night window exists precisely to recover from something discovered late. So: the folder is resolved **by name** and recreated if absent (`CRITICAL — Ber AI Platform Backups (DO NOT DELETE)`, in moose@'s own My Drive so no teammate can see or delete it), Drive's trash gives 30 days to undo an accident, and the status marker records `folder_recreated` so a silent re-create shows on the health page as a warning rather than looking like a first run.

⚠ **AND THE THING NOBODY HAD EVER DONE: READ THE BACKUP BACK.** §12 has said since the beginning that *a backup is not a backup until it has been read back*. Measured this session: **there is no `pg_restore` anywhere in this repo** and nothing had ever read back either copy — 50GB across two machines of artifacts that were assumed good because the script exited 0. `deploy/drive-backup-verify.mjs` streams each artifact down from Drive and compares sha256 against the hash the uploader records, plus checks the `age-encryption.org/v1` header to catch an artifact that is intact but is not an age file at all. Weekly, Sundays 04:00, own launchd agent, own health card.
⚠ **It proves integrity and NOT recoverability, and the card says so in those words.** A restore needs the age private key, which is deliberately off-box — so the Studio *cannot* run a restore drill, by design rather than by oversight. A green card that read as "a restore drill passed" would be worse than no card.

**The mini was decommissioned, and what that cost is written down rather than assumed to be nothing.** It was not removed for security — it only ever held the same ciphertext. It was removed for space. What went with it is a destination with an **independent credential**: the mini push authenticated with an ssh key, where the Drive push authenticates with the OAuth token store — **which is itself one of the files being backed up**, and which a crash destroyed whole on 2026-08-25. Mitigated rather than eliminated: the uploader keeps a second copy of the token store at `~/.config/bw-backup/`, a different blast radius from `~/berwilson-data`, refreshed automatically after every proven token refresh (§12 — a channel whose setup cannot be automated is a channel that is off, so there is no browser step). The tombstone comment in `backup.sh` names that gap as the reason to add a second destination if one is ever wanted again — not space, and not secrecy.

⚠ **`probeOffsite` deliberately does NOT fall back to the mini's `.offsite-status`.** A stale marker from a decommissioned destination would report a copy that no longer happens, which is the exact failure that probe was added on 2026-09-23 to catch.

Verified live rather than reasoned about: folder create, 13-chunk upload of the real 1.5GB artifact, idempotent re-run (skips on name+size), retention prune (proved with a negative retention, which also cleaned up the test artifact), and a full `backup.sh` run end to end in **11m52s**, exit 0, all three artifacts on Drive at 1.78GB. One bug found by its own output and fixed: the nightly line counted artifacts **before** pruning, so it would have reported a window one night longer than Drive actually held — a count lying about the only thing it exists to report.

**The read-back result, which is the point of the session.** All three artifacts streamed back down from Drive and matched sha256 **byte-for-byte** — `db` 134,277,859 bytes, `storage` 1,647,486,668, `secrets` 6,937 — with the `age-encryption.org/v1` header present on each. Exit 0. That is the first verified backup in this project's history; every night before tonight was an assumption.

⚠ **A SHELL TRAP THAT COST SIX TOOL CALLS AND IS WORTH THE LINE IN §12:** waiting on the verifier with `until ! pgrep -qf drive-backup-verify` **never ends**, because the waiting shell's own command line contains the pattern and `pgrep -f` matches it. It reported "still verifying" indefinitely while the job had minutes left, and it reads exactly like a hang. Compounded by piping the job through `| tail -10`, which buffers all output until exit, so the progress log was invisible too — the only way to tell a working job from a dead one was `netstat -ib` on the right interface (`en1`, not `en0`). Wait on the ARTIFACT the job writes, not on the job.

**⚠ THE MINI HELD A 14-NIGHT HISTORY AND DRIVE HELD ONE DAY, SO DELETING IT OUTRIGHT WOULD HAVE SILENTLY SHORTENED THE WINDOW** — and on the day after Richard cleared 119 staged sessions and archived three contacts, which is exactly the kind of thing a fortnight of dumps exists to undo. Richard's words were *"remove any data stored on the mac mini"*; taking that literally while Drive held only 21 October would have met the letter of it and lost the point. So the history was migrated first, split by what is actually irreplaceable: **all 15 nights of database dumps plus their secrets bundles are ~2GB and uploaded in one pass** (30 uploaded, 2 correctly skipped by the name+size idempotency check), where **the 15 storage tarballs are 24GB of near-identical document blobs** whose contents are overwhelmingly sourced from Drive and email in the first place. Fourteen of those were dropped and **the oldest (7 October) was kept and uploaded as a historical floor**, so a document that was deleted at some point in the fortnight is still recoverable from a snapshot bracketing it. **All 33 migrated artifacts were then verified against Drive by sha256 — 33 checked, 0 failed — BEFORE the mini was wiped**, because it was the last independent copy of that history and the verifier existed by then. Final state: **37 artifacts / 6.58GB on Drive** (17 db + 17 secrets spanning 07→21 October, 3 storage), the mini at **61GB free from 35GB** (84% → 71%), and `~/Backups` removed from it entirely.

⚠ **A SECOND SELF-INFLICTED SHELL LESSON, WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT WAS THE SAME ONE TWICE.** After writing the `pgrep` rule above I then launched `sleep N` as a BACKGROUND task and immediately polled its output file — which waits for nothing at all, since backgrounding returns instantly. Several minutes of apparent "still uploading" were really just the same instant re-read. The fix is the same shape as the rule: block in the FOREGROUND on the artifact's own mtime (`until [ "$(stat -f %m marker)" != "$PREV" ]`), which is what finally worked for all three uploads.

Local retention stays at 14 nights and stays **plaintext** — unchanged by this session, now recorded as an open item, because it is the one copy an attacker with the box can read. 667 tests, lint unchanged at 23 (13 errors, 10 warnings).

**⚠ THE GATE WAS MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN, AND THE FIRST INSTINCT WAS WRONG.** `minThreads: 2` is the obvious move and it halves the signal: 176 of 225 staged sessions came from a one-thread cluster, but 2 of the 4 confirmations did too. Six candidate rules replayed over the decided corpus:

| gate | queue | confirms kept (of 4) |
|---|---|---|
| `thread_count >= 1` (shipped) | 225 | 4 |
| an attachment anywhere | 122 | 4 |
| somebody replied (`message_count > 1`) | 114 | 3 |
| attachment AND reply | 62 | 3 |
| `thread_count > 1` | 49 | 2 |
| **(attachment AND reply) OR >1 thread** | **84** | **4** |

Every tighter rule drops a confirmation, so what shipped is the **loosest that keeps all four**, not the tightest that fits. **225 → 84, −63%.** The negative evidence is the strong half and the asymmetry is deliberate: **103 sessions had no attachment anywhere and produced ZERO confirmations**; 111 whose busiest thread was a single message produced one. Four positives cannot validate a gate — they can only rule one out.

**Proved twice, from two different sources.** The table above is SQL over `thread_clusters ⋈ email_threads ⋈ email_intake_sessions`; `scripts/`-style replay then ran `clusterStagingVerdict()` — the real function, through the real `sweepDb()` path — over all 225 clusters and reproduced it exactly: **84 staged, 141 held, 4 confirmed kept, 0 lost.** §12 requires computing both sides from their own sources rather than checking a derivation against itself.

Both conditions are **structural counts the vendor gave us** (`message_count`, `attachment_count`), not a judgement a model made — the same shape §11's recording gate took from 9-wrong-out-of-9 to 0 by refusing to read intent. A reply means somebody here engaged; an attachment means paper moved. A lone unanswered message with nothing attached is a notice, and a notice is already searchable in `thread_chunks` without anybody deciding anything about it, which is precisely Richard's point. **The verdict runs BEFORE the model call**, so a cluster that does not clear the bar costs nothing — roughly 141 extraction-plus-matcher-plus-fit passes that the box was spending to produce rows a human then dismissed.

**⚠ `held`, NOT `dismissed`, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS LOAD-BEARING.** `clusterUnassigned` attaches new threads to clusters in states `open`/`staged`/`confirmed` and deliberately excludes `dismissed`. Had a gated-out cluster been dismissed, the reply that turns a one-message notice into a real deal — the single most likely thing to happen to exactly these clusters — would have formed a FRESH cluster and staged on its own, **with the first message missing from its evidence**. So `held` joins the attach list, a held cluster that absorbs a thread is set back to `open` (after `refreshClusterRollups`, so the stage phase re-reads it against a correct `thread_count`, not the stale 1 it was judged on), and the stage phase reads held clusters back in a **second, separately capped query** — never one `.in()`, because held rows accumulate and share the newest-first ordering, so a single 500-row query would eventually let them crowd out the open cluster that actually needs staging. Re-reading them also means a cluster held under an older version of the rule is re-judged by the current one rather than stranded by a rule that has since changed. `thread_clusters.state` carries **no CHECK constraint** (verified), and both consumers outside the sweep — the `get_intake_status` agent tool and `/api/email-sweep/status` — tally states dynamically rather than enumerating them, so neither needed changing; verified rather than assumed. The held count is **reported** by the status route and explained in the agent's own note, because a gate nobody can see is a black hole and §12 is explicit that a surface hidden because it is quiet is hidden exactly when somebody needs it.

**⚠ MEASURED AND DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT — three of them.**

1. **`/attention` needed nothing.** It was 5 items (3 overdue tasks, 1 milestone, 1 lead) and its lead filter is already tight: `status in (new,reviewing)` AND `fit_recommendation in (pursue,consider)` AND a bid date inside 14 days. The 10-17 reading of 10 items / 8 leads had drained itself (`drainLeadQueue` had expired 247). `attention_dismissals` is still **empty** — the Dismiss button shipped the same morning. And §13 already reserves the `lead_review` question for Richard after a week of use, so pre-empting it would have been answering a question he had explicitly kept.
2. **The `create` verdict's 2% accuracy (2 of 95) is not a prompt problem.** 74 of the 93 rejected creates had **zero** `match_candidates` — §12's *"a model that cannot NAME the record proposes a new one"*, exactly. The cause is measurable and upstream: of **1,881 deal threads, 1,824 are routed and only 174 carry a link to any record**; 7 of 19 projects (Tooele, Delta, Heber, Myton Development, Tonga, DFCM Camp Williams, Alaska Strategic Materials JV) have **zero** linked correspondence; `contact_aliases` holds **0 rows** and `record_identifiers` **14** (10 party, 2 parcel, 2 meeting_title — not one project alias). The platform stages proposals to CREATE records while failing to attach 1,707 threads to the 26 it already has. §12's own remedy is *"do not weaken the bar; assert an alias"*, which is a data act for Richard, not code — and weakening the matcher is the one thing the 10-19 session proved costs nine wrong records out of nine.
3. **A `meetings` lane on `/decide`** — see the finding below. Adding queue items in the session where he said the queue produces faster than two people drain it would have been the wrong answer to the question asked.

**⚠ FOUND: DISMISSING A STAGED *MEETING* IS LOSSY WHERE DISMISSING AN EMAIL SESSION IS NOT, AND THE BUTTON SAYS THE SAME THING FOR BOTH.** Dismissing an email session loses nothing — the threads stay summarized, indexed and routable, which is what makes the new gate safe. But **nine `meetings` rows sit `scope='unfiled'` and `status='draft'`** after their sessions were dismissed: the call is transcribed and searchable, but it is on no record, and the deal, the title learned for the next call in the series, and the follow-up TASKS (8 from the Tensor call alone) were never created. Worse, `/decide` reads `email_intake_sessions`, not `meetings`, so once the session is dismissed **nothing queues the meeting any more**. The nine: *Richard White Introduction* (10-19), *Tensor Site Construction Management* (10-09), *Uintah Basin* (10-07), *Steelton & Riverdale Site Reviews* (09-29 — this is the `Ber Wilson / Zenthium` call, retitled by the model, which §13 had flagged separately), *Rebecca/Merlin Portfolio Review* (09-29), *Partnership & Data Center* (09-23), *Eastern Utah Power* (08-20), *Salt Lake Service Expansion* (08-12), *Delby Digital* (08-12). Raised in §13 rather than fixed, because whether those should be re-queued or left as searchable transcripts is his call. §12 already names the shape: *"a destination that does not carry what creating carries reads as losing the work."*

**Other measurements taken on the way, for the record.** 1,836 leads ever ingested → 1,250 `spam`, 337 `ignored`, 247 `expired`, **1 promoted**. 201 open commitments, only 32 dated, 34 on threads silent 21+ days. 57 of 180 `parties` carry the `auto-contact` tag. 3,722 email threads (1,881 deal / 1,841 lead), 10,049 `chunks` and 8,634 `thread_chunks`. Session production runs 5–10/day, so the queue was never a volume spike — it was a gate that was never there. `lmstudio-check.sh` reports swap at 18.9GB (pre-existing; the check says what to do).

Shipped: `clusterStagingVerdict` + `held`/reopen in `stage-phase.ts`/`cluster-phase.ts`/`db.ts`, the three badge fixes and the 60s cache in `decide/count.ts` + `refile.ts`, `router.refresh()` in `DecideClient.tsx`, the held count in the sweep status route, the corrected agent note, `src/lib/email-sweep/stage-gate.test.ts` (8 cases) and `scripts/verify-decide-badge.mts`. **652 tests** (644 → 652), tsc clean, lint unchanged at 23 problems. DEPLOYED (build 0, kickstart, `/login` 200, `tailnet-setup.sh` and `lmstudio-check.sh` both green) + PUSHED. No migration — `thread_clusters.state` has no CHECK.

**Done 2026-10-20 (the directory joins the audit trail, and the five writers that would have said "system"):**

Richard: *"add parties and entities too."* The decision raised a few hours earlier — nine record-like tables carried no `log_activity()` trigger, two of them the directory, and which registers deserve an attributable history is a scope call rather than something a session should take unilaterally.

**⚠ MEASURED BEFORE APPLYING, BECAUSE THE FAILURE MODE IS A FLOODED LOG.** A trigger on a table some cron rewrites nightly turns `activity_log` into noise, so the question was not "is auditing good" but "what does this table's write volume actually look like". 161 parties and 5 entities; 82 updated in the last 7 days and 104 in 30, 80 created in 30. ⚠ The 7-day figure looked alarming until it was broken down by day: **one 62-row backfill on 10-16 and otherwise five to ten writes a day** — no blanket sweep. Against the 7,902 rows `activity_log` already took in 30 days, the trigger adds roughly 2%. Safe.

**Both tables also joined `_audited_in_full`,** so an UPDATE carries a per-FIELD diff rather than just "someone touched this row": `{"phone": {"old": null, "new": "801-555-0199"}}`. They pass the same test the economics tables passed on 10-05 — narrow and scalar. Measured rather than assumed: rows average **938 bytes** with the longest text column (`relationship_notes`) at **1,333 characters**, nothing like the hundreds of kilobytes that keep `documents` and `updates` permanently out. That diff is the half that answers the question a rolodex actually raises, and §12 records a leak where one phone number was spread across three people.

**⚠ `google_contacts_hash` NEEDED NO EXCLUSION, AND CHECKING THAT WAS THE POINT.** A sync hash that churned on every run would appear in every diff saying nothing, and the generic branch's exclusion list is only `('updated_at','created_at')`. But `workspace-sync.ts:289` skips the write when the hash already matches — the sync is idempotent on it — so a hash change never appears alone; it always travels with the field change that caused it. The honest answer was to measure the writer rather than add a column name to a list that would then need maintaining.

**⚠ THE FUNCTION WAS DERIVED FROM `pg_get_functiondef` AND EDITED PROGRAMMATICALLY, NEVER RETYPED** (§12). `log_activity()` is 210 lines of per-table branches and retyping it is how one of them silently disappears. The migration carries the whole function with one array line added, generated by a script that asserted the anchor appeared exactly once and that `'parties'` was not already present. Verified afterwards by diffing the live definition before against after with comments stripped: **exactly one line added, `'parties', 'entities',`** — and `select count(*) from pg_proc where proname='log_activity'` returns **1**, not 2, because the signature is unchanged and `create or replace` therefore replaces rather than OVERLOADING (§12 — a changed signature leaves the old version callable, and a wrapper's retry path can then fail open).

**⚠ THEN THE FOLLOW-THROUGH THE TRIGGER IS WORTHLESS WITHOUT, AND IT IS THE ENTRY.** §12 already says a user-initiated mutation on a tracked table must use `actorAdminClient()` or the log records it as "system". What that rule does not say — and now does — is that **making a table tracked means auditing every write path to it in the same change**. Of 20 files touching `parties`/`entities`, eight mutate, and **five were on the plain `createAdminClient()`**: the contact PATCH and DELETE (the main human edit path), the two creates, and `parties/associate`. Every human edit to a contact would have landed in the brand-new audit trail as `actor_type='system'`. An audit trail whose every row says "system" answers nothing, which is the only question it was added to answer — and these are precisely the rows Pepper also writes on her own (§11, 10-15: she creates a contact when mail is reciprocated, 53 so far, and fills fields on existing ones), so telling her edits from a human's is the entire value.

Switched to `actorAdminClient()` — **mutations only**. The two collection `GET` handlers were switched by the same pass and then deliberately switched back: a read has no actor to record, and resolving the viewer there buys a cookie read and nothing else.

**⚠ AND MY OWN CLEANUP SCRIPT HIT §12's COMMENT TRAP, in the file where I had just written the comment.** After the switch, three `createAdminClient` imports were unused and lint went 23 → 26. The script that was to remove them asserted the symbol was no longer called — and the assertion fired on `parties/[id]/route.ts`, because the docblock I had just added *explaining why the plain client was gone* names `createAdminClient()` in prose. §12: a scan of the source tree must STRIP COMMENTS or it measures its own documentation. Both halves of that rule have now cost time twice. Stripped, removed, lint back to the §9 baseline of **23 (13 errors, 10 warnings)**.

**Verification** (`scripts/verify-record-delete.mts`, extended rather than forked — a fourth near-identical script is the §12 fork this codebase keeps paying for). 20 live checks, all inside one transaction that rolls back, with a final sweep asserting nothing was left behind. New in this pass: creating a contact is logged; an edit carries the exact field (`801-555-0100 -> 801-555-0199`); **the diff holds ONLY `phone` — no `updated_at` noise**, which is the generic branch's exclusion list working; a deleted contact and a deleted entity are both recoverable from `metadata`; and attribution proved in **both** directions by setting `request.headers` in SQL the way the client sets it over HTTP — a header-less write is honestly marked `system`, one with `x-actor-email` names the person. 644 tests, 46 tables audited (from 44), 160 migrations, 105 tables.

**Still unaudited, deliberately, and still Richard's call:** `leads` (1,800 rows), `steel_deals`, `objectives`, `project_parcels` and the three Dino tables. `commitments` (708) is a standing exclusion with its own precedent, as are the four `*_notes` comment feeds. A blanket trigger remains the wrong move — 59 of 105 tables have no business being audited. (DEPLOYED + MIGRATED + PUSHED)

**Done 2026-10-20 (row delete on the last two lists, and the audit trail that made it defensible):**

Richard: *"add row delete to opportunities and investors too."* The measurement from earlier the same day had named exactly these two as the gap: every other list surface carries a row verb, and these could only be deleted by opening the record.

**⚠ THE FIRST FINDING IS THAT THE WORK WAS ALREADY WRITTEN TWICE.** `OpportunityDeleteButton` and `InvestorDeleteButton` were the same ~60 lines — same imports, same `useState` pair, same `ConfirmDialog`, same toast — differing in exactly four strings: the endpoint, the noun, the redirect and one sentence of description. §12's hardest fork to see is precisely that shape: two sibling modules written days apart where neither *looks* like a copy because every identifier was renamed. Adding a row delete to both lists naively would have made it **four** copies. So the change removes a fork instead of feeding one: both files are deleted, and `src/components/shared/RecordDeleteButton.tsx` is what they became, with a target parameter (`{endpoint, noun, name, description}`) and two variants — `pill` for a detail header, `card` for a grid card's corner.

**⚠ IT OWNS NO ROUTER, AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES IT VERIFIABLE.** `useRouter` throws "invariant expected app router to be mounted" outside a Next request, so a component reading it cannot be exercised by `renderToStaticMarkup`. Every class string and all the fetch behaviour therefore lives in the router-free component, and `RecordDeleteAndLeave` is a four-line wrapper that exists only to own the router for the two detail pages. Same split as `AttentionList`/`AttentionClient`, made the same morning, for the same reason. `router.refresh()` after `router.push()` is not redundant: the list being navigated to is a server component and would otherwise render the just-deleted row from cache.

**⚠ THE CARD COULD NO LONGER BE THE `<Link>`.** Both grids wrapped the entire card in an anchor. A `<button>` inside an `<a>` is invalid HTML and browsers resolve it by firing BOTH, so a delete nested in the old structure would have navigated to the record mid-request — with `tsc`, the build and a glance all clean. Each card is now a `relative group/card` div with the `<Link>` and the button as SIBLINGS, which is the pattern `/projects` already uses; matching it beat inventing a fourth. (Three already existed: `/projects`' in-card overlay confirmation, the detail-page pill with `ConfirmDialog`, and the optimistic icon on `/leads` and `/attention`.) The render check asserts no anchor contains a button and that each card still has exactly **one** real link.

**Both grids split into a pure half and a state half**, matching the morning's work: `OpportunityCards`/`InvestorCards` render and know nothing, `OpportunitiesClient`/`InvestorsClient` own the router and the optimistic removal. ⚠ And the state is an **overlay of removed ids, never a copy of the list** — `useState(props.items)` would be a second source of truth that never sees a `router.refresh()`, and syncing it back with an effect is the `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` pattern §9 already carries eleven of. `InvestorCardData` is re-exported from the wrapper so the page's import did not have to move.

**⚠ BOTH ROUTES ARE ADMIN-ONLY, SO THE BUTTON IS GATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO 403.** `canDelete` comes from each page's own viewer — `/opportunities` already computed `viewer?.isAdmin ?? true` and `/investors` now does the same, hoisted to a named const with the reason, so "may delete" has one definition and not two. §12: null renders no button at all rather than a dead one. The render check proves it on BOTH grids (the flag is passed twice, so a wrong default in either would be invisible), and that the default is **closed** — omitting `canDelete` or `onDeleted` renders nothing, so a call site added next year gets the safe answer.

**⚠ THEN THE REAL FINDING, AND IT CAME FROM VERIFYING THE DIALOG'S OWN SENTENCE.** The two confirmations make claims about the schema, not copy: *"removes the opportunity and its attached documents"*, and *"removes the investor, their investments and their notes. The directory contact stays."* Each is a cascade — or the deliberate absence of one — on a foreign key, and nothing in `tsc`, the build or a render check can see whether Postgres agrees. If `investors.party_id` cascaded, a one-tap delete would quietly take a contact out of the rolodex while the dialog promised it would not. Proved in a transaction that rolls back: documents cascade, investments and notes cascade, **and `parties` does not** — all four sentences true.

What the same check turned up is that **neither `investors` nor `investments` carried `log_activity()`**. 42 tables do. §4 is explicit that `activity_log` is append-only and the trigger writes `to_jsonb(old)` into `metadata`, which is the ONLY reason a hard delete in this app is recoverable — and it is what makes a one-tap delete on a list defensible rather than reckless. So an investor delete left nothing behind at all. ⚠ **The drift has a shape worth naming: the cap-table half of the raise machinery was audited and the pipeline half was not.** §4 pairs them deliberately — *"`investments` IS THE RAISE PIPELINE AND `project_spv_participants` IS THE CAP TABLE"* — they join on `investor_id` and are shown side by side; `project_spvs` and `project_spv_participants` both got the trigger when they were built on 10-06, while `investors`/`investments` predate them by three months and were never revisited. **This is the second time in two days**: `opportunities` was 40-tables-audited-and-not-this-one until 10-19. Migration `20261020000002` adds both. `investor_notes` is deliberately excluded — it is a comment feed, and no feed table in this schema is audited (`dev_notes` is a bug tracker and `personnel_notes` a governance register, not feeds). A cascade fires the child's trigger too, so deleting an investor now writes one recoverable row per investment as well as its own.

**⚠ AND THE CHECK WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE THE SCHEMA WAS, which is §12's "when a check fails, suspect the check" twice over.** First it asserted `action = 'deleted'`; `log_activity()` writes `action = TG_OP` verbatim, which is `'DELETE'` in upper case — so `opportunities`, which *does* carry the trigger, reported as unaudited and nearly earned a redundant migration. Then two column names were guessed from the UI rather than read from the schema (`opportunity_documents.name` is `file_name`; `investor_notes.note` is `body`). The script also died on `ERR_INVALID_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX` because a **backtick inside an SQL comment closed the JS template literal holding the SQL** — a new way to break a verification script, and one the error message does not point at. It now asserts the log row actually CARRIES the deleted row (`metadata->>'name'`), because a tombstone with no body makes "recoverable" a word rather than a fact.

**Measured and NOT built — a finding for Richard, not a silent expansion.** Audit coverage across the record-like tables: unaudited are `parties` (153 rows — the rolodex), `entities`, `leads` (1,800), `steel_deals`, `objectives`, `project_parcels` and the three Dino tables. `commitments` (708) is a deliberate exclusion with its own §4 precedent, as are the four `*_notes` feeds. Which of those registers deserves an attributable history is a scope decision, and a blanket trigger would have been the "broader and wronger" move §12 warns about — 63 of 105 tables legitimately have no business being audited. Raised as an open item.

**Verification.** 36 render checks across both grids (`scripts/verify-record-cards.tsx`): every optional field absent, every one present, a **zero** value distinct from null, an investor with no commitments, the targets overflow counted rather than truncated, the admin gate on both grids, the closed default, `size-[2.75rem]` tap targets rather than `size-11`, the `group-focus-within` keyboard reveal, and no `NaN`/`undefined`/`Infinity`/`>null<` in either. 13 live-database checks (`scripts/verify-record-delete.mts`), all inside one rolled-back transaction, asserting afterwards that nothing was left behind. 644 tests, lint unchanged at 23, 105 tables, 159 migrations, routes unchanged at 192 (no route added — the delete goes through the handlers that already own these records). **Done 2026-10-20 (a list of urgent things with no verbs, and the two it needed):**

Richard: *"When looking in the 'attention' section, it shows me leads and other items that are urgent, but I don't have a quick button to simply delete them. Same with tasks, I suppose i can just mark complete but if we are tracking the activity, I don't want to mark complete a task that really just needs to be deleted. Make sure I have quick actions everywhere needed on the platform."*

**Measured the breadth before building any of it, because "everywhere" is the part that could have been a week.** Across the list surfaces: `/leads` already has an X on the card (optimistic, restores on failure), and `/decide`, `/contacts`, `/objectives` and `/commitments` all carry row verbs. `/opportunities` and `/investors` can only be deleted from the detail page, and `/projects` is partial. **`/attention` had no verb of any kind, for any of its ten kinds** — every row was a bare `<Link>`, so the only thing a reader could do with it was open it. `/tasks` had the complete circle with an Undo toast and nothing else; delete was three interactions deep inside the detail sheet. Richard chose to scope the session to those two and leave the rest measured and reported.

**⚠ THE ENGINE'S OWN COMMENT HAD BEEN PROMISING THE MISSING VERB ALL ALONG.** On the lead branch of `computeAttention()`: *"A bid date is a hard wall — urgency climbs steeply as it approaches, and an already-closed one stays loud until somebody dismisses it."* Nothing ever built the dismiss. Live today the list is 10 items, **8 of them inbound leads**, which is the 10-17 open item about whether leads belong here at all — now answerable from the screen rather than by editing `ATTENTION_KINDS`.

**Four of the ten kinds can honestly be deleted, and that was the design question.** A task, a lead, a diligence item and a compliance item each have a row and a route that owns it. The other six do not: a milestone and a cross-project dependency are real records a triage screen has no business destroying (the dependency has a working DELETE route and still does not get the button, because removing a link changes the graph the project page and the timeline both read); `investor_followup` and `dino_payment` are DERIVED from records nobody would delete to quieten a list; and **`stale_waiting` and `stale_decision` are entries inside an `updates` jsonb array with no row of their own at all.** So delete where delete is honest, and `attentionDeleteTarget()` returns null for the rest — no button rather than a dead one.

For those six, Richard chose a **two-week dismissal**, and §12 decided its shape. `computeAttention()` rebuilds all ten kinds from live rows on every call, so there is nothing to tick: a dismissal in component state dies on the next navigation, one in `localStorage` would be the only copy the page can see AND invisible to the three readers that matter most — the dashboard rail, the sidebar badge and Pepper's 06:50 note. The harder version of the same rule is that an automatic pass and the undo for it are a LOOP unless the undo leaves a mark the pass respects. So `attention_dismissals`, keyed by the item's own id, upserted on a unique index (a second dismiss extends the quiet, never stacks), with `dismissed_until` a DATE rather than a boolean — a milestone dismissed in March that matters in June must return on its own. Precedent: `commitments.snoozed_until`, which took the same shape for the same reason; the difference is that an attention item has no row to hang a column on.

**⚠ AND THE SIDEBAR BADGE IS THE READER THAT COULD ONLY BE FIXED IN SQL.** `countAttention()` is four `head: true` counts and never receives a row, so there is nothing for a JavaScript filter to run against — §12 already records this exact shape, because it is how a confidential project reached that badge on every page. Dismissing an overdue task and watching the sidebar keep counting it would have been the fourth contradictory "needs attention" number, which is what this module's whole docblock is about. The dismissed ids go into a `not.in` per source table, with a 200-id URL cap that returns the query UNFILTERED and logs rather than silently stopping (a 37KB GET is `URI too long` from Kong). `certifications` is deliberately not filtered: nothing can dismiss one, because no attention kind points at it.

**⚠ THE BODY IS TRUSTED FOR ONE FIELD.** The dismiss route takes an item key and reads the title, project name and project id off the LIVE item — the same rule as `/api/records/[child]/[id]`, where a client that can name its own parent can write onto a record it may not. Here it would be worse: `project_id` is what contains the dismissed list from a `confidential` project, so a fabricated one would write a protected milestone's title into a surface every viewer reads. **And that is also the access check, structurally** — `computeAttention()` has already dropped every protected item before the handler sees the list, so a key that is not in it cannot be dismissed. You can only silence what you can see, which is a fact about the choke point rather than a condition a future route can forget.

**⚠ THE PREFIX DISCRIMINATOR, AND THE TWO PLACES IT HAD TO BE ASSERTED.** The item ids are `task-<uuid>`, `comp-<uuid>`, `waiting-<uuid>-<text slice>` and seven more — a registry with no type behind it, which is exactly what cost three switches and a silently-`unfiled` meeting on 10-19. So `idPrefixes` moved into `ATTENTION_KINDS` (investor_followup has TWO, `investor-next-` and `investor-cold-`, which a single-prefix assumption would have left half unparseable), and `attentionRowId()` REFUSES anything that is not a bare uuid after the prefix — stripping `waiting-` yields `<uuid>-Sign the MNDA`, which must never reach a DELETE and would answer `22P02` on the whole badge count, which returns null, which reads as zero. ⚠ The unit test holds one sample id per kind **transcribed by hand from `attention.ts`, so it is a COPY and proves only self-consistency**; `scripts/verify-attention-dismiss.mts` asks the engine what ids it is really producing. Live: all 10 resolved to their own kind, and the deletable ones were checked to have a row actually behind them, because a 404 from a route the UI offered reads as the button being broken.

**⚠ THE ROW COULD NO LONGER BE A `<Link>`, AND THE SECOND-ORDER EFFECT IS THE INTERESTING ONE.** A `<button>` inside an `<a>` is invalid HTML and browsers resolve it by firing BOTH, so the first Delete press would have navigated away mid-request — with `tsc`, the build and a glance all clean. The title now carries the anchor and stretches over the row (`after:absolute after:inset-0`) with the actions above it on their own stacking context (`relative z-10` — without it the overlay sits on top and every press navigates instead of acting, a control that looks present and does the wrong thing). **The effect nobody would look for: the row's hover-reveal fallback was `group-focus-visible:opacity-100`, which asks whether the GROUP ELEMENT is focused.** That worked while the row was a Link. A div cannot take focus, so the variant would have stayed in the class string, passed the existing check that greps for it, and revealed nothing to a keyboard user. `group-focus-within` is the one a row of buttons needs. The render check now asserts the count of keyboard reveals is at least the count of hover reveals, and that `group-focus-visible` is gone.

**On `/tasks`, delete beside the complete circle — and Richard's reason is exactly right.** Ticking the circle stamps `completed_at`, writes a `done` row into `activity_log`, and where the task came from a commitment calls `settleCommitmentForTask`, which settles the obligation on the counterparty's thread as though the work had happened. A task that should never have existed must not leave that trail. Confirmed, unlike complete: completing is one tap with an Undo because the row survives it, while this destroys the task and its notes and the only way back is `to_jsonb(old)` in `activity_log`, which is not a button — so the dialog NAMES the task, and no Undo is offered that could not honour itself.

The suite went 637 → 637 and then to 644, and **a count that holds or rises is not evidence nothing was lost** — I had added about as many as I destroyed.
