**The gate is deliberately not the one that was asked for.** "Talks about moving forward" is said on nearly every call, and 10-17 had already measured what happens when intent language decides: 110 of 126 staged sessions proposed CREATE against a register of 26. So intent is necessary and not sufficient, and two conditions must both hold, both facts:

1. **Nothing in either register resolves the name** — through `resolveMeetingTarget`, the same ladder `/decide` was pointed at on 10-17. A `target`, a `suggestion` **or** an `ambiguous` verdict all refuse. §12 says ambiguity must mean no match; here it has to mean no CREATE too, or the ambiguous case manufactures the duplicate the resolver just declined to pick. A resolver that *threw* also refuses — fail closed.
2. **One hard fact**: a follow-up task carrying a `due_date`, a document that came back EXECUTED in correspondence within ±14 days naming the deal or counterparty, or a follow-up already on the calendar inside 60 days. "Signature requested" is deliberately not on the executed list — that is a fact about an intention, which is the thing the gate exists not to act on.

**Proven on the real case.** With no dated task and no calendar read, `findHardFact` for "Synetra" came back `executed_document: eSigned Document Ready: "BW MNDA Synetra (with Non-Circumvention).docx (2026-10-19)"`, and the full dry run produced one `opportunity` named Synetra tagged **joint_venture** off the MNDA/non-circumvention language. That is the pattern Richard described, decided on evidence rather than enthusiasm.

**What a created record carries.** `auto_created_from` = the recording's source ref (`voicememo:<id>` / `driveaudio:<id>`), doing three jobs: the undo handle (one WHERE clause retires a run, as `auto-contact` does in `parties`), the idempotency key (`unique (auto_created_from, name)` — a plain UNIQUE, so unlimited NULLs leave human rows untouched; deliberately **not** `nulls not distinct`, which is the shared-children convention and exactly wrong here), and an honest label on a thin new row. The description says it was read from speech and names the gate's own fact, so the create is auditable on the record itself and not only in a log. Writes go through `provDbAs(PEPPER_ACTOR)`.

⚠ **Which is how the verification found that `opportunities` has no audit trigger.** The script asserted `activity_log` named Pepper and got an empty set. Forty tables carry `log_activity()` — `projects`, `tasks`, `meetings`, `documents`, `updates` among them — and the opportunity register was not one of them, so **every edit to a pursuit since the table was created has been unattributed**. It becomes load-bearing here, because §11's whole safety argument for an autonomous CREATE is that it is attributable *and* reversible and `auto_created_from` only answers the second. The trigger was added; the function needed no change, its `project_id` branch falling through to `to_jsonb(new)->>'project_id'` (checked against the live definition, not assumed). Not added to `_audited_in_full`: `description` now carries recording prose, so an UPDATE lands as "someone touched this row", exactly as it does on `projects`.

**The destination defaults to the opportunity side.** §12 says the model's `kind` is a guess and a match is a fact — and here, by construction, there is no match to read instead, since gate 1 only passes a name nothing resolves. So the guess is all there is, and the prompt that produced it states the test in the model's own instructions. A first recorded conversation about something we do not have is a PURSUIT; a project is work we hold. `opp_type` is read off what was actually said (joint venture / acquisition / investment) and **left null when the call was silent** — Richard asked for partnership and acquisition calls to be tagged as such, and inventing the tag where nothing was said is worse than leaving the question open on the record.

**No second model call.** The TLDR is composed from prose the recap already paid for — the per-record `discussion` paragraph, which the prompt asks for as "what this meeting said about THAT deal and nothing else". LM Studio serves one request at a time, so a model call here would queue in front of whatever a human is asking Ber AI; and §12's Steelton-narrative-on-Riverdale's-feed trap is the same trap in 150 characters. `recordLocalRecording` now returns its `extraction` so the caller needs neither a query nor a model.

**One text per recording, not one per record.** A broker call names several sites, and three texts in one minute is how a channel gets muted. One record leads with its own line; several are listed, each with its own link. `notification_log`'s `unique (kind, dedupe_key)` is keyed on the SET of record ids rather than the day — `sent_date` only ever meant one-a-day and two recordings on one morning are two pieces of news. Both texts come from Pepper at `info@` (Richard's choice), so each executive gets one clean Pepper thread; the assistant seat is skipped so she cannot text herself. The confidentiality filter is applied at the compose step though nothing this pass creates can be `confidential` — §12, a security filter on an OUTBOUND channel belongs at the choke point as a default, because that is the path that can never be unlocked after the fact.

**And the surface.** `/dashboard` leads with a **Just in** band, above the objectives: the objectives are what we said matters and do not change between mornings, while a recorded call attached to nothing has the shortest useful life of anything on the page. It is deliberately **not** a recordings list and not an attention score — `/attention` ranks ten kinds 0–100 and answers "what is most urgent"; this answers "what arrived, and is it on a deal yet", two quantities named apart and never summed. It shows the recording and anything created from it, because they are the same news at two stages. A created record carries a **"Pepper created this"** chip: the row most likely to be wrong is the one no human approved, and a reader who cannot tell it from one they typed has no reason to check it. The band renders nothing when nothing arrived.

⚠ **The ratchet caught its own author again.** The first draft of `JustIn.tsx` hand-rolled both chips as `text-[11px]` spans: 258 against the 10-17 baseline of 256. Rewritten on `Chip` with real tone names, which is what the convention was for.

**Verification.** 21 unit tests on the rules (which table, which tag, whose next step, what the text says) and **30 live-database checks** — an existing project refusing a duplicate, intent-only refusing, a new name with a hard fact creating exactly one row with its undo handle and its gate written down, the re-run creating nothing, the activity log naming Pepper, the composed text carrying name + signature + tappable link under 600 characters, both executives addressed with the assistant seat skipped, and the row appearing in the dashboard band with no `NaN` or `undefined` in the markup. Rows created by the script are removed through the same `auto_created_from` handle a human would use. Plus **11 render checks** on the band itself (`scripts/verify-just-in-render.tsx`) — behind auth `/dashboard` returns the same 307 whether the band works or throws, so every row shape is rendered directly, including the empty list, which must produce no markup at all. **606 tests pass**, lint unchanged at 23, build exit 0.

**Done 2026-10-19 (sixty-one routes were one route, and twenty-two of them disagreed about security):**

Richard asked how to simplify the platform, a day after the entry above established that **empty is not unused** and a pre-live system cannot be audited by row count. So this pass looked at duplicated WORK rather than unused features, measured four candidates, and built the largest one. Nothing was deleted that anybody uses.

**The measurement.** 200 route handlers across 20,083 lines, against 100 pages — §3 of `CLAUDE.md` still said "~85". Only **3 are dead** (`admin/backfill-embeddings`, `risk-scores`, `steel/quote-template/seed`), so the bloat is not abandoned code. It is repetition: **61 route handlers touch exactly one table with exactly one write verb**, 3,934 lines of them. And the tell was not the line count — it was that **22 of the 61 carry no record-level access check at all**.

**What the twelve files replaced had drifted into.** Four different directions, in the same shape of route:

- `milestones/[id]` resolved the row's parent and called `canAccessRecord`. `dd-items/[id]`, `financing/[id]`, `compliance-items/[id]`, `project-players/[id]` and `entity-projects/[id]` asked **nothing** — any authenticated session could PATCH or DELETE one of those rows by id, on any record, including a project marked `confidential`, which is the one thing `canAccessRecord` exists to refuse. ⚠ The docblock on that function had already called it: *"Checking it in each of them is seven chances to miss one, and the eighth route added next year would miss it by default."* **Six of the seven had missed it.** Latent rather than live — all three auth users are executives, `access_grants` is empty and no project is protected today — which is exactly why nothing reported it.
- `financing/[id]` built its update as `body.x ?? null` for **all twelve** of its columns, so any partial PATCH would have blanked the rest of the row (§12 — a field the caller never mentioned must be OMITTED, not nulled). It survived because its single caller sends the whole form.
- `entity-projects/[id]` and `project-players/[id]` wrote through `createAdminClient()`, so a human's edit was attributed to **"system"** in `activity_log` (§12). Neither checked `auth.getUser()` either, relying wholly on middleware.
- `dd-items` validated `severity` against its Postgres enum at the edge — added after a live 22P02 surfaced as a 500 with raw Postgres text — while `compliance_items.status`, also an enum, went unchecked.

**What was built.** `src/lib/records/children.ts`, one spec per child table of a project or opportunity, plus one dynamic route pair at `/api/records/[child]` + `/api/records/[child]/[id]`. Six tables — milestones, dd_items, financing_structures, compliance_items, project_players, entity_projects — **12 route files and 660 lines down to 2 files and 185**, with 387 lines of spec and guard behind them. The precedent is in the repo and was followed rather than invented: `src/lib/governance/registers.ts` has run twelve registers through one route pair since 2026-09-30.

⚠ **AND THE COERCION WAS EXTRACTED, NOT WRITTEN AGAIN.** The governance registry already held 120 lines of field coercion — dates, money with separators, tribool, uuid, textarray — and writing a second copy for these six tables is §12's hardest fork to see: *two SIBLING MODULES written days apart, because neither looks like a copy*. It moved to `src/lib/registry/fields.ts` and governance imports it; `normalizeRegisterPayload` is now a six-line wrapper whose only remaining job is stamping `author` from the viewer. One new kind was added for `draw_schedule` (`json`, which takes a structure and refuses a scalar).

**The access check is now the default, in one place.** A create reads its parent from the BODY (`scopeFromBody`, already shared); a PATCH or DELETE reads it off the **ROW**, because the id in the path is all a client sends. `project_id` and `opportunity_id` are absent from every `fields` map, so **re-parenting is not expressible** — a writable `project_id` would let a caller move a child onto a record they may write and edit it there, which is the access check defeated by its own payload. A test asserts that for every spec.

⚠ **`/api/records` IS NOT THE PATH THE ROLE GATE NAMES.** `project_manager` was allowlisted `/api/milestones`, the only one of the seven in any `ROLE_API_PREFIXES` list. `matchesPrefix` is a prefix match and is NOT method-aware (§12), so allowlisting the shorter string would have handed a project manager diligence, financing, compliance, players and entity links in one line. It names `/api/records/milestones`, and a test asserts no child's path sits underneath another's.

**Deliberately not generalised further.** `project_dependencies` names TWO projects and is the relationship between them — its guard has to hold at both ends and its list drops a row when either end is protected — so a second parent shape for one table would be a concept earning its keep in one place. It keeps its own file and **got the guard it was missing instead**: `PATCH` and `DELETE` there had no check of any kind, not even `auth.getUser()`. And DELETE is offered for only the four tables that had a delete route; milestones and financing did not, and the registry 405s rather than quietly granting two new destructive verbs (§11).

**Three duplicate lists folded in passing.** `DiligenceTab.tsx` carried its own copies of `SEVERITIES` and `SEVERITY_LABELS` — already in `constants.ts` — and the only definition of `DD_STATUSES` anywhere, inside a component where the registry validating that column could not see it. `dd_items.status` is plain text with no CHECK, so that list IS the schema; it is in `constants.ts` now and both read it.

⚠ **THE VERIFICATION FOUND THE SESSION'S REAL FINDING, AND IT WAS A FIFTH WAY TO BREAK A SCRIPT.** §12 lists four load-time failures a verification script hits that neither `tsc` nor the build can see. Here is the fifth: **`next/server` and `next/headers` do not resolve under the script loader at all**, and a top-level import of either poisons the whole module — *including its pure functions*. `children-access.ts` imported `NextResponse` only to build refusal responses, so it became `Response.json` (a route handler may return either, and `forbiddenJson` already did exactly that). Then `src/lib/auth/viewer.ts` failed the same way one layer down: it imports `@/lib/supabase/server`, which reads cookies through `next/headers`, at the top — so **the entire access layer was unloadable by any test or script**, including `canAccessProject` and `canAccessRecord`, which need no request whatsoever. Only `getViewer` does. Its import is now inside it, the same idiom the file already used for `confidential.ts` one function below.

**Verified against the live database, not asserted.** `scripts/verify-record-children.mts` creates a scratch project, runs **34 checks** through the identical normalise-then-write pipeline the handlers run, and deletes everything it made. The two that matter: *"the unmentioned column SURVIVED"* (patching only `lender` left `senior_debt` at 1,250,000 and the note after it intact) and *"an admin with no step-up is refused a row on a protected project"* — proven by flipping `confidential` on the scratch project mid-run and back, because asserting a guard against zero protected projects proves nothing. Also proven: a parentless compliance item is admitted for an admin and refused for a member; a project manager with no grant is refused on both create and edit; a missing row answers 404 rather than 403; `severity: "high"` is refused before any query reaches Postgres; and resolving a diligence item stamps `resolved_at` server-side and reopening clears it. Plus 14 unit tests on the spec's own invariants — every required/default/enum column is declared, no stamped timestamp is also writable, and `getChild('__proto__')` is nothing.

**Measured after:** route handlers **200 → 190**, thin single-table CRUD handlers **61 → 49**, unguarded ones **22 → 16**. `npm test` 566 → **580, all passing**; build clean; lint unchanged at the documented 23 problems. The 16 that remain are `parties`, `entities`, `media`, `objectives`, the intake sessions and `updates/[id]` — and `updates` is the interesting one, since a typed note is a project child whose table 23 call sites read, four of them with no project filter at all (10-18). That is the obvious next pass and it is in `OPEN-ITEMS.md`, not done here.

**Three candidates measured and NOT built**, in the order I would take them:

1. **Four morning messages, three composition stacks, one GPU.** 06:30 Monday Chat brief → 06:45 text → 06:50 email note → 07:00 Chat digest, all from the same tables, on a server that serves one request at a time — the route comments show the schedule is load-bearing for exactly that reason. `pepper-text` already does this right (it shares the note's assembly and only decides what fits in four lines); `digest/` and `briefs/` do not. One assembly, three renderings, ~1,200 lines and two crons. Held because the audiences genuinely differ and that is Richard's call.
2. **The lead pipeline asks the cheap question after the expensive one.** `junk-senders.ts` computes a sender verdict from facts the database already holds (`bulkShare`, `everProducedLead`) and correctly spares the plan rooms — which is why bidnet, 219 spam leads and a real bid source, is not in the set. But it is consumed only by the LAST phase (hygiene), while triage calls the model on every pending thread first. **49 senders account for 581 lead threads and have never once produced a non-spam lead** — realtor.com 106, Zillow 101 across four addresses, NYTimes 63, Alignable 38, Slidebean 37, and `info@berwilson.com` 24 of its own mail. ~8.7 GPU-hours spent; 53 of the last 277 leads (19%) still come from them.
3. **`cron-deal-intake` fires every 900s against an unset `GOOGLE_DEAL_INTAKE_FOLDER_ID`** — **3,941 identical 503s, 299KB of one sentence**. That is the exit-28 lesson the brief's own docblock tells: a log that always says failure teaches you to stop reading logs. Plus an orphaned 883KB `cron-google-tasks.log` whose agent no longer exists.

**Done 2026-10-19 (asked what to simplify, measured it, and three of the four answers were wrong):**

Richard asked whether the platform could be simplified — *"we likely have old legacy ideas that we don't really need or use anymore"* — with the goal restated as the CRM/BI platform that ingests, organizes and presents automatically. So the session began with measurement, and the first pass of recommendations was **mostly wrong**, which is the entry's main finding.

**What the measurement said.** Real `count(*)` across all 104 tables, not `n_live_tup` (§12 — it reported 1 against a real 15 once, and here it said `projects` = 0 against 19). **40 tables hold zero rows:** all ten economics tables bar the eight seeded benchmarks, eleven of twelve governance tables, all three Dino tables, `investments`, every `steel_*` but `steel_deals` (7) and `steel_quotes` (2). Against that, the consumption side: **72 questions have ever been asked of Ber AI** across 46 conversations, 15 of them this month, and a human touched **499 rows in 60 days** against 9,541 system writes — concentrated in five tables (tasks 88, review_queue 71, documents 71, updates 41, projects 32). ~2 GPU-hours/day, spiking to 5.3.

**The wrong recommendation, and why it was wrong.** The first answer proposed deleting Dino, Steel, Investors and Proposal intake — ~12,000 lines and 14 tables — on the evidence that they hold no data, with §9's removed Equity & Portfolio modules as the precedent. Richard's correction: *"part of the reason some of these aren't being used yet, is because we are not really using this system yet. We are also still onboarding dino plumbing."* ⚠ **EMPTY IS NOT UNUSED, AND A PRE-LIVE SYSTEM CANNOT BE AUDITED BY ROW COUNT.** The whole delete list was withdrawn. Dino was the sharpest miss — it was about to be deleted in the week it goes live. The lesson generalises: a usage measurement reads adoption, and adoption of a system nobody has started using measures nothing. What survives such a measurement is only what is *actively* wrong: redundant, misleading, or duplicated.

**1. Pursuit fit stops judging correspondence.** `assessFit` ran on EVERY thread `email-ingestion/analyze.ts` staged: **230 of 251 sessions carry a verdict and 112 of them say `pass`** — about Steelton, Weirton and Riverdale, deals already under way. 92 of the 230 also set `profile_incomplete`, so the card read "pass, and I am not sure" above a live PSA. "Should Ber Wilson pursue this?" is the wrong question to ask of correspondence on work in hand, and the wrong answer is worse than none, because `predecide` **reads the verdict as an input** — the one thing that stopped this being dead code. It is also the most expensive call here: 1,258 invocations, **17.9 GPU-hours**, ~50s each on a model that serves one request at a time, which every interactive Ber AI question then queues behind.
  - ⚠ **The first diagnosis was also wrong.** `decideWeight` does not read `fit_score`, and `DecideClient` deliberately never prints it (§12 — ±20 points of noise), so it looked like 18 GPU-hours producing a number nothing consumes. Grepping one level further found `predecide.ts` reading `fit.recommendation` and `fit.fit_score` into its prompt. A removal would have silently degraded the pre-decision. **Check what consumes a value before calling it dead** — and the prompt already labels it "advisory only", which is the tell that someone had thought about its weight.
  - The gate is the **matcher's own answer, not a model's**: `matchCandidates.length === 0`. If an existing project or opportunity matched, we have the deal and fit is moot. Measured honestly, that skips only **48 of 251 today** — much less than hoped, because the history predates the 10-17 matcher fix that first let an opportunity be a candidate at all (merges went 7 → 16 on the 19 sessions re-decided). The share grows from here; the shape is right regardless of the ratio. `predecide` still reads the verdict where one exists, and `str(undefined)` → null makes its prompt omit the line entirely, so the null path needed no change.

**2. `/intake` was a second Decide queue over the same rows.** Both pages listed the same pending sessions — **101 email and 14 meeting** — `/intake` ranked by `DISPOSITION_RANK` (create, merge, none, dismiss), `/decide` by `decideWeight` (overdue, urgent, verdict, value), each with its own dismiss buttons, each implying it was the queue. §12: one quantity, one definition, or the reader trusts neither. The split is now by **who the row is waiting on**: a `running` or `failed` session is this page's own job and belongs beside the form that started it; a `pending` one is waiting on a human judgement, which is Decide's whole purpose, and is a count and a link from here. Same treatment on the Meeting tab. People and Cards were left alone — they have no pending rows and `/decide` has no lane for them, so that tab is their only home and is not a duplicate.
  - ⚠ **Caught by the verification script, not by review, and it was one of this file's own rules.** The first version filtered `pending` out in TypeScript after `.neq('status','dismissed').limit(25)` — and the 25 newest undismissed rows are **all pending**, so every confirmed run fell outside the window and "Recent runs" rendered empty. §12 states it exactly: *an exclusion must be applied in SQL, BEFORE the `LIMIT`*. Fixed to `.in('status', ['running','confirmed'])`. `running` is a stored status; `failed` is a stale `running` derived by `effectiveEmailIntakeStatus`, which is why it is not in the list.
  - `scripts/verify-one-queue.tsx` asserts it on live rows, because behind auth a curl returns the same redirect whether a page answers or throws. Four checks: no pending row on either tab, the pointer has a count, the list is **not empty while finished runs exist** (added after the bug above — an empty list is legitimate only when nothing has finished), and pending + confirmed still accounts for every undismissed session so nothing was hidden rather than moved.

**3. One recording pipeline instead of one per recorder.** `voicememos/` and `driveaudio/` were written three days apart and were the same two functions twice. `transcribe.ts`: ~90 of ~110 lines identical — whisper-configured check, cheap guards before moving bytes, fetch, refuse an empty file, transcribe, trim, a result whose field is named `skipped` so a skip never reads as "there was no recording" — **down to the wording of the paging advice** on a failure. `to-thread.ts`: a byte-identical `ResolvedThread` construction carrying the two ⚠ comments that matter most, that participants are the owner alone and never guessed from the transcript, and that the id carries no modification stamp unlike a note's. That copy-paste had already cost a real bug: a recording's `meetings` row never followed its filed thread (fixed 10-18, in both sweeps separately). Now `src/lib/audio/transcribe-source.ts` (one whisper call, any source) and `src/lib/audio/to-thread.ts` (one thread shape, any recorder); each source keeps only what genuinely differs — where the bytes come from, which cheap guards it can answer first (a memo knows its duration and a disk that can fill; a Drive file knows its byte size and a quota), and its own provenance sentence. A third recorder is ~25 lines rather than a third copy. Line count barely moved (479 → 465); the win is that the next fix is one edit.

**What was deliberately NOT done, and why.** Economics, Governance, Steel, Investors, MSPA, Dino and `/timeline` all stay untouched — pre-live, not clunky. `/review` was examined and kept: it looked redundant (0 open rows, aliased to `/decide` in nav) but it is the **resolver** for that lane, the way `/email-ingestion/[id]` is for email, and it already has no sidebar entry of its own. `meetings/transcribe.ts` was examined as a third copy of the whisper chain and is not — it is the meeting-record pipeline (Storage upload, embed, extract), a different job. The iMessage and Notes readers keep their own decoders, which are genuinely different work (SQLite decoding, a credential filter); only the recording tail is shared.

**Two findings for Richard that are not code.** (a) **The queue grows faster than two people drain it** — 115 pending intake sessions and 58 live leads against **8 sessions ever confirmed**; the production side is far ahead of the consumption side, and that is the adoption question, not a bug. (b) **Six triage destinations now sit in one nav group** — Decide, Attention, Tasks, Commitments, Dashboard — which is the "overlapping attention surfaces" debt §9 records as resolved on 07-03, returned. Left alone deliberately: the UI was redrawn on 10-17 and Richard is still judging it, so restructuring his nav two days later is his call, not a refactor to slip in.

**Also measured, for the record.** 1,800 leads ingested: **1,226 spam (68%), 270 ignored, 241 expired, 62 new, 1 promoted**, at ~1,900 triage calls and ~25 GPU-hours. Not cut — `info@` is a real lane and the Dino lanes are live — but the ratio is worth knowing before anything else is built on it. 749 of 3,644 threads (21%) are filed on a record. The non-email doors: iMessage 187 threads / 108 commitments / **9 links**, voice memos 10, **Apple Notes 1** (and it is a recorded call — the nominated-folder door has produced nothing because the folder does not exist yet), **Drive audio 0** (same, the folder is empty). Microsoft Graph is genuinely gone from the code; `CLAUDE.md` §2 still lists it as a stack layer, and `/capacity` is listed in §3 but the page no longer exists — both doc drift, not code debt.

567 tests pass. Build clean, deployed, pushed, `tailnet-setup.sh` and `lmstudio-check.sh` both green — both models resident (idle, paged out, which is why they do not appear in `ps` by RSS), swap 17.8 of 19.5GB, which the check reports as the standing condition it is.

**Done 2026-10-18 (an opportunity's typed note does what a project's does, and the measurement picked the design):**

**The ask.** *"Fix the opportunity notes extraction too. Do what you think is
best."* — the ⚠ I had flagged an hour earlier and deliberately not closed.

**The defect, restated precisely.** `/api/opportunities/[id]/notes` wrote
`opportunity_notes` and called `embedOpportunityNote`. That is all it did: the
text became searchable and nothing else happened. The identical paragraph typed
on a project went through `PasteInput` → `/api/ai/extract` → `/api/updates/save`
and produced a summary, `waiting_on`, `risks`, `decisions`, a confidence, and
**real tasks on the board** via `createTasksFromActionItems`. So one typed
paragraph yielded follow-up work on a project and none on a pursuit. Invisible
from every angle: the screen looked right, `tsc` was happy, and the only symptom
was work that never appeared.

**Three ways to close it, and the measurement chose.** I had written them into
`OPEN-ITEMS.md` with "measure which notes would actually have produced a task
before building any of the three". Doing that is what settled it:

| | |
|---|---|
| notes | **90** across 6 opportunities |
| median length | **2,096 characters** (80 of 90 over 300; max 42,829) |
| written by **`Ber AI`** | **86** |
| by `Email ingestion` | 2 |
| **by a human** | **2** |

So the corpus is not one-liners — these are substantial — but it is almost
entirely **the mail sweep's own output stored as prose**. Two consequences,
both of which changed the plan:

1. ⚠ **No backfill, deliberately.** Re-extracting 86 Ber AI summaries is the
   model reading itself — the self-loop failure that turned out to be 27% of
   the commitment ledger on 10-09. The feature is for what gets typed NEXT.
2. ⚠ **The table does not move.** Making `updates` a shared child (§4) was the
   architecturally pure option and `updates.project_id` is *already* nullable,
   so it looked cheap. It is not: 23 call sites read or write `updates`, their
   `chunks` point at `opportunity_id` + `source_type='opportunity_note'` rather
   than `update_id`, 5 writers would need rewiring — and **four readers
   (`attention.ts`, `daily-brief`, two in `agent-tools.ts`) select `updates`
   with no project filter and then `dropHidden(rows, r => r.project_id)`**,
   whose predicate is `!id || !hidden.has(id)`. An opportunity-attached update
   has a NULL `project_id` and passes straight through — precisely the §12 rule
   about a nullable pointer breaking a security filter without touching it. All
   of that to relocate **2 human rows**.

**So the tables stay two and the PASS becomes one**, which is what §12 actually
demands ("never fork a shared pass — add a target"; "if two paths differ only
in WHERE the work lands, they are one pass with a target parameter"):

- **`src/lib/records/log-entry.ts`** — `logEntry(supabase, target, input)`,
  `target` being `{kind:'project'|'opportunity', id}`. It picks the table,
  stores the extraction beside the raw text, creates the tasks, touches the
  parent and indexes it. In `src/lib`, not the route, per the rule that agent
  tools never fetch the app's own HTTP routes.
- **`createTasksFromActionItems` takes a record target**, not `{ projectId }`.
  `tasks.opportunity_id` has existed the whole time and nothing could reach it
  — that was half the defect on its own.
- **`/api/updates/save` takes `project_id` XOR `opportunity_id`** and refuses
  both (the exactly-one rule the shared-children tables carry as a CHECK).
  ⚠ The two arms take *different* access checks and that is not an oversight: a
  project can be `confidential` so it goes through `requireProjectAccess`,
  which can answer "locked — step up first"; an opportunity has no such flag
  and its gate is the access grant. **`/api/opportunities/[id]/notes` is
  retired** — one door.
- Migration `20261018000001`: `opportunity_notes` gains `summary`,
  `waiting_on`, `risks`, `decisions`, `confidence`, shaped to match `updates`
  exactly (arrays NOT NULL default `'[]'`, same `numeric(3,2)`). All five
  existing writers insert `(opportunity_id, body, author)` only, so the
  defaults mean none of them changes. `npm run gen-types` regenerated 104/104
  and touched exactly those three row types.
- **`ExtractedItems`** is ONE renderer for both cards — they were about to be
  two copies of the same 60 lines — and severity goes through `chipTone`
  instead of a sixth local colour map spelling the same four levels in the
  theme-blind `slate` ramp.
- ⚠ **The brief had two formatters for one shape and they disagreed.** A
  project's updates rendered as `summary` plus risks, waiting-on and decisions;
  an opportunity's notes as **500 truncated characters of raw prose**, because
  there were no extracted columns to render. One `commentaryLines` now, falling
  back to the body — which is what a saved-as-is note and all 86 sweep notes
  carry. The brief and `get_opportunity` both now **select** the columns they
  render: a new column is worth nothing if nothing reads it.
- "Save as-is" keeps the instant path this tab used to be. The extract pass is
  30–60s on a 35B local model and is never forced.

**⚠ Findings.**

- **§12's script-loading rule prescribes a fix that is wrong here, and I
  reproduced both failures before finding the cause.** `import { logEntry }`
  from a `.mts` script threw *"does not provide an export named 'logEntry'"* on
  a plain `export function`; appending `.ts` to the path (which two existing
  scripts do) did not help; and **adding a default export merely moved the
  failure one step**, to *"logEntry is not a function"*. Probing the namespace
  showed why: under `npx tsx` the module resolves as CJS and the ESM namespace
  holds `{ default, 'module.exports' }` with the real exports nested inside
  `default`. **It is the loader, not the import.** Run it under the repo's own
  `deploy/register.mjs` — what `npm test` already uses — and a named import
  resolves normally. The rule is amended rather than extended.
- **The conventions ratchet caught me**, 231 → 232: `NoteCard` hand-rolled
  `rounded-lg border border-border bg-card` instead of `<Panel>`. §12 forbids
  absorbing that by raising the baseline, so both it *and* the project
  `UpdateCard` beside it moved to `Panel` — the ratchet goes down, not sideways.
- **`useRouter()` made the component unrenderable**, so the only honest check
  was impossible (a record page is behind auth; a curl returns the same
  redirect whether it answers or throws). Split into `OpportunityNotesView`
  (pure) and a thin router wrapper — the same split `/attention`'s list needed
  on 10-17, for the same reason.
- **A deleted opportunity note's chunks are unreachable forever.** My cleanup
  left 4 orphans in the corpus, because `chunks` has `update_id` with
  `ON DELETE CASCADE` for a project update and **no pointer to a note at all**
  — a note chunk names only its opportunity, so an orphan is indistinguishable
  from a live one. Latent, not live: there is no delete path for
  `opportunity_notes` anywhere in the app, and the corpus has 153 note chunks
  against 90 notes (several per note). Recorded in `OPEN-ITEMS.md` rather than
  reaped, because there is no producer of the problem yet.
- `updates` holds **32 rows with a NULL `project_id`** — all `source='email'`,
  all `review_state='rejected'`, all from 3–5 May, dead output of the scraper
  removed on 06-25. Correctly invisible; chased because a nullable pointer with
  live rows behind it would have changed the design.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-log-entry.mts` — 28 checks against the LIVE
database, calling the producer rather than building the row (a fixture that
builds the field directly cannot catch a producer that never fills it, §12).
It asserts both arms store the same summary and the same risks from the same
payload; that the opportunity's tasks carry `opportunity_id` and NOT
`project_id`, and the project's the reverse; that a named assignee resolves and
an unnamed one stays unassigned; that saved-as-is stores a NULL summary and
NULL confidence but empty arrays, never nulls; and it deletes every row it
made, with a `finally` that does **not** call `process.exit` (that swallows the
throw it is unwinding, §12). `verify-record-log.tsx` grew to 63 checks covering
the new card in both states. `npm test` 567/567, `tsc` clean, lint unchanged at
23, `npm run build` exit 0 captured unpiped.

**Done 2026-10-18 (one obvious place to log by hand, and the tab bar reads in order):**

**The ask.** *"How do I manually log a meeting on a project? There are times
where I will want to type notes, paste in a summary etc… I don't see a clear
and obvious way to log activity manually. Make sure that is there and make
sure that when I view a project, that the order of things displayed makes the
most sense. How would you organize it? Do the same for opportunities."*

**Measured first, and the premise was half wrong — which changed what got
built.** Nothing was missing. The Meetings tab has carried a complete form
since it shipped: title, kind, date, time, location, attendees picked from
`team_members` and `parties`, a transcript box, summary, minutes, decisions, a
`confidential` flag, an `index_ai` flag, a recording upload that spawns
whisper, and a **Draft from transcript** button that runs `/api/meetings/draft`
and fills the summary, minutes, decisions and attendees from pasted text. The
project Updates tab has carried `PasteInput` — extract with AI, or save as-is —
which writes `updates` with `source='manual_paste'`, embeds into `chunks`, and
turns confirmed action items into real tasks. An opportunity's Notes composer
writes `opportunity_notes` and embeds through `embedOpportunityNote`.

So this was never a build gap. It was a **discoverability** one, and the cause
is a rule this file praises elsewhere: `RecordTabBar` hides a tab with no rows
under **More**. Counted on the live database:

| tab | projects with ≥1 row (of 19) | rows |
|---|---|---|
| documents | 17 | 682 |
| updates | 14 | 179 |
| players | 13 | 70 |
| tasks | 4 | 31 |
| milestones | 2 | 5 |
| **meetings** | **2** | **3** |
| vehicles | 1 | 3 |
| parcels | 1 | 11 |
| financing / entities / economics / dd_items | 0 | — |

And on opportunities (of 7): documents 6, notes 6, tasks 3, **meetings 2**,
everything else 0. So on **17 of 19 projects and 5 of 7 opportunities the only
door to logging a meeting was two clicks down a menu labelled "More"** —
exactly the question asked. ⚠ **Count-gating a tab is right for READING a
populated record and exactly wrong for the first WRITE.** By rows alone
Meetings and Tasks belong under More, and they are the two tabs a human types
into. A rule that ranks by what a record already holds cannot see the act of
putting the first thing in it.

**What got built.**

- **`RecordLogMenu`** in both record headers — a primary **Log** button,
  present on every tab, independent of every count: Meeting · Update (Note on
  an opportunity) · Task · Milestone · Document, each with a line on what goes
  in it. Creation lives in the header; the count-gating stays for reading.
- **`src/lib/records/log-menu.ts`** holds what the menu offers and where each
  entry lands. In `src/lib` rather than exported from the `'use client'`
  component so the verifier can read it (§12), and carrying **`autoOpens`** per
  entry: `?new=1` is appended **only** where the destination page reads it.
  Meetings, Tasks and the record's own feed open their form from it; Milestones
  and Documents are offered without it, because their add control is already in
  place on arrival and a param nothing reads would make the menu a promise the
  page fails to keep.
- The param is read on the **server** and passed in as `startNew` / `startAdd`
  / `autoFocus`, so the form is in the first paint — no `useSearchParams` in an
  effect and no flash of the empty list. `MeetingsView` honours `canEdit`
  first, so a non-admin arriving at `?new=1` gets the read-only list rather
  than a form they cannot submit.
- **The project header gains the action row the opportunity header already
  had** (Log, Brief, Edit, Protect). They had sat mid-page on the Overview tab,
  right-aligned, **below the photo gallery** — so Edit and Generate Brief were
  unreachable from any of the other twelve tabs, and the stage/sector chips
  moved down under the name where they read as identity rather than competing
  with the buttons for the same corner.
- **`PasteInput`'s placeholder and the Updates buttons were pasting-only in
  their wording** — "Paste Update", "Paste an email, meeting notes…", "Paste
  First Update" — against a box that has always accepted typing. Richard's
  words were *"type notes, paste in a summary"*, and two thirds of the label
  described the half he was not asking about. Now "Log an update" over "Type
  notes, or paste an email, a meeting summary, or a call recap…".

**Tab order — the reading order, not the row counts.** Both records now read
Overview → *the pulse* → *the file* → *the structure*:

`Overview · Updates|Notes · Meetings · Tasks · Documents · Players ·
Milestones · [Land] · Economics · Vehicles · Financing · Diligence · Entities`

Documents moves from third to fifth on purpose, despite being the heaviest
tab: it is a surface you go to deliberately, by name, where the first four are
what you scan. Five tabs are `always`, and the verifier **ratchets that at
five** — past it, an empty record shows a bar of empties again, which is the
bug the gating was built to fix. Vehicles still precedes Economics: the
structure is settled before anything is priced.

**Overview section order.**

- An **opportunity now leads with Next Step.** It was the *last* block on the
  page, under the facts grid, the description and two prose cards — the one
  line saying what to actually do, below the fold, with everything above it
  reference.
- A **project's Contract block moves above Sub-Projects**: how big and by when,
  then what it is made of.
- ⚠ The project's audit section is renamed **Change History**. It was "Recent
  Activity" — and the tab three inches above it is where a human reads what
  actually happened on the deal, while that table is `log_activity`'s
  who-changed-which-column. Two surfaces called activity meaning different
  things is the one-quantity-one-definition rule (§12); the collision was there
  before this session and would have got worse the moment the Log menu made
  the feed easy to reach.

**Found while measuring, not fixed here.** An opportunity's Notes are embedded
but **never extracted** — `opportunity_notes` gets `embedOpportunityNote` and
nothing else, where a project's Updates run `/api/ai/extract` and produce
tasks, risks and decisions. So the same typed paragraph yields follow-up work
on a project and nothing on an opportunity. Listed in `OPEN-ITEMS.md`; it is a
real asymmetry, not a bug, and worth a measurement before it is closed.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify-record-log.tsx` — ⚠ a record page is behind
auth, so a curl returns the same redirect whether it answers or throws (§12).
It renders the components directly and asserts: the trigger is a closed menu
on both records; **every entry names a segment that exists in that record's
tab registry**; **`?new=1` appears on exactly the entries whose page reads it**
(the check that stops the menu rotting — a href is a string and `tsc` cannot
see either failure); `startNew` shows the form and hides the list; a non-admin
gets no form; the composer's "save as-is" is offered alongside the AI pass;
all five manual tabs are visible on a record holding nothing; no more than five
are always-on; and the two registries carry the same tabs in the same order bar
Land. 41 checks, all passing. `npm test` 567/567, `tsc` clean, lint unchanged
at 23 problems, `npm run build` exit 0 (captured unpiped — §12).

**Done 2026-10-18 (a hardware recorder gets a door, and the register was not following the thread):**

**The ask.** Richard has a Plaude recorder and wants the raw mp3 of a sensitive
call read by the platform rather than by a vendor — exporting either to Apple
Notes or to a Drive folder, and asking which. Measured both before building:

- **Notes cannot carry it.** The notes sweep transcribes a note's audio only
  when `isCallRecording` passes, which is iOS's own generated title
  (`/^call with\s+\S/i`) plus an attachment — a deliberately narrow door, because
  that title is a signal iOS writes and not a human's prose. A Plaude export is
  titled with a timestamp, so it would fall to the nominated-folder path, and
  that path has no whisper call in it at all (`sweep.ts:127` gates the
  transcription loop on the same test). The result would be a thread whose body
  is a timestamp. Notes also only syncs while Notes.app is open, which is already
  a live open item.
- **Drive could not either.** `meet-import` *counts* `recordingsWithoutTranscript`
  and never transcribes one; a knowledge folder runs an mp3 through
  `documentKind`, which returns `'unsupported'` — a `documents` row with no text
  and a null `ai_summary`, which §12 calls a document the agent never opens.
- So the only manual door was a project's **Meetings tab → Recording**, which is
  per-record (what Richard wanted to avoid) and is the THIN path: transcript,
  summary, indexed — no commitments, no tasks, no attendee links.

**Built: `src/lib/driveaudio/*` + `/api/cron/drive-audio-sweep`.** A nominated
Drive folder, read hourly in business hours, downloaded, transcribed on-box by
whisper, then handed to the eight mail phases — so a recording becomes a thread,
a `meetings` row, an `updates` entry on the deal, and its obligations. The new
code is the reader, the transcriber and the ordering; every phase is the one the
mail sweep runs (§12: add a caller, not a pipeline). `recordLocalRecording`'s own
docblock had specified this case since 10-14 ("audio dropped in Drive and an
in-app recorder are both specified"), so the expensive half was already written.

Folder created on the shared drive as **Ber AI Recordings**
(`scripts/setup-audio-intake.mts`, idempotent) — on "Ber Wilson Proper" rather
than a My Drive so either executive can drop a file and the sweep, which reads as
`moose@`, sees all of it.

**⚠ THE FOLDER HINT, AND WHY IT NEEDED MORE THAN A SUBJECT.** A subfolder's name
is read as the deal, because a Plaude export — like a voice memo — is named with
a timestamp and "rename it after the deal" is a habit nobody keeps, while
dragging a file into a folder survives being in a hurry. First live run, with the
file in a subfolder called `Tooele`, the exact name of a real project:
**`linked: 0`**. `bestMatch` was working exactly as designed — a ONE-WORD record
name is ambiguous evidence by nature ("GridEdge" is a brand, "Tooele" is a
county) so it needs a shared CONTACT to corroborate it, and a recording
structurally has no external participants at all. That is §12 arriving for the
third time: *a two-signal bar makes a record invisible where one signal cannot
exist for the source* — documents hit it (38 M&A documents sat as company
knowledge), and the rule's own text already names Tooele as the example.

The bar did not need weakening, because a folder name is not a DESCRIPTION the
platform extracted from prose — it is an assertion a human made by dragging a
file, which has the standing of an alias. So the hint resolves through
`resolveMeetingTarget` (bar 1: a title a human already filed; bar 2: an exact
record name unique across both tables) and the sweep writes the `thread_links`
row itself at `linked`. A `suggestion` is deliberately NOT acted on — that bar
exists to pre-tick a checkbox, never to file. `routeThreads` already respects an
existing `linked` link and skips guessing, so nothing in the matcher changed.

**⚠ AND THE FINDING THAT WAS NOT MINE: A RECORDING'S `meetings` ROW HAS NEVER
FOLLOWED ITS FILED THREAD.** With the folder hint working, `updatesPosted: 1` and
`meetingsFiled: 0`. Every recording sweep writes the register row LAST, because
the recap costs a model pass — so at the moment `applyThreadUpdates` visits the
link there is no meeting to move, and by the next run the link is caught up on
text AND attachments and `continue`s at `apply-phase.ts:228`, never visited
again. The comment at `apply-phase.ts:327` says the call sits outside the
`needsText` block *on purpose* because "the meeting may still be sitting
unfiled" — true, and not enough: it is inside the loop that skips a caught-up
link entirely. §12, third occurrence: **a cleanup that is a side effect of having
work to do never reaches the rows with no work.**

Checked against the live database rather than assumed, and it was real and
pre-existing: **both voice memos on the box had a `linked` thread and an
`unfiled` meeting**, including the 67-minute Tensor construction-management
meeting the 10-15 session recorded as "filed as the Tensor Site Construction
Management meeting". `search_meetings` filtered by project answered that there
had been no calls on either deal. Fixed forward in
`fileMeetingFromThreadLinks` (`meetings/attach-recording.ts`), asked from the
side that just changed, called by BOTH sweeps at the moment they write the row,
refusing on ambiguity (a recording names 2–8 deals, and the register holds the
event once). Backfilled with `scripts/one-shot/file-stranded-recording-meetings.mts`
— 3 stranded, 3 filed. ⚠ Worth Richard's eye: one of the two is a *Helper, Utah*
recording now on **Box Elder Quantum Campus**, which is the thread's own
human-asserted alias link (`known as "Quantum Campus"`, confidence 0.99), not a
new guess — the register now agrees with the thread instead of saying the call
belonged to nobody, but the thread may itself be on the wrong deal.

**Verified end to end on a real mp3**, twice, against production: a 54-second
`say`-generated call named `2026-10-18 141500.mp3` (435KB, 64kbps mono, real
MPEG container) in a `Tooele` subfolder. Downloaded, **transcribed in 3.1s**,
summarized, filed on Tooele by the folder name, update posted to the project's
feed with `source: 'recording'` (the `thread-source.ts` arm, confirmed on the
live row — without it the feed would read "Email — Tooele — 2026-10-18"), a
`meetings` row written and then moved onto Tooele, **2 commitments extracted and
1 promoted to a task**: *"I will send the surveyor the scope… by Wednesday"* →
`side='us'`, `due 2026-10-21`, a task; *"Can you ask the title company…"* →
`side='them'`, correctly NOT a task (§11). All test rows and the Drive file were
then removed; `activity_log` keeps the trace, as it should.

**Two reporting bugs in my own first draft**, both caught by reading the output
rather than the code: the dry-run line printed `recordedAt.slice(0,16)`, so a
file named `141500` listed as `20:15` and read as a failed parse (it is UTC —
the siblings do this harmlessly because nothing is there to compare against);
and `Math.round(bytes/1024/1024)` printed a 435KB file as **`0MB`**, which reads
as an empty upload. Both now print what they mean.

**Smaller decisions, each with a reason:**

- **The gate is the folder, not the summarizer.** Every voice memo is read
  because a memo library is a personal archive with no filing decision in it;
  here somebody chose the file, which is the Notes and knowledge-base control
  model (§7). A `noise` verdict still discards the TEXT, because the prefix is in
  `LOCAL_THREAD_PREFIXES` and `summarize-phase` redacts there by default — a
  filter at the choke point, not a parameter each caller passes. The AUDIO is
  never touched: `redact.ts` gates deletion on `isVoiceMemoThread`, and the
  platform does not get to delete a document a human deliberately filed. Which
  also makes a wrong verdict recoverable, and the report says how (upload a
  copy — a copy is a new Drive id; re-dropping the same file is not).
- **`driveaudio:` maps onto the existing `recording` ThreadSource**, so there is
  no `update_source` enum migration and no new arm in `curator/evidence.ts` or
  `commitments/chase.ts`. The prefix still had to be named in `thread-source.ts`
  twice — once for the source, once for `LOCAL_THREAD_PREFIXES` — which is the
  file whose header exists because this bug has cost hours three times.
- **The thread id is Drive's file id with no modification stamp**, following
  `voicememo:` and not `note:`. Audio never changes, and the id survives a rename
  AND a move, so renaming the file after it has been read costs nothing.
- **A date is parsed out of the file name** (`2026-10-18 10-30-00`,
  `20261018_103000`, `Plaude 2026-10-18T10.30`), bounded to 2020..now+2d,
  rejecting a rolled-over `2026-02-30` and refusing eight digits that are merely
  an invoice number — falling back to Drive's modified time and REPORTING which,
  because an export that sat on the device for three days would otherwise file a
  Tuesday call above the mail that answered it. Date-only names land at midday,
  never `new Date('YYYY-MM-DD')`.
- **`RECORDING_EXTENSIONS` is now one list** with `isRecordingFileName()` over
  it, shared by the file picker and this sweep. `.qta` is why: a recent iOS
  writes it, there was no branch, and 39 of 111 voice memos — every 2026
  recording — read as a quiet corpus.
- **Guards the local sources do not need:** a 24KB floor (Drive reports no
  duration for audio, so the 5-second floor has no measure here, and whisper
  answers confident hallucinated text on silence) and a 500MB ceiling, because
  this folder is a place a human can drop a 4GB screen recording and
  `fetchDriveFile` buffers the body on a box that already pages.
- **Watched on the BACKLOG, not a clock** (`probeDriveAudio`). The local sweeps
  watch a snapshot's age because their faults are invisible otherwise; this one
  has no snapshot, but the folder itself says what is owed, which is a direct
  read on whether the consuming half of the loop runs rather than an inference
  from silence. Exercised directly, since the health page is behind auth.
- Cron at **:35 hourly in business hours**, clear of the email sweep and of the
  three local sweeps at :40/:45/:50 — LM Studio serves one request at a time and
  whisper holds a CPU beside it, so a latency measured while another sweep runs
  is measuring the queue.

⚠ **What is NOT built, deliberately:** nothing moves or deletes the file after
reading it. A move needs the `drive` scope that is marked TEMPORARY, and the
"already ingested" check makes the folder self-limiting anyway — the report says
the file can be trashed or dragged into an `Archive` subfolder, which
`isArchiveFolder` already skips. Also unbuilt: Richard's audio has already left
his hardware via Plaude's own cloud before any of this runs, so the local-only
guarantee here covers PROCESSING, not the recording (said plainly to him rather
than designed around). (DEPLOYED + AGENT INSTALLED)

**Done 2026-10-17 (Phases 4 and 5: the palette reaches the screens, and the agent can finally point at things):**

**Phase 4 — the colour migration, and it is the shape of the change that made it safe.**

324 raw bg/text/ring triples down to **149**, and the theme-blind `slate` ramp
from 572 uses to **365**. 39 distinct spellings over 12 hues folded to 13 tones,
the vocabulary DERIVED from the corpus rather than invented (§12): slate 34,
emerald 26, amber 26, blue 17, violet 16, red 16, indigo 13, cyan 10, sky 10,
teal 8, rose 8, orange 6.

⚠ **IT REWRITES THE VALUES, NOT THE TYPE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DECISION.**
Measured before touching anything: of the 71 sites consuming a `*_BADGE` map,
only **22** pass it to `<Chip tone=>`. The other 49 hand-roll their own chip as
`cn('inline-flex … ring-1 ring-inset', MAP[x])`. So converting the map VALUES to
tone names — the obvious move, and what the plan called for — would have meant
editing all 49, each with a visual shift as `Chip`'s own padding and text size
took over. Keeping `Record<K, string>` and sourcing the string from `chipTone()`
changes nothing downstream and buys the identical correctness win. The
type-level completion proof (narrowing `Chip`'s prop to `Tone`) is deferred, not
lost.

⚠ **`avatar.ts` IS EXCLUDED BY NAME.** Its eight values are a hash ramp — a
contact gets a colour from their name so that two people look different — and
three of those hues map to STATUS tones. Folding them in would render someone's
initials as `positive` or `caution`: a person's face reading as an alert.
Decoration and status are different questions and this palette keeps them apart.
The avatar classes already carry both themes, so there was nothing theme-blind
there to fix anyway.

⚠ **`TIER_CHIP.live` CARRIES ITS OWN `ring-1`** because its consumer does not add
one, while `chipTone()` omits it because `<Chip>` supplies it. The codemod
preserves it rather than silently removing that chip's ring.

⚠ **THE CODEMOD'S FIRST RUN PUT THE IMPORT INSIDE A MULTI-LINE `import type { … }`
BLOCK** — 40 syntax errors in `constants.ts` — because it matched the last line
that STARTS an import rather than the last that CLOSES one. Reverted from the
codemod's own manifest, fixed, re-run. ⚠ And I hit the same trap again later in
the session, by hand, in a one-off script, writing the fix a second time instead
of reusing the one I had just written: a trap you have just fixed is still a trap
in the next file you open manually.

Then the single-class maps the codemod could not see, and those were real bugs:
`bidDueColor()` returned `text-red-700` / `text-amber-600` / `text-slate-600`
with **no dark variant at all**, on the most time-critical figure on a project —
murky in exactly one theme. Same for `SCORECARD_RATING_COLORS`. (Its two red
levels, 700 for overdue and 600 for within a week, were also imperceptibly
different; urgency is carried by the words beside the date.)

**One card radius.** `Panel` was `rounded-xl` while 145 hand-rolled shells were
`rounded-lg`, so two card radii appeared on one screen. Under the chosen palette
`--radius` is 0.25rem, which makes `rounded-lg` exactly 4px — the radius the
direction specifies — so the base was right and the 85 xl outliers were wrong.
The ratchet changed shape with it: a card at `rounded-xl` is now an INVARIANT at
zero rather than a count to drain, because after this it would be a NEW second
radius rather than inherited debt.

**Phase 5 — reach.**

**Print.** There were 15 `print:*` utilities in the whole app and four were the
print toolbars, so printing any ordinary page emitted the sidebar, the header,
the mobile tab bar and the docks. Five classes across five chrome components
makes all 98 pages printable instead of 5.

**`/tasks` had neither a skeleton nor an error boundary**, despite being one of
the five routes in the mobile tab bar: a throw replaced the whole page and eight
queries ran with the previous screen frozen. Its 4-deep serial tail is now 2.

**`contacts/[id]` was the worst waterfall in the repo** — 18 awaits, zero
`Promise.all`, and its `loading.tsx` was the one bare three-bar skeleton in the
app, so the slowest route also had the least informative wait. The activity
tab's six serial reads are two stages now; only the two `updates` queries
actually need `projectIds`. Every hard-won comment in that block survived — the
jsonb `::text` cast PostgREST silently drops, and the `in.(null)` that errors on
a uuid column.

**Ber AI can link to the record it is discussing.** `BriefMarkdown` was written
for the brief prompt's vocabulary — headings, bold, bullets, bracketed tags —
and then reused for free-form chat, where it has rendered every agent answer
since the agent shipped. So `[Steelton](/projects/abc)` reached the reader as
that literal string, a numbered list rendered as a paragraph, and a pipe table
rendered as prose. Added links, ordered lists, inline code and fenced blocks,
additively, so both print views render byte-identically.
⚠ **A LINK MUST BE INTERNAL:** an href in an agent answer is a string a model
composed, so `https://`, `javascript:`, `mailto:`, protocol-relative `//` and
`../` traversal are all rendered as plain text — asserted, because a brief is a
document that gets emailed. ⚠ And the LINK alternative has to precede the TAG
alternative in the inline split, or `[WATCH]` claims the label half of a link.
⚠ Then the prompt had to be told, because a renderer that accepts links is
useless while the model believes it cannot use them (§12: a stale prompt example
is a lie the model repeats with confidence). A new test asserts every path the
prompt offers is a real route, checked against the filesystem — it caught the
first draft offering `/documents` as a suffix the model would have to assemble,
and `/opportunities/<id>`, whose index lives under a `(detail)` route group that
is invisible in the URL.

**An answer's sources are clickable.** Every stored message has carried
`toolCalls: { name, args }[]` all along and the UI printed
`Data sources: query project data, search documents` — the names, joined with
commas, args discarded. So an answer about Steelton's lease could not be checked
against the record it came from. ⚠ The mapping is pure and tested because a
citation pointing at the wrong record is worse than none: **the KIND decides the
route, never the shape of the id** (a project uuid is indistinguishable from an
opportunity uuid, and §12 records one being sent to the wrong branch), a value
that is not a uuid never becomes a route, and a uuid in a term field is not
printed at the reader as a search term.

**The sidebar is four labelled groups** — Today, Pipeline, Divisions,
Intelligence — instead of 13 unlabelled rows mixing triage, records, two
business units, a strategy board and a map, while the three groups that WERE
labelled were the three small ones. Leads left "Intelligence", where it sat
between a calculator and the agent. Declaration order is the reading order.
`aria-current="page"` on the sidebar and both mobile link sets: there were ZERO
in the entire codebase, so the active row was a background colour and a screen
reader could not tell which page it was on. Collapse is remembered — it was
`useState(false)` while the lead-lane disclosure three lines below it, a far
less consequential preference, was already stored. A new nav test makes the
file's own two ⚠ comments mechanical: no path lights two rows, no `alsoMatches`
duplicates an href, every destination is a real route, every group is labelled,
no visible group exceeds seven rows, the mobile bar holds exactly five.

**A filtered board is a link.** The task board's six filters were `useState`, so
"Eric's overdue Weirton tasks" could not be sent to the other executive,
bookmarked, or survive a refresh. Three decisions in the new `useUrlState` hook,
each reversing a specific bug: it REPLACES rather than pushes (with `push`, Back
walks the reader through every dropdown they touched); the default is DELETED
from the query string rather than serialised (or every shared link carries four
redundant params and the bare case never occurs); and the incoming value is
VALIDATED against an allow-list, because a query string is user input that
reaches `.eq('status', …)` and §12 records that a value outside an enum fails
the WHOLE query with `22P02` and a null row set.
⚠ **And `ProjectFilters`' localStorage replay is deleted.** It mirrored the URL
filters into localStorage and replayed them on mount whenever someone arrived
with none — so a bare `/projects` rendered DIFFERENTLY for each executive and the
sender could not tell, and because the replay ran after hydration the list
visibly re-rendered on arrival. ⚠ Correction to the plan: this was supposed to
drop one of the 11 `set-state-in-effect` warnings. It does not — that effect
called `router.replace`, not setState. Counted after: still 11.

**`?` opens a shortcuts overlay**, generated from a new typed dock registry. The
best-executed interactions in the app were the least findable: ⌘/ was
discoverable only through a `title=` attribute, which never appears on keyboard
focus and does not exist on a phone. ⚠ The four dock events were untyped string
literals dispatched from eight sites, and the convention check written to catch
them matched `new Event(` only — so the two dispatches carrying a payload used
`new CustomEvent(`, and **one of those was the single site that also kept its own
second copy of the event name** (`QUICK_CALC_EVENT`, exported from the dock and
dispatched by hand from the header). The hardest case hid behind the narrow
pattern. Checked both directions now: an entry nothing listens for is a dead
dock, a listener nothing can dispatch is a dock that never opens.

**17 nameless icon buttons**, including the SEND BUTTON ON THE AGENT — the
most-used control in the app's headline feature — and three modal closes in
`UserAccessManager`. Plus two byte-identical hand-written input constants in the
mail and meeting review screens: wrong radius, no 44px mobile height, and **no
focus ring at all**, so a keyboard user could not see which field they were in
on the two screens that stage records.
⚠ **The check for this took three narrowings and each broad version cost
evidence** (§12). Reading the text after the icon flagged all 20
`<Plus/> Add Requirement` buttons. Stripping `{expressions}` flagged every
`{saving ? 'Saving…' : 'Save Profile'}` button, because the label is a literal
INSIDE the expression. Counting those literals still flagged the multi-line
`{cond ? (<Icon/> Text) : (…)}` form, because a non-greedy brace match stops
inside `size={14}`. The shipped version matches only children that are exactly
one self-closing element: it misses a button labelled through a conditional, and
that is the right trade — a narrow check that is trusted beats a broad one that
gets muted. ⚠ And `title=` DOES count toward the accessible name, so the audit's
figure of 34 was overstated; the real number was 17.

**Eleven skeletons** for the routes that actually wait — the whole /steel detail
family, /vendors/[id], the four /intake confirmation routes,
/email-ingestion/[id], a named raise. ⚠ `/opportunities/[id]/(detail)` left
alone: it is the app's only route group and §12 records that a `loading.tsx` at a
route group's ROOT 500s the whole route. The Phase 1 conventions test enforces
that, which is the only reason this pass could be run mechanically.

**Deleting a task asks first.** Measured rather than assumed: 40 files issue a
DELETE, 15 had no `ConfirmDialog`, but three of those are fine — two use an
inline two-step and `LeadsClient` carries a documented decision that the
friction is why the queue stalls. So 12, not the audited 16. The task sheet was
fixed because it is touched daily; the other 11 are recorded in OPEN-ITEMS with
the measured list, worst first, because each needs its own dialog wired to its
own handler in a differently shaped component and twelve careless edits to
destructive paths is worse than none.

**Measured and deliberately NOT done**, each with the measurement:
  * **The dashboard rail on the attention engine.** The plan called it "likely a
    net query win"; the opposite is true. `ddRaw` and `overdueRaw` also build
    the per-project CARD badges (blockingCount, overdueCount, nextDeadline), so
    they cannot be removed — adding `computeAttention()`'s dozen queries to the
    most-visited page in the app would buy ranking at a real latency cost. Only
    a larger restructure of the card-badge derivation makes it pay, and the
    single-definition problem it was meant to solve is already addressed.
  * **Collapsing the rail's ~200 lines of near-duplicate markup.** Each of the
    eight row shapes genuinely differs (a review row shows confidence, a Dino
    row an amount, a lead a bid date), so the shared part is the
    header-and-overflow shell rather than the row — worth extracting, not worth
    a blind rewrite of a 506-line file in the same pass as a behaviour change.
  * **h1 → PageHeader.** The chrome already renders the page `h1` from
    `nav.ts`, so the 69 page-level ones are SECOND h1s: the win is consistency,
    not a defect.
  * **aria-invalid on ~33 forms** — `field-classes.ts` already ships the
    styling, so each is a one-line prop beside an existing `setError`.
  * **~30 mutating components worth a toast**, ordered by blast radius.

Twelve commits, each deployed and asserted. **557 tests pass**, up from 528;
lint unchanged at the documented 23 throughout; `tailnet-setup.sh` green on every
deploy. ⚠ CLAUDE.md went 140,777 → 144,095 and was pruned to 141,932 — and for
the second time in one day the bloat was this session's own Recent-sessions
entry, under a heading whose stated contract is one line. The window is now ~5
days rather than a week, which is the honest trade and is recorded there.

**Done 2026-10-17 (Phase 3: the record bar stays put, and the attention engine gets a face):**

Three things, two of them long-standing complaints and one of them a surface
that should have existed since September.

**3.1 — the record bar is sticky, and you can walk the register.**

The worst thing about a populated deal: scroll to the bottom of Steelton's
181-document Documents tab and you had lost the project name, the stage and
sector chips, AND the tab bar — there was no way to another tab without
scrolling all the way back up. `main` is the scroll container
(`app/layout.tsx`) and `AppHeader` is its SIBLING, so `sticky top-0` inside
`RecordTabBar` pins to the top of the content area, just under the chrome, and
both record layouts get it from the one component.

⚠ **The negative margins are load-bearing.** `main` carries `p-5 sm:p-6`, so
without `-mx-5 sm:-mx-6 px-5 sm:px-6` and an opaque background the bar sticks
*inside* that padding and the canvas shows through a 20px strip beside and above
it as content passes under. ⚠ And `PursuitSnapshot` was `lg:sticky lg:top-4`,
which would have slid the Overview rail underneath the new bar — both now read
`--record-bar-h` from globals.css, because a magic number in a component
silently stops matching the thing it was measured against. ⚠ The More menu also
used `elev-2`, which this palette made transparent; a floating menu is exactly
what `elev-3` survived for.

The header above it deliberately still scrolls away. The full block is ~130px,
which is most of a phone screen; the tab bar alone is ~44px and carries the
navigation, which is the part a reader actually loses.

**Prev/next** closes the other gap: there was no way to get from one deal to the
next, so comparing two records meant a round trip through a 19-card grid every
time. Ordered by NAME, deliberately — a chain has to be stable and `updated_at`
reorders itself as you work — and the control says so.

⚠ **The interesting half of a prev/next control is containment, not the arrows.**
The chain is a cross-portfolio list, and §8 takes a protected project out of
every one of those: so a confidential project is not in the chain, and standing
on one renders nothing at all, because a position in a list the record has been
removed from is not a meaningful number and a chain drawn around it would leak
its neighbours' order. The filter and the TOTAL are decided together inside
`pagerPosition()` so the count can never be taken before the exclusion — the
shape §12 records as how a disclosure happens. That function is pure and in
`src/lib` precisely so the rules are asserted rather than reviewed: seven tests
cover the hidden-current case, the hidden-sibling count, a record missing from
its own register, and no-wrap at the ends.

Folded in while the opportunity layout was open: its three inline bg/text/ring
triples became tone names, so the colour ratchet dropped 326 → 324.

**3.2 — `/attention`, for an engine that never had a UI.**

`src/lib/attention.ts` has scored ten categories of falling-through-the-cracks
work 0–100 since it was written, and its consumers were an API route, the
sidebar badge, and an agent tool. The one place any of it reached a reader was
the dashboard rail, which truncated six of its eight sections at six items with
no overflow link — so **there was no way in the product to see attention item
number seven**, and the urgency score had never been shown to anyone at all.
CLAUDE.md §3 has listed the route as existing since September.

`ATTENTION_KINDS` replaces three hand-written lists: a ten-member category
union, eleven lines building the summary, and the chip row the UI would have
added as a third. The category type, the summary's field names, the counts and
the chips all derive from it, so a new kind appears everywhere or nowhere — §12
records this failure twice, most recently `/decide` shipping a kind that got a
count and no chip.

⚠ **Deliberately no `counted` flag in that registry.** What the sidebar badge
sums is a separate, narrower question that `COUNTED_ATTENTION_KINDS` already
answers, in a vocabulary that is genuinely different: the badge head-counts
`certifications` (a company record) while the registry's `expiring_compliance`
reads `compliance_items` (a project child). Two near-identical names over two
different tables. A second answer in the same row is the drift the registry
exists to prevent.

⚠ **THE REGISTRY NEEDED ITS OWN MODULE.** A client component reads it, and
`attention.ts` imports the service-role Supabase client and the leads client —
importing the registry from there drags all of that into the browser bundle.
§12 states the mirror of this rule (a helper shared with a server page must not
live in a `'use client'` file); it runs both ways.

⚠ **AND THE LIST HAD TO BE SPLIT FROM ITS URL WRAPPER TO BE VERIFIABLE.**
`useSearchParams`/`useRouter` throw *invariant expected app router to be
mounted* outside a Next request, so a component that reads them cannot be
rendered by `renderToStaticMarkup` — and §12 is explicit that a listed route is
not an answering one and that a curl behind auth returns the same redirect
either way. `AttentionList` takes the active filter as a prop and the two
navigations as callbacks; `AttentionClient` supplies them from the URL, which is
where a filter belongs because a view has to be a link.

⚠ **That render check immediately found a real bug.** `cn()` is tailwind-merge,
so the cursor row's `bg-accent` and the urgency band's `bg-critical-surface/40`
are the same utility group: the later one wins and the earlier is **deleted from
the class string entirely**. The most urgent row lost its colour at the exact
moment you navigated onto it. Invisible to `tsc`, to the build, and to a glance
at the source, where both classes are plainly present. The check counted 3
tinted rows against 4 at `now`. The cursor is a ring now — a different group,
which composes.

⚠ **And the page's first draft asserted something false with confidence.** It
derived the sidebar badge's number by filtering the engine's items to four
categories and said *"that is the number on the sidebar badge"*. It is not, and
cannot be: the badge counts milestones already OVERDUE while the engine scores
milestones approaching within 30 days, and it counts certifications where the
engine reads compliance items. **And the wrong derivation returned 3 while the
real badge is also 3** — two overdue actions plus one approaching milestone,
against one overdue task plus two expiring certifications. Checking the screen
by eye against that day's database would have confirmed the bug. §12's rule
about a worked example whose figures coincide, met in the wild on a derived
number rather than a reference case. Both quantities are now measured from
their own source and printed side by side: **badge 3, list 9**, Decide counted
separately, none of the three ever summed.

Copies `/decide`'s idioms on purpose, because that surface is this app's quality
bar: chips derived with counts, `j`/`k`/`↵`/`esc` with the shortcuts STATED
rather than discovered, an empty state that says you are done, and only the
`now` band tinted so red still signifies. The sidebar badge moved off Dashboard
onto this route — it had always counted attention, so a reader saw a number
beside "Dashboard" and had no way to reach the thing it counted.

Verified against the live database: 9 items, ranked — an overdue task at 100,
three inbound leads at 95/95/79, and Steelton's PSA closing (dated that day) at
74, each resolving to a destination that exists.

**3.3 — the rail stops naming numbers you cannot reach.**

Phase 0 gave two sections their true COUNT in plain text; this makes all five
overflows real links, including the two that had no destination in the world
until `/attention` existed. The card header links out too, because the card is
a six-per-section slice and `/attention` is the whole thing ranked. The Critical
block came off the theme-blind reds onto tone names.

⚠ **MEASURED AND DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: feeding the rail from the engine.** The
plan assumed it would be "likely a net query win" and the opposite is true —
`ddRaw` and `overdueRaw` also build the per-project CARD badges (blockingCount,
overdueCount, nextDeadline), so they cannot be removed, and adding
`computeAttention()`'s dozen queries to the most-visited page in the app would
buy ranking at a real latency cost. Only a larger restructure of the card-badge
derivation makes it pay. The single-definition problem it was meant to solve is
already addressed: the badge moved, and the page names its quantities apart.
Also left: collapsing the ~200 lines of near-duplicate section markup. Each of
the eight row shapes genuinely differs (a review row shows confidence, a Dino
row an amount, a lead a bid date), so the shared part is the header-and-overflow
shell rather than the row — worth extracting, not worth a blind rewrite of a
506-line file in the same pass as a behaviour change. Recorded as debt.

The render check now forbids the regression: every truncating section must offer
the rest, and that offer must be an **anchor** rather than text, asserted by
finding each "+N more" and checking which tag opens it.

Four commits, each deployed and asserted. 528 tests pass, up from 514; lint
unchanged at the documented 23 throughout. ⚠ CLAUDE.md reached 144,071
characters and was pruned to 140,287 — and for once the bloat WAS where the rule
said to look, because it was this session's own: three entries totalling 7,426
characters under a heading whose stated contract is one line each, with the full
versions already here.
