**Done 2026-10-17 (the redraw lands — direction C, and three things that only surface when you turn the knob):**

Richard reconsidered A, then asked for the call outright: *"I don't mind if it is
radical change. Just give me what you think will be the best for utility and to
impress anyone that looks at it."* **C**, for a reason that is not visible in a
swatch: at high density a shadow on every card turns a list of 181 documents into
mush, so C's hairline borders are what keep it readable where A's and B's
elevation starts working against them. It is also the only direction that makes
§12's "colour only for status meaning" **structural** rather than remembered —
nothing else on screen is coloured, so there is no decorative colour left to
mistake for a signal. And monochrome-with-one-accent is the register that reads
as technical and current to the people he screen-shares with.

⚠ **One deviation from the candidate, and it mattered.** Stock C set `--primary`
to near-black, which throws away the Ber Wilson blue and leaves a primary button
unfindable beside black text. Monochrome done well is **zero-chroma neutrals plus
exactly one chromatic role**, not the absence of colour — so the accent is the
brand hue at real chroma: 8.68:1 as link text, 8.44:1 for a white label on the
button, 7.02 / 7.37 in dark. The neutrals are *literally* chroma 0, asserted in
`contrast.test.ts` rather than trusted, because a faintly blue grey is invisible
in isolation and obvious in aggregate.

Values were derived from the direction block programmatically rather than
retyped, then every palette comment was rewritten: they described navy, a warm
cream hover and "soft tinted shadows read more premium than a flat box-shadow",
all false now, and §12 is explicit that a comment claiming a control that is not
there is worse than no comment. Scaffolding deleted — `directions.css`, both
preview components, both measuring scripts — which is exactly why they were
separate files; and `readDirectionTokens()` went with them rather than being left
pointing at a deleted path.

⚠ **Turning the density knob shrank 66 touch targets below 44px, in 32 files.**
`h-11` is `calc(var(--spacing) * 11)`: exactly 44px at Tailwind's 0.25rem default
and **38.7px** at this palette's 0.22rem. So the change that makes more fit on a
screen silently broke the tap target on the one device Richard actually carries,
and nothing could report it — `tsc` passes, the build passes, and it only shows
up under a thumb. A touch target is a PHYSICAL constraint and was never a spacing
step; all 66 are now absolute `h-[2.75rem]` / `min-h-[2.75rem]` /
`size-[2.75rem]`, the login logo is excluded as decorative, decorative `size-12`
icon circles are deliberately left to scale, and a ratchet keeps them that way.
The general lesson is in §12: before changing a token that feeds a `calc()`,
enumerate what else derives from it — `--spacing` alone backs every padding,
margin, gap, width and height class in the application.

⚠ **WCAG contrast cannot see surface separation at the dark end, and that is a
property of the metric.** The dark rail sat 1.03:1 from the canvas and visually
merged into the page. Dropping it from L 0.155 all the way to L 0.085 moved the
ratio to **1.031:1** — because the formula's `+0.05` offset swamps any lightness
difference down there. The instrument was wrong, not the palette. Added
`lightnessDelta()`: OKLCH lightness is perceptually uniform by construction, so
one threshold works at both ends of the range, and the tests now assert surface
separation that way. The rail recedes ΔL 0.035 below the canvas, which reads as
recessed chrome. ⚠ And the new check immediately caught the **light** theme,
where white cards on a 0.985 canvas is ΔL 0.015 — with no shadow at rest, that
left a hairline border carrying a whole screen full of cards. Canvas deepened to
0.962, ΔL 0.038. Neither of those would have been found by eye on this machine,
and both would have been found by Richard.

⚠ **A second `.dark` block, 120 lines further down `globals.css`, was winning.**
The elevation tokens are declared in the `.dark` palette block *and* again under
an "Elevation utilities" heading, so the new dark shadows sat at line 264 doing
nothing while the old deep ones kept rendering — no error, light mode changing
correctly, and the symptom reading as "dark mode just looks the same". One home
now, with a comment saying it wins. The Postgres analogue was already in §12
(`create or replace` OVERLOADS a changed signature).

⚠ **Two tests were verifying a copy of the palette.** `contrast.test.ts`
hardcoded the oklch values it asserted on, so the redraw changed every one of
them and the test **kept passing while measuring colours that no longer existed
anywhere in the codebase**. It reads `globals.css` now. The tell is a literal in
a test that also exists in source: that is a duplicate, not a fixture.

Checked before shipping, not after: only **4** elements used `elev-1`/`elev-2`
without a border or ring, and all four are filled `bg-primary` buttons that need
no shadow to read — so removing resting elevation left nothing invisible.
`.lift` still uses `elev-3`, so an interactive card now rises from flat on
hover, which suits the direction.

Measured, both themes: body 20.3 / 17.9:1, muted 8.5 / 7.1:1, accent-as-link
8.7 / 7.0:1, every status ink ≥ 5.6:1 on its own surface, rail label 15.7 /
16.8:1, ΔL card/canvas 0.038 / 0.045. 514 tests pass (up from 510; four new
assertions are about this palette's own stated rules — zero-chroma neutrals,
shadowless resting surfaces, perceptible surface separation, and no
spacing-derived tap target). Lint unchanged at 23 throughout. ⚠ **What is left is
the half no measurement reaches:** whether 12% tighter is right on the dense
screens, whether the accent stays scarce enough to mean "this is the action", and
whether the recessed rail reads as chrome. That is Richard's to say, and the
palette is one file now, so a change is cheap.

**Done 2026-10-17 (a measured token layer, and three directions to choose from):**

Richard: *"How can I enhance the user interface and the user experience to make it
truly impressive?"* Three parallel audits first — design system, high-traffic
surfaces, polish layer — and the headline finding was worth stating plainly:
**this is a high-craft codebase with systemic drift, not a sloppy one.** 396
`focus-visible:` against 0 real `focus:`. Zero `window.alert`, zero
`window.confirm`, zero empty catch blocks. 63 `loading.tsx` files containing no
spinners and no "Loading…" strings. `/decide` renders its own keyboard legend
because "the shortcuts, stated rather than discovered". `AgentChat` recovers a
dropped SSE stream by polling for the answer the server finished persisting. The
problem was never taste — it was that the good decisions are **bypassed at
scale**: `Panel` is the card but the shell is hand-written 229 times; the OKLCH
tokens are the palette but 3,489 raw palette utilities and a 572-use theme-BLIND
`slate` ramp run beside them; `field.tsx` is excellent and 12 files import it.

Richard chose: audience is both execs **plus** partners on screen-share, a third
user arriving, and the phone; dark mode is in real use; scope is everything,
systematically; and the visual identity should be **redrawn**, not merely
enforced. That last answer reorders everything, because of one dependency worth
recording: **a redraw cannot land while 3,489 colour utilities and 229
hand-rolled shells bypass the token layer.** Change `--primary` today and most
of the app does not move. The convergence work is not a rival of the redraw, it
is the mechanism by which a redraw reaches the screen at all.

**Phase 0 — three defects that were not cosmetic.**

⚠ **A containment leak wearing a UI costume.** `countAttention()` ran four
*unfiltered* head counts while `computeAttention()` filtered confidential
projects with `dropHidden()`. That badge renders in the ROOT LAYOUT on every
page for every viewer, so a protected project's overdue milestones, tasks and
critical diligence were reaching a portfolio-wide aggregate — and §8 is explicit
that containment keeps such a project out of "every aggregate". **A head count
never receives rows, so `dropHidden()` has no equivalent: the exclusion has to
happen in SQL**, and two traps meet there. A malformed `.or()` returns an empty
set with no error; and a bare `.not('project_id','in',…)` is NULL for a NULL
column and therefore not true. `milestones`, `dd_items` and `tasks` are all §4
shared children with a **nullable** `project_id`, so the naive form would have
silently discarded every opportunity-attached row. Confirmed against the live
schema, then proved against the live database inside a rolled-back transaction —
two synthetic overdue tasks, one on a hidden project and one with a null
project_id: baseline 3, **this filter 2** (hidden gone, null kept, matching
`dropHidden`'s own `!id || !hidden.has(id)` exactly), **naive bare `not in` 1**.
Re-proved end to end through PostgREST: 1 unfiltered, 0 excluding the row's own
project, 1 excluding an unrelated one. `certifications` stays unfiltered because
it is a company record with no `project_id` at all, and now says so —
and note it is a *different table* from `compliance_items`, which
`AttentionSummary` counts as `expiring_compliance` under a similar name.

⚠ **Two saves that lied.** `OpportunityStatusControl` and `InvestorStageControl`
awaited a `fetch` with no `res.ok`, no catch and no toast, so on a 500 the select
showed the new value, the spinner stopped, and `router.refresh()` then reverted it
with nothing said. Both now run on `useApiCall()` — which already encoded
status-check → the route's own error sentence → success → refresh, and was used
by exactly three files while 107 other mutating components hand-rolled it. Moved
to `src/hooks/` (NOT `src/lib`, which is where a server page would import a
`'use client'` export and throw at request time), and the optimistic value is
restored when the save actually fails.

⚠ **A badge that under-reported itself by construction.** `NeedsAttention`
summed `.length` of three lists the dashboard had **already sliced to 6** at
`dashboard/page.tsx:366-369`, while the true total (`reviewCount`) was passed in
beside them and ignored — a badge cap inventing a third quantity. Rendering the
real component with 20 review / 14 milestone / 9 diligence rows now reads **24**
rather than the old capped **19**, the section headers read 20/14/9 rather than
6/6/6, and the two sections that truncated in silence say how many they hide. It
also no longer adds the review queue: that is the Decide backlog, counted by
`countDecideItems()`, and folding it in is the exact mistake `HealthPanel`'s own
docblock records making once already (the tile read 197 while the sidebar read 1).

Also: `dashboard/loading.tsx` was animating an 84px radial health gauge removed
from `HealthPanel` on 2026-07-03 plus a stat-card row that is not on the page, so
every load animated one layout and snapped to another. And `global-error.tsx` did
not exist — the only boundary that catches the ROOT LAYOUT failing, which matters
precisely because that layout awaits three database reads on every page; styled
inline on purpose, since the layout is what imports `globals.css`.

**Phase 1 — the token layer, measured rather than chosen.**

Four status tones (positive / caution / critical / info), each with three slots:
`ink` for text, `surface` for a tinted block, `edge` for the ring. A new pure
module `src/lib/ui/contrast.ts` converts OKLCH → OKLab → linear sRGB → sRGB and
computes WCAG contrast, verified first against values whose answer is known
(white/black = 21.00 exactly, a mid grey neutral in all three channels,
out-of-gamut clamping rather than wrapping) — because a colour conversion that is
subtly wrong produces plausible numbers and would certify an unreadable palette.
It also confirmed the palette's **existing** documented claims: `--primary` on
white is 6.5:1 as its comment says, `--muted-foreground` 6.1:1.

Every tone was then tuned against the surface it actually sits on. Light:
ink/card 5.20–6.52, ink-on-its-own-surface 4.74–5.87. Dark: 7.38–10.89 and
5.76–8.03. `caution` had to come down from L 0.55 to L 0.52 to clear 4.5:1 on its
own surface at all — yellow always does. ⚠ **Found while measuring: in LIGHT mode
a tinted surface reads at just 1.02–1.06:1 against the canvas** (0.976 vs
0.964–0.968), where on a white card it is 1.10:1. So off a card the ring is the
only thing giving the block an edge — it is load-bearing, not decoration, and
there is now a test saying so, because that is exactly the kind of thing a later
session "simplifies" away.

The dark values are **real second values**. `--chart-1..5` are byte-identical in
`:root` and `.dark` and only get away with it because nothing renders them yet;
a test now asserts no status token can repeat that. `--critical` is deliberately
**not** `--destructive`: a status and a destructive action are different
questions, and aliasing them is how a Save button turns red.

**Tone names, derived from the corpus rather than invented.** Measured 46
distinct bg/text/ring triples over 192 uses in 12 files, resolving to 14 hue
families — slate 34, emerald 27, amber 26, blue 17, red 16, then violet 15,
indigo 12, cyan 9, sky 9, teal 7, rose 7, orange 5. The first five carry meaning
in every map that uses them; the rest only ever mean "a different kind from that
one", so those stay Tailwind classes with both halves explicit rather than
earning 21 CSS tokens nobody can name. `neutral` maps the **34 theme-blind slate
uses** onto `bg-muted / text-muted-foreground / ring-border`, which is the single
biggest dark-mode correctness win available and is one line. `chipTone()` throws
on an unknown name (§12). `Chip` now accepts `Tone | (string & {})`, so all 192
existing call sites keep working untouched and conversion goes one file at a
time; narrowing that to `Tone` later makes `tsc` enumerate the stragglers, which
is the only completion proof worth having.

**The type ladder is tokenised at Tailwind's exact defaults.** Only `--text-xs`
and `--text-sm` had ever been tokenised, so the five sizes above them lived
nowhere and the scale could not be adjusted in one place — which is why the top
end reads unconsidered (69 `h1` elements in 25 spellings). ⚠ **The first draft of
this changed the numbers** — `text-2xl` 24 → 27px — which is a visual change to
every heading and would have destroyed the one property making Phase 1 safe to
deploy mid-week. Caught and reverted: all ten values verified field-by-field
against `node_modules/tailwindcss/theme.css`, identical including the `calc()`
line-height form. Tokenising is structural; moving the numbers is a design
decision and belongs to the phase where a direction gets chosen. Same discipline
for motion: `--dur` was set to **200ms**, the value `.lift` already hardcoded, so
repointing it moved nothing and the token gained a real consumer.

**`/settings/ui`** renders every tone, type step, elevation, button state and
callout in **both themes side by side**, the right column wrapped in `.dark` —
which is all the theme switch is, so it is genuinely the dark theme rather than a
mock-up of one. The contrast ratios are computed **at render** from
`globals.css` through the same module the tests assert on, so the page cannot
claim a ratio the palette does not have. URL-only, in `TITLE_EXTRAS`, in no nav
group: a style guide is an instrument, not a working surface.

**Conventions as ratcheting tests.** `src/lib/ui/conventions.test.ts` asserts
each count is at or below a recorded baseline — never equality, because two
sessions share this repo and a test demanding perfection would block the other
one's unrelated work while a test forbidding regression never does. Zero-tolerance
invariants: no `focus:`, no `window.alert`/`confirm`, **no `loading.tsx` at a
route group root** (§12's rule made mechanical for the first time — it had
already cost the hours once as prose), no Tailwind class built by interpolation.
Ratchets recorded: card shell 145 at `rounded-lg` + 84 at `rounded-xl`, raw
`shadow-*` 15, local input-class constants 39, `text-[11px]` 256, raw colour
pairs 326, `slate-*` 572.

⚠ **Three findings from writing those checks, all of them about the checks.**
First, **the counts must strip comments**: a naive grep for `focus:` returns 2
hits and *both are docblocks explaining why it is banned*, and the only
`window.confirm` in the repo is the line recording that `confirm-dialog.tsx`
replaced it — so a ratchet on the raw numbers could never reach zero and would be
permanently ignored. Real usage of both is zero; the audit's "2 focus:" was the
rule's own documentation. Second, **the scan counted itself**:
`conventions.test.ts` holds every banned pattern as a regex literal, which
reported three false regressions on the first run, all its own source — test
files are now excluded. Third, `(?:bg|text|ring|border)-\$\{` matched
`` `pepper-text-${Date.now()}` `` in `notify/text.ts`, a temp **filename**, which
is §12's own trap about a substring matching any word that contains it (the one
that put `title` inside `Entitlements`); the pattern now requires the prefix to
start a token rather than end one.

⚠ **And the ratchet caught its own author within minutes of existing.** The style
guide's elevation swatches pushed the card-shell count 84 → 86. They cannot be
`Panel`s — `Panel` bakes in `elev-1`, so a swatch demonstrating `elev-2` would
show two elevations at once — so that one file is exempt **by name, with the
reason recorded**. Raising the baseline was the easy move and would have retired
the ratchet on day one.

Both new test groups were verified to **fail** when the palette is deliberately
broken (paling an ink; making dark identical to light), because a check that
cannot fail is not a check.

**Phase 2.1 — three directions, for Richard to choose.**

⚠ **The enabling discovery: Tailwind v4 emits every utility as a `var()`
resolved at USE time**, confirmed by reading the built CSS — `.text-sm` →
`var(--text-sm)`, `.rounded-xl` → `calc(var(--radius) * 1.4)`, `.elev-1` →
`var(--elev-1)`, and `.p-4` → `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)`. That last one is the
surprise: **`--spacing` (0.25rem) is a single multiplier behind every padding,
margin and gap in the application**, so DENSITY is a token like any other. A
whole visual direction is therefore ~30 declarations in a scoped selector, not a
rewrite — which is what made showing three of them tractable at all.

  * **A — Institutional.** The navy lineage sharpened: cooler neutrals, 6px
    radius, elevation cut almost to hairlines so the borders carry the
    structure, spacing in 6%. The most information per screen.
  * **B — Editorial.** Warm paper canvas, 14px radius, real layered elevation,
    10% more air, type scale a notch up. Best for the narrative brief and long
    diligence text; costs roughly a fifth of the rows per screen.
  * **C — Engineered.** Near-monochrome with one accent, 4px radius, **no shadow
    at all** on resting surfaces, tightest spacing. Colour can only ever mean
    status because nothing else is coloured. Densest on a phone, and the most
    legible of the three — body text 20.3:1 light / 17.9:1 dark.

All three were measured before being shown, through the same module Phase 1's
tests use (`scripts/measure-directions.mts`), and all three clear every
threshold in both themes on the first pass: body 16.3–20.3:1, muted 6.9–8.5:1,
every status ink ≥ 5.14:1 on its own surface.

The preview is a **real record**, not tidy fixture data: Steelton —
Cleveland-Cliffs (PA), capture stage, 99% win probability, 181 live documents,
PSA closing dated 17 Oct 2026 against Ber Wilson's 1 Nov revision, the
Cleveland-Cliffs / Paul Finan / JPMorgan / 4% broker facts, and the 900 MW
capacity flag — all read out of the live database. So each direction is judged
against a title that wraps, an address that truncates, a capture value that is
genuinely unset, and a figure that must not read as a failed render. The
**current** look renders alongside as the baseline, because three options with
nothing to measure against is a mood board.

⚠ The selector shape is load-bearing: the theme class and the direction
attribute sit on the **same element** (`[data-direction='a']:not(.dark)` /
`.dark[data-direction='a']`). Written as a descendant selector, the light rule
would also match inside `.dark` and the dark column would silently render the
light palette — the exact failure a side-by-side view exists to catch.

⚠ And `scripts/verify-directions.tsx` exists for **token purity**, not for "does
it render". A single `text-amber-700` in the preview would sit unchanged across
all three columns while everything around it moved, so the screen would show
three directions that differ less than they really do — a mock-up pretending to
be a measurement. Nothing else catches it: it builds, it typechecks, it looks
plausible. Verified to fail when a hardcoded colour is deliberately planted.

⚠ **The ratchet caught me a second time, and this time it was right and I was
wrong:** the preview hand-rolled the card shell five times. `Panel` is exactly
`rounded-xl border border-border bg-card elev-1`, every class token-backed, so it
varies per direction correctly and there was never a reason to imitate it.
Converted, and the count fell back under baseline on its own.

`directions.css` is deliberately its own file: when a direction is chosen, its
values move into `:root` / `.dark` and the file is deleted along with the two
rejects, so the cleanup is `rm` rather than a careful excision from a file two
sessions share.

Four commits, each deployed and asserted (`tailnet-setup.sh` + `lmstudio-check.sh`
green; the LM Studio check reports the box paging at 197MB free / 15.7GB swap,
pre-existing and unrelated). 510 tests pass, up from 479; lint unchanged at the
documented 23 problems throughout. ⚠ **Still open for Richard: the direction
choice.** Phases 3–5 of the plan (sticky record header, `/attention` as the UI
for an engine that has none, the mechanical colour and card-shell retrofit, nav
IA, URL state, `BriefMarkdown` links and agent citations) all follow from it.

⚠ Noted in passing, not fixed: `src/lib/security/confidential.ts` carries a
comment saying `npm run gen-types` is a disabled stub, which §4 contradicts — it
works and covers 104 of 104 tables. That is §12's "a workaround's recorded reason
must be re-tested before it is inherited" shape, and six modules once grew 1,290
lines of workaround around exactly that note.

**Done 2026-10-17 (the ports under the proxy, and the matcher under the queue):**

Richard: *"what can we improve?"* — so the session began by measuring the live box
rather than reading §13, and most of what §13 worries about turned out to be fine.
All 26 launchd agents had run that day, 456 tests passed, backups were nightly and
offsite (the alarming `backup.err.log` was stale from 1 October), both models were
resident at the documented 131072/parallel-1 with no orphaned `llama-server`, and the
1,203 `fetch failed` lines in `platform.err.log` were ONE contiguous outage block
rather than an ongoing fault. The `note:`-id Gmail bug found on 10-14 no longer fires.
Two things were genuinely wrong, and both were invisible to every check that existed.

---

**1. "Tailnet-only" was a claim about the proxy, not about the ports underneath it.**

`tailscale serve` was configured exactly right — `:443 -> 127.0.0.1:3000`,
`:8443 -> localhost:8000`, both "tailnet only" — and §2, §8 and §13 all described the
platform as tailnet-only on the strength of it. Measured from the box's own LAN
address, `192.168.86.38`: **Postgres (5432), the Supabase gateway (8000/8443), the app
(3000) and LM Studio (1234) were all listening on `*` and all answering.** §8 says
plainly that middleware is the auth boundary, because app traffic uses the service role
and RLS is defence-in-depth only — so any device on that network reached PostgREST
underneath the gate, and the model server was a free unauthenticated LLM to the
building. Nothing had ever reported it because every existing check tested the proxy.

⚠ **The obvious fix is the wrong layer, and it cost an outage.** Binding the CONTAINER
to `127.0.0.1` in `docker-compose` was tried first — and lima only forwards a guest port
it can SEE on `0.0.0.0`, so the host lost Kong entirely: `curl` exit 56, the app unable
to reach its own database, `supabase-rest` unhealthy. Reverted inside two minutes
(`docker-compose.lean.yml.bak-20261017`, service restored, data intact at 19 projects /
10,033 chunks) and fixed at the forwarder instead. The container must keep publishing on
0.0.0.0 *inside* the guest; it is the HOST side that gets narrowed. An abandoned
`deploy/supabase-compose.override.yml` was deleted rather than shipped — a file carrying
"INSTALL TO:" instructions for an approach that takes production down is worse than no
file, and the dead end is recorded in the header of the one that works.

Also found while reading the compose files: the live stack is `docker-compose.lean.yml`
with **no supavisor container at all**, so the first override was written against ports
the running system does not even publish.

Three layers hold the fix and **not one of them is in this repo**:

| port | layer | file |
|---|---|---|
| 5432 / 8000 / 8443 | lima's catch-all forward, `hostIP: 0.0.0.0` | `~/.colima/_lima/_config/override.yaml` (kept at `deploy/colima-lima-override.yaml`) |
| 3000 | `next start` binds `::` | `deploy/com.berwilson.platform.plist`, `-H 127.0.0.1` |
| 1234 | LM Studio's "Serve on Local Network" | `lms server start --bind 127.0.0.1` |

lima's global `_config/override.yaml` was chosen deliberately over editing the generated
`lima.yaml`, which colima rewrites on every start. ⚠ Worth knowing: the override is
merged at RUNTIME and never appears in the generated file, so `lima.yaml` still reads
`hostIP: 0.0.0.0` and looks untouched — the proof is in the host agent log,
`guestAddr 0.0.0.0:5432 -> hostAddr 127.0.0.1:5432`, and in the listeners themselves.

Both deploy scripts now assert it, because all three layers come back on an upgrade, a
reinstall or a GUI click: `tailnet-setup.sh` §6 fails on any non-loopback listener
across the six ports, and `lmstudio-check.sh` §5 asserts the bind and `--fix` repairs
it. That `--fix` reload is now gated on a new `MODEL_BAD` flag, so a binding-only drift
no longer pays for a 22GB model round trip. **The §6 assertion was itself tested
against a deliberate `0.0.0.0:6543` listener** — it names the address and exits 1.

Verified after: all six ports refuse from 192.168.86.38 while loopback answers; tailnet
443 and 8443 still serve; kong REST with the anon key returns 200; models still resident
at 131072/parallel 1. What remains on all interfaces is macOS's own — AirPlay (5000,
7000), Continuity (63001) and lima's DNS (53).

**And the deploy footgun beside it.** CLAUDE.md line 39 recorded
`deploy/deploy-to-studio.sh` as retired when the Studio became the repo, while §2
(line 68) and §7 (line 308) BOTH still named it as *the* deploy command — two of three
places pointing the next session at a script that would ssh to this box from this box,
`rsync -az --delete` the repo over itself and `scp` a `.env.local` over the live one.
Guarded rather than deleted, because a deleted file takes its warning with it: it now
refuses on `LocalHostName == Richards-Mac-Studio` and prints the real runbook. Both
CLAUDE.md lines corrected.

**2. The intake queue could not offer a merge, and that is why nobody worked it.**

`/decide` has carried a "Select the N Ber AI is sure about" button since 09-24 and it
has **never been pressed**. The measurements killed two plausible explanations before
finding the real one:

- *Mis-calibration?* No. Of 106 "dismissals" in the table's history, **102 were the
  model's OWN `disposition='dismiss'`**, which `/decide` skips by design. The human
  verdict history is 8 confirmed and ~4 dismissed — there is barely any human behaviour
  to calibrate against.
- *Duplicate fear?* No. The confident block holds no exact-title duplicates;
  `dedupe.ts` is doing its job.

The real cause was one matcher. `findMatchingProjects` built `match_candidates` — the
CLOSED LIST the pre-decide model must choose a merge target from — and it searched
**`projects` only**. `MatchCandidate` had no `opportunity_id`/`opportunity_name` field
at all, so none of the 7 live opportunities could ever be a merge target. ⚠ And
`resolveMergeTarget` had been reading exactly those two fields since the day it was
written: **a branch nothing could ever satisfy, with no test and no error**, because an
unreachable branch reports nothing. Its name bar was trigram at threshold 0.3, the exact
cliff §12 documents.

A model that cannot NAME the record proposes a new one. Measured 2026-10-16: **110 of
126 pending sessions proposed CREATING a record, at 0.93 average confidence**, against a
register of 19 projects and 7 opportunities — so pressing the button would have made
~105 projects. 53 of those sessions were a month old.

The fix already existed, wired to one surface. `resolveMeetingTarget`'s bars 2 and 3
were never a meetings question: they read BOTH tables, asking for an exact unique name
and then a single identity-bearing word, with an ambiguity refusal that names the
records that collided. Extracted whole to **`src/lib/records/resolve.ts`**; the meetings
path keeps bar 1 (a title a human filed before) and delegates the rest. Not forked.

⚠ **Measuring it on the real queue is what corrected it.** The first run produced 21
matches and reading them found **three wrong — all on a word that QUALIFIES a noun
rather than naming a deal**, which is the compass-direction argument again:
*"General Stillwell … Bldg 1520"* matched *"DFCM Camp Williams Bldg. 4140"* (two
different buildings on two different bases), and both *"Golden Rock"* and the DoD
*"Golden Dome White Paper Pursuit"* took *Alaska Golden Summit*. `building` was already
stopworded; the **abbreviation** was not. Added `bldg`/`bldgs`/`golden` and then proved
nothing was lost — the real Englert Mining thread still reaches that record on `summit`.
The matched WORD is now carried out of the resolver into `match_reasons`, because
`0.55` tells a reader nothing and `record_name_shared_word:steelton` is checkable.

After that correction, over the live backlog: **24 of 113 sessions got better
candidates, 15 gained one where there had been none, 7 reached an opportunity for the
first time, and ZERO lost a candidate** — the word bar only adds. Two show the cliff
outright: trigram had ranked *Heber Development* (0.51) and *American Energy Rail
Corridor — Community Development* (0.61) **above** the right answer, *DUBHES Helper*, on
the words "Development" and "Community Development".

⚠ **A prompt-version bump was the wrong tool, and `match_candidates` is written by the
SWEEP, not by predecide.** Re-running the model over the old rows would have re-read the
same stale candidate list and reached the same conclusion. And predecide only revisits a
session whose verdict is null or whose `prompt_version` is stale — all 118 carried the
current `intake-predecide-2.0`, so a bump would have re-decided all 118 to re-derive 94
answers that could not change, at ~90 minutes of exclusive LM Studio time.
`scripts/restage-intake-candidates.mts` recomputes candidates with **no model call**,
and `--redecide` nulls the verdict on only the rows that can actually move — a predicate
derived from the data (candidates carrying a `record_name_` reason, verdict still
`create`), never remembered, which makes it idempotent.

**The result, end to end: 19 sessions re-decided, 9 of them flipped to `merge`, 1 to
dismiss, 0 failed. Merges in the queue went 7 → 16**, and every one is a pairing a human
would recognise — Steelton, three Helper threads, two Myton, two West Wendover,
Stockton, Box Elder Quantum, and four onto OPPORTUNITIES that were structurally
unreachable that morning: Elite Solutions, GridEdge, Zenthium Partnership and Alaska
Golden Summit.

**Found on the way:** `resolveMergeTarget` **threw** on a null element in the jsonb
candidate array — `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` — which would have 500'd
the merge button on a human's click. Caught by the first test ever written for that
function, in the same commit that made its opportunity branch reachable.

**Verified:** 472 tests (456 → 472), all passing. ⚠ The stopword tests were checked for
TEETH rather than assumed: deliberately dropping three words from the list fails exactly
3 of them, and restoring brings 472/472 back. (A first attempt at that probe reported
"0 failures" and was itself wrong — it grepped for TAP's `not ok` against a reporter
that prints `✖`, and its `python3 replace` printed success without asserting the edit
had applied.) `scripts/verify-record-resolver.mts` exercises 18 real queue titles
against the LIVE register, 18/18, including both §12 pairs — *Eagle Mountain
Development* must NOT take Myton Development, *Delta, Utah Campus* must reach Delta
Industrial Campus — and the controls that must stay unresolved. The restage is
idempotent on both halves. `/decide` renders with a clean console. ⚠ Its rows are not
ARIA-exposed, so the accessibility tree reads `main` as empty and a screenshot is the
only honest check.

**Deliberately not done:** the economics backlog (`deal_economics` still has 0 rows, so
0 of 26 records carry a capture value and the pipeline reads $0) — real, but data entry
against a working engine rather than a build task. And a `/decide` lane for the 208
unfiled deal-relevant threads: this change should reduce that number as a by-product, so
it wants re-measuring before anything is built for it.

Richard: *"We don't have a COO. Get rid of traces of Tarek or Nancy or anyone else.
The company is just Eric and Richard right now."*

**What was there.** Measured before touching anything, because the question is which
of these are CLAIMS about who we are and which are RECORDS of what happened — and the
two deserve opposite treatment.

| Where | What it said |
|---|---|
| `org_people` | `Tarek "Rick" Nosseir — Director`, leadership tier, detail reading *"joint CFO oversight with Nancy"*. Plus Amy Clark (Director, Real Estate), Brooke Stonebraker (Director of Underwriting), and Colton / Rocky / Dr Gary Samuelson / Doc Elements attached to four SPV nodes |
| `project_players` | Tarek on Myton Rail as *"New COO overseeing operations, strategy, and international expansion"*; Nancy on Myton Rail, and on Stockton as *"Ber Wilson Evaluator"* |
| `parties` | a bare `Tarek` stub with no email or phone, and `Nancy Thunnel — ASEA, Advisor`. Separately, four contacts carried `company = 'Ber Wilson'`: Jerrod Ewell, Jerry Chizmadia, Jonathan Sipe, Taylor Scalley |
| `20260718000001_org_structure.sql` | still SEEDS Nancy as Chairwoman / interim CFO, Tarek as COO and Dennis Allen as a director — fires on any rebuilt database, so all three come back |
| `src/lib/curator/contacts.ts`, `fold.ts` | two comments stating Tarek **is** our COO, used as the standing justification for the `namesOurselves` rule |
| `scripts/measure-rolodex.mts` | *"Tarek is COO and corresponds from a gmail address"* |
| `docs/OPEN-ITEMS.md` | a live row instructing a future session to **put Tarek's address on his contact row** so `internalAddresses()` would treat him as one of ours |
| `signatures.test.ts` / `MeetingForm.tsx` | Nancy's real gmail and real phone as a test fixture; *"e.g. Nancy Norton"* as a form placeholder |

`team_members` was already clean (Eric, Richard, Pepper), and `personnel` is empty.

**⚠ THE DOCS WERE WORSE THAN THE DATA.** A stale row in `org_people` is a wrong chart
somebody looks at once. The open-items row was an instruction to a future session to
*wire a departed COO into `internalAddresses()`* — which is the function that decides
whose correspondence is internal, and therefore ingested rather than scored. Of the
eight places the names lived, the three that would have caused new wrong work were all
prose: the open-items row, and the two code comments offering Tarek as the reason the
`namesOurselves` test exists. §12 already says a workaround's recorded reason must be
re-tested before it is inherited; this is the same failure with a person in it.

**The split.** Richard's calls, taken before any delete: strip **every** name from the
chart but keep the three vacant seats (they are roles, not people); **archive** the two
contact rows rather than delete them, and keep the correspondence.

Kept, deliberately: **82 email threads, 16 commitments, 2 meetings and 245 indexed
passages** name these people. They really did correspond, and that is a true record.
What went is only the claim that they work here. Archiving (`status = 'archived'`) is
the app's own soft delete — the same thing the Archive button on `/contacts` does — so
it is one `update` to reverse.

**`20261016000001_roster_is_two_people.sql`.** Deletes every NAMED `org_people` row
other than the two executives, matched **by name rather than by id** so it also catches
the seeded copies on a rebuilt database, where the ids are freshly generated. Drops the
three `project_players` roles, archives the two `parties` rows, and clears
`company = 'Ber Wilson'` off the four contacts that were never employees (the contact
itself is untouched — only the employer claim). Applied: `DELETE 7`, `DELETE 3`,
`UPDATE 2`, `UPDATE 4`.

⚠ **`parties` AND `project_players` CARRY NO AUDIT TRIGGER** — only `org_people` does —
so `activity_log` cannot recover any of this. The full row snapshots are written into
the migration file as comments, which makes git the undo. That is also why the four
`company` clears were done as an UPDATE of one field rather than anything broader.

⚠ **The seed migration was left alone.** It is history, it has been applied, and the
new migration runs after it in both directions — on the live database now, and on a
rebuild after the seed re-inserts. Editing an applied migration to make the past look
different is how a rebuild and a running database stop agreeing.

**What survived and why.** The `namesOurselves` test itself stays: `berwilsonllc@outlook.com`
signs *"Ericson Tua'one"* and is on no `team_members` row, so a display name carrying
our own company name is still the structural tell. Its docblock now says so — a roster
is a list of logins, not a list of addresses — instead of citing a COO who does not
exist. The `EVP/COO` **persona** in the four AI prompts is untouched: that is how the
agent is told to think, not a claim about anybody's job.

**Verified:** `tsc` clean, 456 tests pass, `next build` exits 0 (unpiped, per §12).
Chart re-read after the migration: leadership is Ericson Tua'one and Richard White, the
three vacant director seats remain, no SPV node carries a name. Every `staff` render
path was already guarded by `staff.length > 0` and `staffByNode.get(id) ?? []`, so the

- `scripts/measure-rolodex.mts` — the reciprocity question and the info@ question.
- A throwaway fill-rate read over all 40 registry columns.

Both premises were wrong, in opposite directions.

- **The real gap is the rolodex.** `parties.phone` blank on **82 of 97** — the

**What was built.** `src/lib/curator/contacts.ts` — the reciprocity sweep, and the one
pass that creates a record. The gate is a rule, not a score: `pipeline='deal'`, one of
the two executives must have personally SENT a message on the thread, and the person
must have written too. `info@` is unreachable by construction rather than by a flag,

notes — which land in the deal pipeline as ordinary threads — cannot read as a reply.
A confidential project's threads are skipped for the reason `run.ts` gives: what makes
unattended writing safe is that every change is reported, and the note is an outbound
channel a protected deal may never reach.

`applyPeople` gained `allowCreate` as a TARGET rather than being forked (§12), so
every guard that makes it safe runs first — a creation only happens after `matchParty`
has declined, which is what stops it duplicating a contact under another spelling.

⚠ **A DETAIL BELONGS TO THE MESSAGE IT WAS IN, NOT TO THE THREAD — and the first
version shipped the opposite.** It searched a whole thread for the target's address and
took the nearest number, guarded by "only if this address is the closest one", which
sounds sufficient and is not: a rendered thread puts a `To:` line directly under every
message heading, so a signature's number at the FOOT of one message is nearer the NEXT
message's recipient than its own sender. The live dry run offered Eric's own cell
`385-436-6519` as the phone number for **Merlin Corbin, Ocean Patel, Amy Clark and
Courtney**, spread one `410-991-1469` across three unrelated people, and gave
Christopher Johnson the number Mark Welsko had been seen with seven times. Splitting on
the `### <ts> — <From>` headings and attributing only to the SENDER took it from 14
recoveries with 7 wrong to 7 with 0 wrong; Merlin got his own `949-637-7555`. Two
further guards were still needed: a number two addresses claim goes to the one with
strictly more sightings and the other gets nothing (a quoted forward puts somebody
else's signature inside your message), and a number belonging to one of OURS is never
written onto a counterparty — that leak is a NUMBER, not an address, so
`internalAddresses()` cannot see it and the set has to be read off the directory.

⚠ **`c.isOrg ?? nameTest` LET A MODEL'S `is_organization: false` SILENTLY DISABLE THE
RULE.** `??` only falls through on null, so a summary asserting "this is a person"
skipped the name test entirely — and `Wallace Incorporated`, `Dino Plumbing HVAC &
Electrical` and a `Consulate of Israel` desk were each about to be created as PEOPLE by
a pass that had an explicit rule against exactly them. The model's flag is the
unreliable half here, so it may convict and never acquit: the tests are now additive,
and where no flag exists at all the rule is to SKIP rather than guess.

⚠ **`noteIsEmpty` IGNORED CURATION ENTIRELY.** It tested the reader's own work —
obligations, tasks, meetings, cracks, the queue — so a morning whose only news was that
Pepper had changed records or added contacts sent **no note at all**, and the change
went unreported. That is the one failure mode the whole unattended-write design may not
have (§11, and `curator/run.ts`'s header). Her open questions were in the same hole.
Fixed, and a `CONTACTS I ADDED FROM MAIL YOU REPLIED TO` section added to the note —
read from `parties` by the `auto-contact` tag, because a creation is not a field write
and `record_field_provenance` cannot see one.

Richard asked for a calculation layer: read the correspondence, populate the deal details and the
revenue opportunities, and build the formulas in — what a data center or power opportunity is worth
to Ber Wilson under the TensorIQ Master Strategic Partnership Agreement, plus a sanity check on the
project economics TensorIQ presents. He supplied a long specification of the fee schedule, the role
protection stages, and TensorIQ's own project model, with two validation cases to reproduce.

**The first thing measured was whether the specification was true**, because it arrived as prose and
the authority is a signed document. Both are in the corpus: the executed
`BerWilson_TensorIQ_Master_Strategic_Partnership_Agreement_v6.5` (147,079 characters) and
`PCA_01_Steelton_PA_signed`, signed by Jonathan Houk and Sterling Orr on 2026-10-12. Schedule 1 and
Sections 8.5 / 8.7 / 8.9 / 8.12 / 9.4 check out line for line — the marginal tiers, the 7.0% EPCM and
12.0% converted Scope B rates, the 9.0% aggregate fee cap and its reduction order, the 0.5%
preconstruction fee, the 1.5% utility coordination fee, the 10/25/40% protection stages, the
$50k/$150k per-MW fallback and the 3.0%/2.5% cap. Nothing in the paste had drifted. **So the
agreement's own $1.0B fee illustration became the test**, and `fees.test.ts` now asserts every line
of that contract table: A $26.0M on $700M, B $14.0M at 7%, C $6.0M, D $30.0M, preconstruction $5.0M,
total $81.0M (8.1%), and the converted case at $91.0M with Scope A–D at 8.6% still inside the cap.

⚠ **THE ILLUSTRATION CANNOT DISTINGUISH THE PRECONSTRUCTION FEE BASE FROM TPC, BECAUSE ITS NUMBERS
COINCIDE.** The base is "estimated Cost of the Work for the engaged Scope", and in the illustration
A+B+C is $700M + $200M + $100M = $1,000M, which happens to equal the $1.0B TPC exactly. Both
readings give $5.0M, so the worked example is no evidence of which is right — and on any real phase
carrying soft costs inside TPC, or with land excluded from it, the two diverge. Implemented off the
scope costs, with a test that moves TPC to $1.2B and asserts the fee does not follow it.

⚠ **STEELTON'S PLANNED IT CAPACITY AND ITS OWN GRID ROADMAP DO NOT MEET.** PCA item 3 reads "Planned
IT Capacity and phasing — Up to 900 MW", and the MSPA defines Planned IT Capacity as IT load, so the
basis is contractually settled: 900 IT MW needs about **1,260 utility MW** at PUE 1.4, and 1,080 even
at immersion's 1.2. But the same record's Grid Expansion Roadmap reads Phase 1 300 MW / Phase 2
500 MW / Phase 3 700 MW, PPL's interconnection "supports up to 300 MW" today, the existing
configuration is 120 MW, and $135,000,000 at closing buys the first 120 MW. Either the 900 is utility
load mislabelled as Planned IT Capacity in a signed agreement, or the project needs roughly 560 MW
more than its own roadmap plans for. Nothing in the corpus resolves it, and it is the single most
consequential open question on the deal — a factor-of-1.4 error on every fee, cost and return below.

⚠ **AND SEEDING THE PHASES FROM THAT ROADMAP IS HOW THE ERROR PROPAGATES.** Entered as increments,
300 / 500 / 700 is 1,500 MW against a 900 MW cap, and every fee downstream inherits it — the smoke
test produced $1.40B of fees that way before anything noticed. Nothing in the chain was watching, so
`assess.ts` now refuses a phase list summing past the project's own capacity and says the figures are
probably cumulative rather than incremental.

**TensorIQ's model was reimplemented beside the contract half and deliberately kept at a different
confidence.** The tearsheet Sterling Orr sent at 00:03 on 10-15 (`TLH_74MW_14OCT2026`) was already
indexed in `thread_chunks` — 27 passages, 52,584 characters — and publishes every intermediate
figure, so `sizing.test.ts` reproduces it rather than trusting the paste: 3,384 servers, effective
overhead ×1.47, **52.9 IT MW**, **74.0 utility MW**, 177,688 sqft, 3,203,145 available GPU-hours per
utility MW-year, **$3.26B** hardware at $120K/GPU and $61.6M per IT MW, **$586M** direct facility and
**$710.3M** loaded at 21.1% — the last to within 0.03%. The annual stack reproduces too: $127.9M
lease, $58.4M power, $74.0M opex, $186.2M rack rent, $260.3M total.

⚠ **STERLING'S "~$10.5M PER MW" IS THE RE DEVCO FIGURE, NOT THE FACILITY FIGURE.** His covering note
said to extrapolate from the example at that rate. The loaded facility is **$9.6M per utility MW**;
the RE DevCo, which adds property at $1M/MW, is **$10.6M**. Land purchase price is excluded from Total
Project Cost by Section 8.6, so extrapolating a Cost of the Work base at $10.5M/MW quietly puts
excluded land into a Schedule 1 fee base. A test asserts which of the two figures the number is nearer.

⚠ **WE CANNOT RECONSTRUCT THEIR 14.9x MOIC / 72% IRR, AND DO NOT PRETEND TO.** Their expense stack
reproduces to within 1%, but the equity base does not: $149.4M against $3.97B of capex is under 4%,
and it depends on the drawdown timing of a ~$1.9B customer prepayment, the tax and depreciation
schedule, the community-benefit charge and the IT sustaining reserve — none of which we were sent. At
that leverage small changes in those internals move MOIC by multiples. Every scenario therefore
carries the divergence as a caveat naming their published figure beside ours. **A reconstruction
presented as their number would be the worst of both.**

⚠ **THREE INCONSISTENCIES FOUND IN THE MODEL ITSELF.** (1) The stated power blend does not produce
the stated rate: 80% grid at $0.09 and 20% behind-the-meter at $0.18 blends to **$0.108/kWh**, against
the $0.09 used — a 16.7% understatement of a $58.4M/year line, about $11.7M. (2) The RE DevCo's
construction loan-to-cost and permanent loan-to-value are **both 65%**, which makes leverage exactly
multiple-neutral, since (value − 0.65·value) ÷ (cost − 0.65·cost) reduces to value ÷ cost. Levered
and unlevered multiples are identical by construction, so a published 5.0x levered against ~2.0x
unlevered cannot come from this capital structure. (3) At an 8% cap rate the permanent loan ($1.02B)
**exceeds total cost** ($784M), so the refinance returns every dollar of equity and $235M besides —
a result produced entirely by the cap-rate assumption, not by the development. Also corrected a basis
error of our own on the way: striking the RE lease on improvements net of land gave NOI of $113.7M
against the published $125M, and on total cost it gives $125.5M and a $1.569B value, matching both.

⚠ **AND A LISTED ROUTE IS NOT AN ANSWERING ONE.** `/mspa` is admin-only by default-deny, so a curl
returns 307 exactly as `/calc` does — which proves middleware works and nothing else, and the Chrome

directly for all 26 records across three input modes — **78 renders** — and asserts no `NaN`,
`undefined` or `Infinity` reaches the markup, since a bare em dash reads as a failed render and `NaN`
reads as a number. Getting it to run cost three tooling failures none of which `tsc` or `next build`
can see: Node's own TypeScript handling does not do JSX, so a `.tsx` import dies with

`require()` the component (`ERR_REQUIRE_CYCLE_MODULE`); and the component importing from the

imports directly. It is a `.tsx` run under tsx, importing specific modules, with default exports added
to `assess.ts` and `params.ts` for the same reason `register.ts` already had one.

**A window, because scope and relevance are different questions.** The header's rule stands —

not a work corpus that happens to be old: 59 of the 111 (~31 of the 45.7 hours, the longest a

instruction nobody re-tests is how a repo asks for work that was already done.

**Done 2026-10-15 (Pepper's four weak edges, each measured before it was built):**

Richard asked what else would make Pepper more efficient, helpful or accurate. The whole
assistant layer was mapped — `src/lib/pepper/*`, the curator, the commitment loop, the five
morning crons — and then the live database was measured rather than reasoned about, which
changed what got built and in one case changed the design completely.

**What the measurement said.** Open commitments 444 (`status='open'`; the 527 first counted was
`settled_at is null`, which includes the 83 the extractor had already machine-`resolved` — two
different questions and the first one wrong). Of those 444, **294 sat on threads with no message
in 14 days and 82 on threads silent 90+**, with 246 of the 294 carrying no due date. Against that,
**14 had ever been settled by a human** — the other 131 "settled" were the 10-09 self-loop repair
script. Contacts: 97 rows, **72 with no title, 54 no email, 45 no company**, while
`curator_cursors` held 23 rows and **every one was a project or an opportunity, none a party** —
though `parties` has been in the writable registry with all six of its columns on the OPEN tier
since 10-12. `field_update_proposals`: 0 rows ever, and **no reader anywhere in the codebase**
outside its own writer. `pepper_text`, the curator and the chase: no health card of any kind.

**1. The ledger could only grow.** A commitment is re-judged exactly once, when its thread grows:
`email-sweep/fetch-phase.ts` clears `commitments_at` on a refreshed thread, `extract-phase.ts`
re-reads it and auto-`resolved`s any open row the new extraction no longer claims. That machinery
is right and is why the live half of the ledger stays honest. But a thread that goes QUIET is
never re-read, because nothing clears the marker again — those 294 obligations were immortal, and
the number only going up is why nobody was working it (§13 had recorded exactly that of the note).

`src/lib/commitments/aging.ts`, no model call, riding on the existing 05:30 chase cron — which is
where it belongs, because the chase and the retirement are two halves of one question and have to
agree about the order: a row must be chased BEFORE it can be aged out, or Pepper closes things she
never asked about. Running them in one job in that order makes it true by construction rather than
by two cron times happening not to collide.

⚠ **The threshold was measured, not chosen** (§12), and the sweep is in
`scripts/one-shot/dry-aging.mts`: at 30 days 174 rows, at 45 days 151, at 60 days 119, at 90 days
80, each printed with its eight closest boundary cases so a human could read what was about to be
closed. Split by side: `them` 95/86/65/34, `us` 100/86/73/48. Richard chose 45 for both sides —
two full chase cycles past the 21-day undated chase bar, so everything it closes has had its
follow-up composed and three more weeks of silence after it. **444 → 293 open.**

It writes `status='resolved'` rather than inventing a status, and that single decision is what
made the rest fall out for free: `CommitmentStatus` already separates the machine's verdict from a
person's, every reader already filters `status='open'`, the human-progress counts already filter
`HUMAN_SETTLED`, and a thread that revives puts the obligation back through re-extraction. The
reason travels in `settled_by` ("aged out — conversation silent since 2026-08-12"), where the
10-09 self-loop repair put its own reason for the same purpose: the table carries no audit
trigger, so the column IS the record.

⚠ **AND THE UNDO AND THE PASS WERE A LOOP.** Found by verifying the documented undo rather than by
reading the code. `settleCommitment(id,'open')` clears `settled_at`, `settled_by` and
`snoozed_until` and returns the row to `status='open'` — which is to say it restores the row to
EXACTLY the state the pass selects: open, on a thread that is still silent. The undo worked once
and the platform overruled it the next morning, and every morning after, with the reader watching
a row they had deliberately reinstated disappear again. The snooze was already immune and nobody
had noticed why: `snoozed_until` survives the pass because its whole job is to persist, while the
undo's whole job is to clear columns. Fixed with `reopened_at` (migration
`20261015000003`), which permanently exempts a reopened row from the AUTOMATIC close while leaving
every human verdict available. ⚠ **Two runs cannot catch this.** The standing idempotency check —
run the pass twice, assert the second reports nothing — passed perfectly, because the loop needs a
human action BETWEEN the runs. `scripts/one-shot/verify-aging.mts` now reopens a row between two
passes and asserts it survives; it reported `✗ the undo is a loop` before the fix and
`✓ the undo holds — reopened row survived a pass (2 exempt)` after.

Retired rows needed somewhere to be seen or the undo was theoretical, so `/commitments` gains a
**Retired** tab with its own total chip — deliberately not folded into Settled, because a person
deciding something is done and the platform noticing a conversation died are two different events
and summing them would make "settled" measure nobody's work.

**2. The curator had never walked the rolodex.** It gathers person-mentions from the evidence of
each DEAL it walks, and that evidence comes strictly from `thread_links` — so a contact's title is
learned only if some linked project happened to have new correspondence that cycle, and a
signature block on an unfiled thread is invisible however often it appears. `src/lib/curator/people.ts`
walks the CORRESPONDENCE instead: 1,680 summarized deal threads, their structured `people` already
extracted by the sweep (§12 — check whether the data is already on the row before calling it an
extraction problem), one cursor row keyed on a sentinel because what has to be remembered is how
far through the MAIL the pass has read, paged ascending on `last_at` so a partial run still
advances to a point everything before which was genuinely read. No model call. It reuses
`applyPeople` rather than forking it, because everything that makes that function safe lives
inside it.

⚠ **Its dry run is why it is fill-only, and this is the whole value of dry-running a pass.**
Unrestricted over 1,919 sightings it proposed 20 changes to 14 contacts, and reading them was
alarming: `Timothy Seibert: Managing Member → CEO`, `Rebecca Leonardi: Transaction lead → CEO`,
`Nancy Thunnel: ASEA → Aurevia LLC`, `Ocean Patel: Myton Land Owner → Energence`,
`Michael W. Moyer: Associate → Partner` and, worst, **`Mark Urbina:
mark.urbina@noircgrp.com → mark.urbina@gmail.com`** — trading a work address for a personal one
off a single passing mention. §12 says which act is safe turns on whether the source DESCRIBES its
subject or merely mentions it; a corpus-wide sweep is structurally the mentioning kind, while the
record pass reading one deal's own correspondence is the describing kind. So `applyPeople` took a
`fillOnly` parameter and **the broad source fills while the narrow source decides**. 20 proposed
changes became **8 blank-fills, all correct** (Merlin Corbin → Advisor, Elizabeth Hales → Real
Estate Broker, Sam Wadsworth → Wadsworth Development, Christopher Johnson → Co-Founder /
c-link.world, Jerry Chizmadia → HVAC Expert, Ken Berg → PE, Mark Urbina → Manager). Blank titles
72 → 66, blank companies 45 → 43. Second run wrote nothing.

⚠ **And it proposed writing our own company onto a party row as a person** — `Title = CEO/Founder`,
`Company = Ber Wilson`, `Email = info@berwilson.com`, the assistant's own seat. Two pre-existing
bugs in `fold.ts`, both now fixed where BOTH passes benefit: `matchParty` selected
`id, full_name, email` and never `is_organization`, so a person-shaped sighting could resolve to an
organization row with no column in hand to refuse it (§12 says decide on the FLAG, never the name —
but the flag has to be selected on the row the matcher RETURNS, not only checked on the source);
and the internal-person guard tested only the party's STORED address, so an internal person whose
contact row has no email yet walked straight through, which is exactly the row most in need of
filling.

**3. The guarded tier wrote into a void.** Three module headers — `cron/curator/route.ts`,
`provenance/fields.ts` and `provenance/write.ts` — all argue that what makes unattended CRM
writing safe is that every change is REPORTED, and the route's own comment says the run "RETURNS
what it changed, which the morning note reads out". It did not:
`grep -rin 'curat|provenance' src/lib/pepper/` was empty. Richard's 10-12 direction traded the
approval gate for legibility and the legible half was never built, so a guarded field — money,
ownership, a legally effective date, the things the registry protects precisely because being
wrong costs something — raised a question that accumulated as a pending row with no screen, no
note line and nowhere to answer it.

`src/lib/provenance/report.ts` reads both halves: what she wrote (off `record_field_provenance`,
not `activity_log`, because `opportunities` and `parties` carry no audit trigger — 17 live writes
on 10-12 left exactly one activity row, which is why `previous_value` lives on the provenance row)
and what she is holding. The note carries both; the email itemises the questions **from the rows,
never from the prose**, the pattern the settle list beside it already establishes; and `/decide`
gains a **Field question** lane. `KIND_META` is the registry the chip row and count map both derive
from, so the lane picked those up for free — the 10-15 fix for that drift paying for itself one day
later. The new `/api/provenance/proposals/[id]` route keeps `fieldSpec` as the boundary (a
proposal names its own table and column, and this must not become a way to write an arbitrary
column by posting a crafted id), checks `allowedValues` before writing because a non-member value
fails the WHOLE update with 22P02, and carries THE READER as the actor.

Answering one is the **first real caller of `recordHumanWrite`**, which had zero — so until now
protection rested entirely on the "unknown provenance reads as human" default, and a field a
person had just explicitly approved would have read as Pepper's to revise. Verified end to end:
the registry refuses `confidential` and an unknown column, the enum guard rejects a non-member
`stage`, accepting marks the field `written_by='human'` with the reader's address, and `canWrite`
then answers `propose` rather than `write` on the next pass.

⚠ **The first thing the reporting surfaced was a bad write**: `Dino Plumbing | Sector: (blank) →
technology`. Dino is the acquired plumbing/HVAC operating company. 31 of Pepper's writes became
visible for the first time.

**4. The morning channel.** One real bug first: `composeWeekAheadText` filtered a seven-day window
over `note.meetings`, which `assembleMeetings` only ever populated with TODAY
(`dayEnd.setHours(23,59,59,999)`). **Monday's week-ahead text was structurally incapable of naming
a meeting later in the week**, the `weekdayOf()` formatter beside it had nothing but Mondays to
format, and "N meetings this week" could only ever be Monday's. Three tests covered that text and
all three passed, because **each one injected a Tuesday meeting straight into `note.meetings`,
bypassing the one-day fetch that WAS the defect** — a unit test of a pure renderer proves the
renderer and says nothing about whether anything upstream ever puts that shape in the field. One
calendar fetch now covers the week and splits into `meetings` (today, with counterparty context)
and `weekMeetings` (the week, bare, because the week-ahead text names subjects and days and
nothing else). The regression test fails against the old code in both directions.

⚠ **And one meeting arrived under two Google event ids.** Found in the end-to-end dry run: Eric's
text rendered "6:00 PM KAVA Talks" TWICE inside a four-line budget. Google returned four events
for his week and they were two meetings — the same recurring series exists on his calendar twice,
under `_60q30c1g…_20261016T000000Z` and `tln6evvl…_20261016T000000Z`, because a duplicate invite
was accepted. Same start, same subject, different id. Deduped in `fetchCalendarEvents` itself
because every caller had it: the note doubles a line, the brief counts it twice, and the
pre-meeting nudge keys its one-per-meeting latch on `eventId` and **would have sent two nudges for
one meeting**. Attendees are MERGED rather than discarded with the duplicate — two invites to one
meeting can carry different guest lists, and keeping the first would silently drop a counterparty.

Then the accuracy items. `assembleMeetings` built "us" as `new Set([member.email])` while
`meeting-prep.ts` builds domains plus every roster address *precisely because* that bug announced
one executive as the other's external counterparty and recited his own commitments back as the
counterparty's — the fix landed in the nudge on 10-09 and the note, assembled by the same module
five minutes earlier, was never converted. `internalSet`/`isExternalTo` now live in
`attribution.ts`, which is the module whose job is who-counts-as-whom. The text's `clockOf` called
`toLocaleTimeString` with no `timeZone` while every other renderer pins `America/Denver`.

`loadMentions` was only ever called with `'commitment'`, so the `kind='task'` mentions written
after every successful send since 10-09 were **read by nobody** — a task raised four mornings
running got no escalation clause while a commitment beside it did. And the 06:45 text recorded
nothing at all, so for anyone whose email note `noteIsEmpty` skips, the same two task titles went
out every morning with `times_named` stuck at zero: no escalation, no rotation, forever. It now
records what it NAMED (the two titles `nameList` actually prints, not everything the assembly
held — recording the rest would claim she named what she summarised). ⚠ That ordering then made
`mentionClause` able to say "4 PREVIOUS MORNINGS" on the fourth morning, since the text counts
today before the email reads memory — already reachable with `?force=1`. `Mention.previousMornings`
derives the figure the clause means rather than relying on which cron ran first.

⚠ **The merge of the two morning crons was deliberately NOT done**, against the plan. The stated
gain was one assembly instead of two; re-reading the code, both routes see the same mention state
(recording happens only after the email sends), so the two provably cannot disagree, and the cost
would have been a single point of failure for both channels against a design whose header
explicitly says the email "still goes at 06:50" when the text channel is absent. The substantive
half of that item — the text contributing nothing to memory — is fixed above without the
resilience trade.

**Three unwatched channels.** `pepper_text` had no card since the channel went live on 10-13, the
curator had none at all, and the chase had two cards that were both COUNTS. This page has learned
that lesson twice already — its own comment records that a commitment check "printed 476 open in
green for sixteen days" — so all three are clocks now. The chase needed a column first:
`chase_drafted_at` is set only where a Gmail draft is possible, which is 3.5% of the work, so on
~96% of it the pass left no timestamp anywhere and a dead cron was unobservable.
`chase_composed_at` (migration `20261015000002`) is set whenever text is stored, draft or not,
backfilled from `coalesce(chase_drafted_at, updated_at)` for the 49 existing rows rather than
`now()`, which would have dated the whole backlog to the migration.

**Two count-honesty fixes found in the same read.** `loadTotals` counted the raw table while the
list it heads has protected rows removed by the choke point, under a header comment calling them
"honest totals … independent of the current filter" — true of the VIEW filter and silently untrue
of the SECURITY filter. And `withheld` ignored `side`, `threadIds` and `excludeSnoozed`, so
`listCommitments({side:'us'})` disclosed a figure drawn from both sides and a meeting's
thread-scoped read disclosed the whole portfolio's protected backlog against four rows. ⚠ **Worse,
the settled view's comment claimed a confidentiality filter that was not there at all** — "It
still applies the confidentiality filter, in memory — the set is small" over a completely
unfiltered read returning `withheld: 0`, so a protected project's settled obligations rendered on
the page under a disclosure asserting nothing was hidden. Both history views now go through one
`withoutProtected` helper.

**5. Pepper's ears.** CLAUDE.md's highest-leverage item said to email `info@` because it "is
already swept and is the one mailbox that can send". Two of those three premises do not hold:
**every** mailbox holds `gmail.send` (what only `info@` holds is `gmail.modify`, which buys drafts
and labels and is not needed to reply), and `info@` is swept by the LEAD pipeline once a day at
04:30 and runs marketing triage and bid scoring — a question there waits up to 24 hours and is
then scored as a sales lead. Richard's direction this session settled it: `info@` is "mainly junk
and solicitations", while 100% of project and opportunity correspondence is in `moose@` and
`tuaone@`. So the ears are on the deal mailboxes, and no re-consent is needed from anybody.

⚠ **What makes a message a question for her is that it REPLIES to one of hers** — not a subject
convention, which is something a human has to remember on a phone at 7am and which anyone emailing
the mailbox can trip by accident. That needed her sent ids, and nothing had them: `sendMail` threw
on failure and returned NOTHING on success, so the platform had never known the id of anything she
sent. It now returns `{id, threadId}`, accepts `threadId` + `inReplyTo` (lifting the header pair
out of `createDraft`, which documents why Gmail's own threading is not enough for other clients),
and `notification_log` stores both on the row it already writes per send — two columns on an
existing row rather than a second ledger to keep in step.

⚠ **Idempotency is the Gmail thread itself**, which is why there is no latch table: a thread is
only picked up when its LAST message is from the asker, so the moment Pepper replies the last
message is hers and the thread drops out. A send that succeeded cannot be answered twice even if
the logging after it failed.

The sender allowlist did not exist in any form — `grep allowlist|whitelist|allowedSender` over
`src/`, `deploy/` and `scripts/` returns only route-permission and column lists. It is built from
the roster, keyed on ADDRESS (§12's most expensive bug in this repo was a guard keyed on a DISPLAY
NAME, defeated by a rename that was itself a good idea — 27% of the commitment ledger turned out
to be Pepper reading her own notes), excludes the `info@` seat, fails CLOSED, and gives an
unrecognised sender SILENCE rather than a polite refusal: a reply to a stranger is an outbound
egress hole, not a courtesy. It resolved live to `Richard [moose@berwilson.com,
richmwhite@gmail.com] | Eric [tuaone@berwilson.com]` — the personal address included, which is
exactly what `PepperMember.addresses` was added for.

Answering imports `runAgent` directly rather than calling `/api/ai/agent`, which 401s without a
session cookie (and §12 forbids agent paths fetching the app's own HTTP routes). It is cookie-free,
uses the admin client, and already calls `hiddenProjectIds(null)` + `scrubHiddenProjects`, so it is
blind to a protected deal whoever asks — which matters because an emailed answer leaves the box and
containment is the half that can never be unlocked afterwards. All 43 tools were audited read-only:
not one `.insert(`, `.update(`, `.upsert(` or `.delete(` across `agent-tools.ts` or
`agent-tools-modules.ts`. There is no mode to switch off and nothing to switch on; that is the
standing constraint on `answer.ts`, and a mutating tool must not become reachable from it.

⚠ **Caught in the dry run:** a reply typed with nothing above the signature left "Sent from my
iPhone" as the question, which would have spent a whole agent turn — on a box serving one model
request at a time — answering a phone's footer. Seven tests cover the stripper, including her own
note quoted bare, which must yield nothing: handing the agent the note it is replying to is the
self-loop shape again.

Scheduled weekdays 07:30–18:00 every 15 minutes, deliberately clear of the 05:30–07:00 block where
the chase, curator, brief, text, note and digest already queue behind one GPU; `MAX_PER_MEMBER` is
3 so a flurry of replies cannot hold it for an hour; curl times out at 1750s against the route's
own 1800 so a run that completed is never recorded as a failure. And it is watched from the day it
ships — deliberately NOT as a clock, because this channel only speaks when spoken to and silence is
an empty inbox. What the card checks is that the allowlist resolves and that her sends carry the
ids a reply needs; it reads **blind** until the first morning note goes out, then turns green.

**Also found:** `recordMentions` did not dedupe its batch, and one duplicate `(kind, item_key)`
fails the WHOLE upsert with "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot affect row a second time", taking every
other mention in the note with it — unreachable today but a sharp edge for the next caller. And a
loader limit worth recording: tsx loads `src/lib` modules as CJS namespaces and Node's
`cjs-module-lexer` surfaces an `export function` but not an `export const`, so
`import { runAgingPass, STALE_THREAD_DAYS }` fails at link time naming the constant, which reads
as a typo rather than as a limit.

**Verification.** 372 tests pass (7 new on the stripper, 4 on the text's memory and the week-ahead
field). `npm run build` exit 0, captured unpiped. The aging pass run twice plus a reopen between
two runs. The rolodex sweep run twice. The proposal accept path exercised through every guard and
then rolled back, with the test proposal, its provenance row and the project's value all restored.
Both notes assembled end to end against the live database for both executives.

**Done 2026-10-15 (an attachment's text belongs in one corpus, and the jam was never where it looked):**

Richard: *"It seems like some projects are getting jammed with too many documents. since we can query email attachments when asking questions, is it even necessary to upload the attachments into Ber Intelligence? I'd almost prefer that we manually upload the important ones to the drive or the platform and have those sync. What do you think?"*

Measured before touching anything, and the premise held while the diagnosis did not.

**The premise is right, and understated.** `readAttachmentText` (`src/lib/ai/thread-embeddings.ts:232`) has been fetching every email attachment from Gmail at embed time all along, running `unpdf` text extraction with Apple Vision OCR behind it for scans, and writing the verbatim text into `thread_chunks` with `source='attachment'`. That is **5,459 attachment passages from 308 files across 225 threads — more retrieval text than every message body combined (2,921)**. `search_correspondence` reads it. A `documents` row is not what makes an attachment answerable, and never was.

**But mail is not what jams a project.** Of 799 live documents, 105 came from mail. Weirton — Cleveland-Cliffs is 187 documents of which **9** are from email; Steelton 178 of which 22; DUBHES Helper 73 of which 18. Weirton's 187 is a real seller's data room: 100 *Diligence/Rail & Transportation*, 21 *Power & Utilities*, 20 *Geotech & Site Reports*, all Drive-synced. Portfolio-wide the `diligence` doc_type is 480 documents and 5,532 chunks. **Withdrawing the attachment import would have removed ~13% of the rows and left the jam exactly as it was** — and on the opportunity side it would have emptied the records: GridEdge is 22 of 23 from mail, IAN 13 of 13.

**The real cost of importing is duplication, not volume.** The import chunked bytes the mail index had already chunked: **1,191 duplicate passages across 85 documents**, the same prose in two corpora, two agent tools able to quote each of them, and a ~48s local-model summary pass per file that the thread indexer deliberately skips. Read side by side, `chunks` and `thread_chunks` held the same TensorIQ partnership clauses at different offsets.

So the two jobs importing had welded together were split. **Custody** — the artifact on the record, filed to Drive — is unchanged. **Search** stops happening twice: a new `skipEmbed` flag on `runDocumentAiPass` (symmetric with the `skipSummary` flag already there) extracts and summarizes but does not chunk, settling a fourth terminal status, `indexed_in_mail`. The document keeps its file, its `ai_summary` (or `list_documents` would never present it — §12) and its `extracted_text` (or `get_document_content` could not read it).

⚠ **THE DECISION CANNOT BE MADE AT THE IMPORT, BECAUSE `apply` RUNS BEFORE `embed`.** `ALL_PHASES` in the orchestrator is fetch → summarize → cluster → stage → route → **apply** → **embed** → …, so when `importThreadAttachments` registers a file there is not one `thread_chunks` row for that thread yet. Predicting from `documentKind` was the obvious alternative and would have been a projection of what the other half of the pipeline was going to do — §12 is explicit that an orphaned projection looks perfectly live. So the import defers, and `reconcileMailIndexedDocuments` settles it as the tail of the embed phase, when the mail index is authoritative: present in `thread_chunks` → leave it; absent → index it as a document after all, embedding from the `extracted_text` already stored, with no re-download, no second OCR and no model call. **The fallback is what makes the optimisation allowable** — `readAttachmentText` handles pdf/docx/text only, so an emailed `.xlsx`, `.pptx` or image is fetched and discarded (and still burns one of the 8 per-thread slots), a byte fetch can fail outright, and a thread the summarizer judged `noise` is never embedded at all. Being wrong costs a duplicate passage, never a document nobody can find.

⚠ **59 OF THE 85 CARRY A `drive_file_id`**, because the import files them to Drive. So omitting `indexed_in_mail` from `needsAnotherPass` — which reads anything but `complete`/`skipped` as an unfinished pass — would have had the nightly Drive sync re-run a ~48s model pass on all 59, forever, reporting success each time. Not hypothetical; measured. The same one-value-many-readers trap sat in `system-health.ts`, which buckets any unrecognised status as `stuck` and would have reported a 85-document backlog that does not exist. It now says *"725 indexed, 85 indexed with their email thread, 77 not readable"*.

⚠ **`/decide` WOULD HAVE CALLED EVERY MAIL-INDEXED DOCUMENT HARMLESS.** Both queues print a document's retrieval footprint from `chunks` and, at zero, say *"Not indexed, so nothing is answering from it yet"* — which for these documents is false, and false in the direction that makes a misfiled row look free to leave. `MisfiledDoc` and `CompanyKnowledgeDoc` now carry `mailChunks` beside `chunks`, counted on `(thread_id, attachment_name)` and never summed into it: filing the document moves `chunks`, while the mail passages follow the THREAD's links and do not move at all. Summing would have promised the tap does more than it does.

**The backfill, and the guard that nearly was not there.** Resolving the old rows needed a thread, which `documents` did not record — `source` is an `update_source` enum reading `'document'` and there was no pointer at all, so the two corpora could not be compared. New `source_thread_id` on both document tables, `on delete set null` because the thread is how a document ARRIVED, not what it belongs to: dropping a swept thread must never delete a deed. The script resolves each legacy row through its record's own `thread_links` and takes it **only when exactly one of them carries an attachment of that name** — two candidates is ambiguity, and ambiguity means no match, so 5 rows were left fully indexed rather than given a pointer that might be wrong, along with 55 genuinely not in the mail index.

⚠ **PRESENCE IS NOT COVERAGE, and the first version of the script did not ask.** `readAttachmentText` caps an attachment at `MAX_ATTACHMENT_CHARS` (200,000) where a document's stored text is capped at `LOCAL_PDF_TEXT_MAX_CHARS` (2,000,000) — so a long enough agreement could sit in the mail index as a truncated head, and deleting the document's own chunks on the strength of a first page would quietly have lost the rest. Measured across all **91** comparable documents before the guard was written: every one is at **97.2% or better**, so it fires on nothing today. It is there for the document that has not arrived yet. 1,191 chunks reclaimed, 11,028 → 9,837, behind a `pg_dump` of `chunks` read back before the delete.

**Verified end to end, not inferred.** The backfill run twice reports nothing the second time.
