**The text channel — and a platform assumption that expired under us.**

⚠ **APPLESCRIPT TO MESSAGES IS GONE ON THIS OS.** Measured here, macOS **27.0 (26A428)**: `sdef /System/Applications/Messages.app` returns **nothing**. No scripting dictionary at all — no `send`, no `buddy`, no `service`. Every published "send an iMessage from the terminal" recipe is written against a dictionary this machine does not have.

And it does not fail cleanly, which is the dangerous part. Messages accepts the Apple event and never answers:

```
execution error: Messages got an error: AppleEvent timed out. (-1712)
```

Reproduced twice, with an explicit `with timeout of 20 seconds` block, against a running Messages. It is **-1712 (timeout), not -1743 (not authorized)** — so this is not a TCC problem and granting Automation does not fix it. On an unattended 06:45 cron an AppleScript transport would have been a fifteen-minute hang and a silently missing morning, which is worse than no feature.

The transport is therefore the **Shortcuts CLI** (`/usr/bin/shortcuts`, present and working), Apple's sanctioned replacement. It needs one two-action shortcut per recipient, built by hand once — `deploy/pepper-text-setup.md`. That manual step is unavoidable and is the honest cost of keeping the channel on-box; the alternative is an SMS vendor, which means every morning's obligations leaving the hardware against the whole point of the 07-07 cutover.

⚠ **THE SELF-LOOP GUARD WAS BUILT BEFORE THE FIRST SEND, NOT AFTER THE BUG.** The Studio sends as Richard's own Apple ID, so a text to Eric lands in the Richard↔Eric conversation that the iMessage sweep ingests unconditionally (`IMESSAGE_INTERNAL_HANDLES` marks it internal) — and `is_from_me` **cannot** discriminate, because Richard's own real texts are also from him and those are exactly what the sweep is for. This is the 10-09 bug (131 of 481 open commitments turned out to be Pepper reading her own morning notes) in a channel with no Gmail labels to spot it with. So every outbound body is **hashed into `pepper_outbound_texts` before it leaves**, and ingestion drops what it finds there. Structural, not a prefix or a display name anybody might reword — §12, key the guard on what cannot be renamed, including by us. **If the guard row cannot be written, the message is not sent:** an unsent text is a visible problem, a self-feeding ledger is an invisible one. The hash is taken over a normalized body, because a message read back out of `chat.db` is not byte-identical to what was sent (line endings, trailing whitespace) and a guard that misses *is* the loop.

`normalizeHandle` **refuses** anything it cannot be sure of rather than guessing — a wrong handle texts a deal's obligations to a stranger. `deploy/pepper-text-check.sh` asserts the binary, the shortcut names and the handles **without sending**, because a health check that texts somebody is a health check nobody runs. It also avoids §12's `grep -q` SIGPIPE trap by capturing `shortcuts list` to a variable first.

**Why a text is not a shorter email, in Pepper's own data.** Twelve consecutive weekday notes, subject lines only:

```
Richard: 19 -> 28 -> 28 -> 42 -> 51 -> 58 -> 59 -> 71 -> 74 -> 76 -> 82
Eric:    90 -> 93 -> 95 -> 112 -> 116 -> 123 -> 125 -> 122 -> 124 -> 133 -> 154
```

Delivery was flawless — 12 of 12 weekdays, both recipients, no gaps — and the headline only ever grew, because it counted the whole ledger. Across those eleven mornings, `count(settled_by)` on 407 open commitments was **0** and `snoozed_until` was **0**. A text has room for about four lines; spending them on a number that cannot go down is spending the channel on telling somebody they are behind. §12 already records the same shape about colour: when every row is red, red has stopped signifying.

So the morning text carries what is **today's** — overdue, due today, today's meetings, then one line of two per-person quantities named apart — and the queue stays in the 06:50 email, which has room for it and a one-tap link on every row. No model call: deterministic, because a message read half awake must be skimmable and must never be late behind the brief.

**Three more defects, found by actually rendering it:**

1. **`"272 to decide"`** appeared in a four-line text — the exact only-ever-grows number the channel was built to escape. Removed; it lives in the email.
2. **The week-ahead reported September as "due this week".** The deadline filter had an upper bound and **no lower one**, so the dry run told Richard *"Due this week: 9 Sept …; 18 Sept …; 21 Sept …"* and Eric *"11 Feb …; 20 Feb …; 1 Jun …"*. 71 of 407 open commitments carry a date and most of those dates are months gone, so this was **certain** to fire on the first real Monday. Past-dated items are real and belong in the note; what they are not is this week's. They now collapse to one honest line, *"12 already overdue."*
3. **An all-day calendar entry is a deadline, not a meeting.** It said *"3 meetings"* where two were all-day `BID DUE — …` markers. §12: one quantity, one definition. And a counterparty never resolved to a contact has `name` = the address, so it printed `Ber Wilson chat W Taylor (englertmining@gmail.com)` — an address where a person's name goes reads as a failed render, the same way a bare em dash does. Omitted instead.

---

⚠ **DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: A RETIRE-BY-AGE RULE FOR STALE PROPOSALS**, which is half of what Richard asked for by name ("get rid of older crappy data like old proposals"). 212 email intake sessions are staged and 100 are over thirty days old, which looked exactly like the target. Measured the oldest first: **`IAN Acquisition & EMP/Microgrid IDIQ Pursuit`, `Fort Polk Military & Infrastructure Pursuits`, `Myton islanded grid and rail project`.** Those are live deals already on the books — not junk. A clock would have retired real work and called it cleaning. What makes a staged proposal disposable is that its deal **already exists**, which is the duplicate fold's question and not a clock's; so housekeeping calls the **existing** `dedupePendingSessions` (written 09-14, given a UI door 10-08) on a nightly agent rather than adding a second pass. §12: never fork a shared pass, add a caller. The `retired_at`/`retired_reason` columns were added and are currently **unused** — kept because a human "this is not a deal" verdict wants them and they are two nullable columns, but recorded here as debt rather than pretended into a feature.

Also measured and left alone: the "weak deal descriptions" in the same instruction do not exist (1 blank of 19 projects, 0 short), and `leads` is already triaged (1,143 spam, 242 ignored, 223 expired, 60 new) rather than dirty.

⚠ **AND THE LIVENESS GATE PROPOSED AT THE START OF THE SESSION WAS DROPPED RATHER THAN BUILT.** The plan was to split the commitment ledger into live and backlog so the number could fall. A concurrent session was solving the same problem from the board end — `src/lib/tasks/priority.ts` with `LIVE_CORRESPONDENCE_DAYS = 14` and a three-tier ranking, plus `commitments/internal-tasks.ts` promoting the executives' own obligations onto the board. Shipping a second definition of "live" would have been precisely what §12 forbids twice over: never fork a shared pass, and one quantity gets one definition or the reader trusts none of them. Measured anyway, for the record: a 45-day gate removes only 19 of 407 rows because the sweep keeps touching old threads, and the honest split is by provenance rather than recency — **230 of 407 were created in the single week of 09-21** (the historical excavation) against a genuine inflow of ~65-72 a week.

**Shipped:** `record_field_provenance`, `field_update_proposals`, `pepper_outbound_texts`, `curator_cursors`, `enum_members()`; `src/lib/provenance/{fields,write,db}.ts`, `src/lib/curator/{evidence,fold,run}.ts`, `src/lib/notify/text.ts`, `src/lib/imessage/own-outbound.ts`, `src/lib/pepper/text-note.ts`; `/api/cron/curator` and `/api/cron/pepper-text` (both named in `middleware.ts` — §12, a cron route is unreachable until it is, and the tell is which word comes back: both answer the route's own `Unauthorized`, not the gate's `Not authenticated`); three launchd agents (curator weekdays 06:20, pepper-text weekdays 06:45 with Monday's being the week-ahead, housekeeping nightly 23:10 on its own agent because a 45-minute model budget must not sit in front of the brief). 23 agents loaded, tailnet listeners asserted, both models resident, 300 tests passing (was 266).

**Still open, and both are Richard's to close:** the two Shortcuts must be built by hand before a single text can send (`deploy/pepper-text-setup.md`), and nothing reads Apple Notes yet, so the phone-call notes named in the instruction are the one source still not reaching her.

**Done 2026-10-12 (the RFP deadlines left the board, the obligations the two of you give each other arrived on it, and a tapback was carrying Eric's whole message under Richard's name):**

Richard: *"WHen Pepper creates tasks and calendar events, I want it to differentiate between important tasks and things like RFP deadlines for potential projects... In fact, I want all of the RFP type of tasks and emails to dissappear. Let just handle that at the lead level. That way we aren't cluttering our calendars, task lists etc... with things that aren't as important. If you look at my most recent texts from Eric, he laid out all the key things we have outstanding right now. Those should have already ingested and be showing but if they aren't, please fix."*

**MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS WRITTEN, AND THE PREMISE WAS HALF RIGHT IN A WAY THAT CHANGED THE BUILD.** The clutter was exactly as described: **11 of 22 open tasks were unsolicited RFP bid deadlines**. But the complaint about ranking turned out to understate the problem. The four non-lead tasks that sat on a real record belonged to **Alaska JV and Case Garage, whose newest correspondence is 2026-09-12 and 2026-09-17** — while Steelton, Elite Solutions, Helper, GridEdge, Myton Rail and IAN, every one of them with mail through 10-09 or 10-10, had **not one task between them**. So the board was not mis-sorted so much as empty of the live work, and a tier applied to what was already there would have ranked a quiet deal above nothing at all. Nothing writes to Google Calendar or Google Tasks any more (retired 09-21 and 10-11), so "cluttering our calendars" was already solved; the clutter was the in-app board and `/calendar`, which reads it.

**TWO DECISIONS WERE PUT TO HIM, BOTH BECAUSE THEY CHANGED THE BUILD.** How Eric's items should reach the board — a one-tap promote, or automatic creation for internal threads only — and what the colour should key off. He chose **automatic for internal threads, and three tiers derived from correspondence.** The first answer is a deliberate, narrow exception to §11 and is recorded as one.

**⚠ ERIC'S LIST HAD INGESTED, PERFECTLY, AND THAT WAS THE WHOLE POINT.** He texted the rundown at **20:29 on 10-11** — Dino Plumbing, Ber Wilson Ammo / Brass Kisses, Fairbanks Mining, the Tim Seibert and Mortenson teaming agreements, the CoreWeave GC, the Kiewit power agreement — and Richard replied nine minutes later, *"Perfect I'll get these tasks in BI"*. The platform had read all seven within the hour, correctly, every one `side='us'` at 0.85 confidence. They were **commitments 356 to 367 of a 367-row ledger**, attached to no record and on no board. The extraction was never the problem. The ledger had no door onto the board, and the board was full of strangers' RFPs.

**⚠ AND A TAPBACK WAS CARRYING THE WHOLE QUOTED MESSAGE UNDER THE WRONG AUTHOR.** Messages stores a reaction as its own `message` row whose body is `Liked "<the entire text it reacts to>"` and whose `is_from_me` is the REACTOR's. `read.ts` selected every message row without ever looking at `associated_message_type`, so Richard liking Eric's 10-10 rundown at 20:41 produced a verbatim second copy of that rundown attributed to Richard, one minute after the original. The commitment extractor read it twice, from both executives — which is why all five obligations off that thread landed `side='them'` with `owner_name` NULL.

Measured on this box: **46,106 of 305,241 messages are tapbacks, 15.1%**; 1,933 of 13,953 in the last 90 days. Of the 115 text threads already stored, **23 carried at least one**, 67 blocks and 17,934 characters of duplicate text between them. The filter is one SQL predicate (`associated_message_type = 0`), counted rather than merely dropped, and deliberately **not** counted toward `ChatRow.total` — that number is what the classifier reads as conversation volume, and a reaction is not a message.

**THE REPAIR EDITS THE STORED TEXT RATHER THAN RE-INGESTING, AND THAT IS NOT LAZINESS.** `storeFetchedThreads` writes a thread only when the incoming session is LONGER than the stored one, so that a needless upsert cannot throw away a summary the corpus has already paid for. A fixed sweep produces FEWER messages, so it would have skipped all 23 of these threads and the duplicates would have survived every future pass. `scripts/strip-tapback-duplicates.mts` strips the blocks to exactly what the fixed renderer now produces, moves `message_count` with them (a stale "78 message(s)" above 68 blocks is a small lie the summary prompt reads as fact), and queues `summary_state='pending'` + `commitments_at`/`embedded_at` cleared. `routed_at` is deliberately LEFT: a duplicate paragraph never changed which deal a thread is about. Run twice, the second run reports zero.

The re-read is already paying: Eric's 10-11 session went from 7 open items to **8 richer ones**, picking up the Helper financing choice (private capital vs. the Zions bridge), the water-rights negotiation, the Herscher data-centre appraisal, the TRE CFO conversation and Jerron's unanswered email — none of which survived the duplicate.

**THE RFP TASKS ARE GONE AT THE SOURCE, NOT FILTERED.** `src/lib/leads/tasks.ts` is deleted, the `tasks` phase is out of the lead orchestrator and `refreshLeadTask` is out of the lead route; the 10 open lead tasks were closed as `done` rather than deleted, so the decision is reversible and the `log_tasks` trigger recorded it. `LEAD_TASK_OWNER`/`LEAD_TASK_SYNC` are documented as retired in `.env.local` with the reason, which is the third home a bid deadline has had and the last: nothing is lost, because the bid date, the site visit and the RFI cut-off are columns on the lead, shown on `/leads` and published to each lane's Drive sheet.

**THE TIER IS DERIVED, AND IT REACHES 'live' TWO WAYS.** `src/lib/tasks/priority.ts` — pure, tested, no database — reads `live` if the task's RECORD has correspondence inside `LIVE_CORRESPONDENCE_DAYS` (14), **or** if it was promoted from a commitment whose own conversation is that recent. The second route is load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: **277 of 367 open commitments name neither a project nor an opportunity**, so a tag-only test would have filed every item off Eric's rundown as `unattached`, which is the opposite of the truth. `tagged` is anything hung off a record that has gone quiet, `unattached` is a task on nothing.

⚠ **A TAG IS THE ONLY EVIDENCE, AND A TITLE IS NOT.** "GridEdge offer" sits on the board untagged while GridEdge the opportunity has 19 threads through 10-09, and it still reads `unattached`. Matching a record by a word in a title is what put Bloom Energy's logo on bfaenergy.com and claimed a 664-message family thread for a hospital project (§12). The honest answer is to show the tier the tags support.

**ONE NUMBER, ONE DEFINITION, IN FOUR PLACES.** The same 14 days and the same function now decide the board's colour and order, the task sheet's order, which internal obligations are promoted at all, and which undated work Pepper names. A phone that disagrees with the screen about what is important is worse than either alone.

**THE COLOUR IS ONE COLOUR.** Only `live` is tinted — an emerald left border and a chip; `unattached` is dimmed; `tagged` is the ordinary card. §12: when every row is red, red has stopped signifying. Overdue keeps the red edge and is checked FIRST so the two never both apply to one border, and overdue is lifted out of its tier in the sort, because being late is a different and more urgent fact than being important.

**⚠ THE DATE COULD NOT STAY THE SORT KEY, AND THE REASON IS AN ASYMMETRY WORTH REMEMBERING: A DEADLINE IS ATTACHED TO THE WORK LEAST LIKELY TO MATTER.** A bid invitation always carries one; a real obligation between the two executives almost never does. **34 of the 38 promoted obligations have no due date at all** — Eric does not put a deadline on "Finalize the Fairbanks Mining Contract", he just says it is outstanding. So a date-first sort structurally buries the important half, and it did so on three surfaces at once.

**⚠ AND THE SAME ASYMMETRY HAD SILENCED PEPPER'S NOTE ENTIRELY, WHICH WOULD HAVE MADE THE WHOLE CHANGE INVISIBLE WHERE RICHARD ACTUALLY READS IT.** `fetchTasksForDigest` filtered `due_date is not null`, and the note then bucketed what came back into overdue and due-in-7 — so an undated task reached **neither bucket and was never mentioned**. All 38 would have landed on the board and none in the note. The filter is gone, there is a third section (`liveTasks`: live tier, no date or past the horizon), and it renders in the prompt, in the itemised list under the note, in `noteIsEmpty` and in the dry-run counts. The sentence justifying it was **already written one line above in the same function** — *"An obligation with no agreed date is not less real; it just cannot be sorted by one"* — about commitments, and never applied to tasks.

**THE PROMOTION IS BOUND BY FOUR THINGS, EACH MEASURED.** Internal only (every participant one of ours, keyed on ADDRESSES — the Pepper self-loop guard was defeated by a display name, §12); `side='us'` only, because for `them` on an internal thread `attribute()` resolves by mailbox and would put Eric's obligations on Richard's board as things he owes himself; a conversation inside the same 14 days (64 open internal 'us' commitments in all, **38 inside 14 days, 30 inside 7**); and `tasks.commitment_id` unique, surviving the task being completed OR deleted, because deleting a promoted task IS the decision that it is not work.

The assistant seat is deliberately **not** internal. §12 already records that a structural "participants are only info@ plus internal mailboxes" predicate caught 9 real threads of forwarded counterparty correspondence; leaving info@ out keeps this pass away from the whole lead pipeline, which arrives there.

**THE LOOP CLOSES BOTH WAYS, WHICH IS THE POINT OF PROMOTING AT ALL.** A commitment the sweep re-reads as settled closes its task; ticking the task settles the commitment, and un-ticking reopens it. Two ledgers that disagree about the same promise are worse than one — and as of 10-11, `count(settled_by)` across 407 open commitments was still **zero**, sixteen mornings after the closing half was built.

**⚠ AND THE LAST BUG WAS MINE, FOUND BY READING THE BOARD BACK RATHER THAN BY A TEST — THE SAME NUMBER OF DAYS REACHED BY TWO DIFFERENT READS.** `loadLiveContext` built its live-COMMITMENT set out of the thread ids it had already gathered from `thread_links`, which exist only for a thread FILED against a record — and an internal text session between the two executives usually is not filed against anything. So **9 of the 34 obligations promoted minutes earlier ranked `tagged`, while the pass that promoted them had called the very same conversation live.** 25 live / 14 tagged before, 34 live / 5 tagged after, which is exactly the 34 promoted plus the one pre-existing Alaska task whose deal has gone quiet. §12's rule is one quantity one definition, and this is the sharper version of it: the definition has to be the same READ, not just the same constant. Nothing would ever have reported it — the board had colour, the colour was simply wrong on a quarter of the rows.

**THE REPAIR MEASURABLY IMPROVED THE SET IT FED.** Re-extraction over the corrected text: 23 threads, 21 examined, **16 commitments created, 34 reworded, 24 auto-resolved**, 0 failed, and the live internal set went 38 → 34 — but a BETTER 34. *"Bring a couple of shirts for try-on"* and *"Meet at 6 PM in Bluffdale"* are gone, replaced by *"Respond to Jerron's email"*, *"Talk to TRE about CFO responsibilities for Helper and other greenfield projects"* and *"Create a data center page for the website"*. The duplicate was not merely noise in the index; it was costing real obligations.

**⚠ TWO MORE THINGS THE DEPLOY ITSELF FOUND.**

**`strayRows` had reported exactly 1000 on all 41 runs since the task sheet was created — 0 only on the first, before any checkbox existed.** That counter exists to notice somebody pasting their own notes into the shared sheet, and a number that cannot change is not a signal: a real paste was invisible behind it. The checkbox validation covers the whole Done column, so Sheets materialises a real `false` in every row below the data, and **`String(false)` is the non-empty string `"false"`** — so every blank grid row read as a paste. Measured off the live sheet: the *All open* tab returns **246 rows for 45 tasks, 200 of them holding nothing but that bare checkbox**; five tabs' worth sums to the round 1000 that should have been the tell. "Blank" now ignores the Done column, three tests cover it (including the ticked-with-no-id row, which must be a paste and never an instruction), and the live run afterwards reported **0**. Not asked for, found while reading the board back.

**⚠ AND THE FIRST REBUILD FAILED ON THE OTHER SESSION'S HALF-SAVED FILE, WHICH IS A NEW EDGE ON AN OLD RULE.** §12 already records that the runbook builds the WORKING TREE rather than `HEAD`, so a commit that does not compile ships green. The sharper version, met here: the working tree also holds the OTHER session's file **as it is at that instant**. `npm run build` died on `src/lib/notes/decode.ts` — *"BigInt literals are not available when targeting lower than ES2020"* — an untracked file that the other session had already diagnosed and fixed; the build simply caught it mid-edit, and the file now carries a comment saying *"PLAIN NUMBERS, NOT BigInt"*. **`npx tsc --noEmit` had passed minutes earlier on the same path**, which is how the gap presents.

The exposure is the part worth remembering: a failed build **removes `.next/BUILD_ID`**, and `next start` holds its build in memory — so production kept answering 200 while being one crash, reboot or kickstart away from 000, exactly the state §12's `npm run build | grep` entry describes. Gating the kickstart on an UNPIPED `$?` is what made that survivable: the build failed, nothing was restarted, and a rebuild a minute later exited 0 and restored `BUILD_ID`. Nothing was touched in the other session's files.

Verification: 300 tests (up from 251), `tsc` clean, `eslint` showing exactly the 21 pre-existing problems CLAUDE.md §9 records and no new ones. The promotion was printed before it wrote (§12), run, then run AGAIN — second pass 0 created / 34 already promoted. Board after: 45 open tasks, **0 of them RFP deadlines**, 34 promoted, 2 overdue at the top, then 34 live, 5 attached, 6 unattached (*"Talk to Garn"*, *"8a question"*) at the bottom. 32 on Richard, 7 on Eric, 6 unowned.

**Done 2026-10-11 (the task board becomes a Google Sheet you can tick, and the Sheets API had never been enabled):**

Richard: *"Instead of syncing tasks on ber intelligence with tasks on Gsuite. I want the tasks to sync w a google sheet. Can you please make a Google sheet that syncs the tasks?"*

**Three decisions were put to him before anything was written, because each changed the build rather than the polish.** Two-way or read-only (the Google Tasks sync was genuinely bidirectional — 39 live link rows, pulling `status` and `due` back — so a read-only sheet would have cost the phone tick-off and the platform is tailnet-only); keep Google Tasks alongside, trial both, or replace it outright; and one sheet with a tab per person, one sheet per person, or one flat tab. He chose **two-way with a real checkbox, replace outright, and one workbook with per-person tabs.** The third answer is the interesting one and is the reason the whole thing is worth building: the 2026-09-10 migration's own docstring says *"Google Tasks lists are private per account: there is no shared list, no assignee field, no delegation. /tasks remains the only place the whole board can exist."* A sheet is the whole board, on a phone, off the tailnet — the one thing the sync it replaces structurally could not do.

**⚠ THE SHEETS API HAD NEVER BEEN ENABLED ON THE CLOUD PROJECT, AND NOTHING WOULD HAVE SAID SO UNTIL THE FIRST CRON RUN.** `src/lib/integrations/google-drive-write.ts` carried the comment *"the Sheets API accepts drive.file for app-created files, so no broader spreadsheets scope is needed"* — a claim no code had ever exercised, because `upsertSheetFromCsv` goes through the DRIVE API and lets Drive convert an uploaded CSV. That is why the lead sheets have worked for weeks with the Sheets API switched off. Probed before building on it (§12: re-test a recorded reason before inheriting it), it answered `403 — Google Sheets API has not been used in project 247991610437 before or it is disabled`. One click in the console, and no scope change or re-consent: the claim about `drive.file` is still the right bet, it simply had a prerequisite nobody had hit.

**The two 403s mean opposite things and are reported apart.** `SheetsApiDisabledError` is a console switch and needs no token work; `SheetsScopeError` is a mailbox re-consenting in a browser. Google answers both with 403 and prose that reads alike in a hurry, and `explainTokenError` already owned the translation — so the new client matches its OUTPUT rather than re-parsing Google's body, which is how the two would have drifted. The cron route returns the error key plus the exact fix for each. `spreadsheetExists` rethrows both rather than treating them as "the file is gone", because a disabled API read as a 404 would create a fresh workbook on every run and leave a trail of abandoned ones.

**THE PROJECTION BEING REBUILT WHOLE IS WHAT REMOVED THE MERGE TABLE.** The Google Tasks sync needed `google_task_lists` + `task_google_links`, a stored `base_status`/`base_due` per link and a three-way per-field merge — 1,077 lines, and the docstring is explicit that forgetting to rewrite the base is the only way to reintroduce ping-pong. None of that is needed here. After a rebuild the rendered checkbox always agrees with the platform (FALSE on an open tab, TRUE on the Done tab), so **the rendered value IS the base, and which tab the row is on implies it**:

```
open tab + ticked    ->  settle it done
open tab + unticked  ->  nothing (this is the rendered state)
Done tab + unticked  ->  reopen it
Done tab + ticked    ->  nothing (this is the rendered state)
```

The two no-op arms are the whole safety argument and each has a named test. A task completed inside the platform at 10:05, against a sheet rendered at 10:00, is read at 10:15 as unticked-on-an-open-tab — which means nothing, not "reopen". **Nothing can be lost by arriving late.** If that arm were ever read as an instruction, every completion made in the platform would be undone by the next sync.

**Order is load-bearing: read, settle, RE-READ the board, rebuild.** Rebuilding first overwrites the ticks unread, which is the one way this pass could lose work rather than delay it. Rebuilding from the pre-settle board redraws a task somebody just ticked as still open, and they tick it again. The settle itself is guarded on the task's current status (`.eq('status', 'open')`), so a double-read cannot double-count and the counter cannot claim work the platform did on its own — §12's rule that a pass reporting what it did must read before it writes.

**The same task appears on two open tabs, and that resolves rather than conflicts.** "All open" and the owner's tab both carry a checkbox for it. A tick is an affirmative act and a blank is the absence of one, so **a tick anywhere wins** — treating it as a contradiction would have made settling from a person's own tab impossible. A genuine contradiction (ticked on an open tab AND unticked on Done, which takes a copied row to produce) is held back and named, per §12's rule that ambiguity must mean no match.

**Attribution comes from the tab, and the tab order is what makes it work.** A tick on Richard's own tab is written through `createAdminClient({ id: auth_user_id, email })` so `activity_log` names him rather than "system" (§12). A tick on a shared tab cannot be traced to a person by any API Google offers, so it is recorded as the sheet — true, rather than credited to whoever the task happened to be assigned to. This depends on person tabs being READ AFTER the shared one, which is asserted by its own test, because reversing the order would silently move every settle to "the sheet".

**NOTHING IS EVER CREATED FROM THE SHEET**, which is the one place this deliberately does less than the thing it replaced. The old sync imported tasks a member typed into their own Google list, and that was safe *because a list is one person's*. A shared sheet is not: a row somebody pastes in while reorganising is indistinguishable from a task they meant to create, and §11's standing rule is that a record is never created without a human confirm step. A row with no task id in the hidden column is ignored and COUNTED — `strayRows`, because a count that is always zero is the only way to notice people trying to add tasks there.

**Measured decisions in the layout.** One column schema for every tab rather than three tailored ones: a person tab does not need Assignee and an open tab never has a Completed date, but three layouts mean three renderers, three read-back parsers and three sets of column indices that must agree forever — the cost of a blank cell is a blank cell, the cost of a drifted index is a tick read against the wrong task. **Six of 22 open tasks had no owner**, 27%, so Unassigned is a TAB rather than a footnote (§12, 09-24: count unowned records over the whole set). A person gets a tab once they have anything on the board and keeps it when it empties — a tab that comes and goes is worse than an empty one, because the bookmark and the habit both point at it. Nothing ever deletes a tab, which also means a tab somebody adds themselves is left alone rather than tidied away. `readTick` accepts `x`, `yes`, `✓`, `1` as well as a real boolean, because somebody will type into the column on a phone keyboard; anything that is neither ticked nor blank refuses and says so.

**⚠ THE WORKBOOK IS AN OUTBOUND CHANNEL AND THE CONFIDENTIAL FILTER TAKES THE ABSOLUTE ANSWER.** It is shared, in Drive, on phones, and impossible to recall — so `hiddenProjectIds(null)`, with no viewer and no step-up that can unlock a row. Filtered on `project_id` ONLY, deliberately: `confidential` exists on projects and nowhere else, and the 10-11 measurement is that **27 of 46 tasks hang off a LEAD and 3 off an opportunity**, so dropping those would withhold real work and protect nothing. The withheld count is taken on its own rather than as a length difference, per §12 — "0 withheld" beside a trimmed list asserts a completeness it does not have.

**Sharing had to be upgraded, not merely asserted.** The Ber Intelligence root shares with the domain as READER, which is enough to look at a sheet and not enough to tick a box in it. `shareWithAddresses` checked only whether an address held *any* grant, so it would have skipped moose@ and tuaone@ forever at reader. It is now role-aware: it reads `permissions(id,type,emailAddress,role)`, PATCHes an existing permission to upgrade (a second POST for the same address answers 400 `alreadyExists`, so the presence check could not simply be dropped), and never DOWNGRADES — a grant somebody was given by hand is not that function's to take away. Asserted every run, because a grant removed by hand in Drive is invisible from here (§12, 08-26).

**`probeTaskSheet` watches the OUTPUT side.** The commitment loop read "476 open" in green for sixteen days — correctly, extraction is why it was 476 — while nothing had ever been settled by a human (§12, 10-09). The identical shape was available here: a sheet full of open tasks is exactly what a healthy publish produces AND what a sheet nobody can write to produces. So a workbook with open rows and no tick ever read reports `partial` and names the likely cause (writer access), rather than counting as health. A `last_synced_at` of Infinity — built but never completed a run — lands in the stalled arm too, since excluding it is how a never-once-working job reads clean.

**What was removed:** `google-sync.ts` (1,077), `google-push.ts`, `google-body.ts`, `google-tasks-write.ts`, the cron route, `verify-google-tasks.mjs`, the plist, `TASKS_ONLY_SCOPES`, `TASK_MAILBOXES`, `GOOGLE_TASK_MAILBOXES`, and `everyConsentedMailbox`'s reason for differing from `allMailboxes`. The delete route lost its remote-cleanup half entirely (`readRemovableLink`/`queueTaskRemoval`): a deleted task needed a Google task deleting out of somebody's list, where here it simply is not redrawn. `queueTaskPush`'s per-task debounce became one whole-board `queueTaskSheetRefresh` with an in-flight latch and a `dirty` flag.

**⚠ THE 39 TASKS ALREADY PUSHED ARE THE REASON THE LINK TABLES WERE RENAMED RATHER THAN DROPPED.** They are sitting in two personal Google Tasks lists that will never update again, and a frozen to-do list does not look frozen — it looks like a to-do list, which is §12's orphaned-projection failure in about the worst place it could land: somebody works the stale list and re-does finished work. The link rows are the ONLY map from a platform task to its copy, so they survive as `_bw_dropped_task_google_links_20261011` (dumped and read back first — 39 rows verified in the dump). `scripts/retire-google-tasks.mts` clears the remote copies, dry run by default because it deletes from Richard's and Eric's own lists; the live dry run reads **36 for moose@, 3 for tuaone@**. Deleting is the right verb here and unusually so: these are not records but COPIES of records that still exist in full, which is the line `queueTaskRemoval` drew before it was deleted. The script needs the `tasks` scope that the source no longer asks for — tokens minted before today still carry it, since removing a scope changes nothing already stored (§12, 10-11), so it works now and stops working the moment either mailbox re-consents. It probes the scope once per mailbox and says that, rather than reporting 39 identical 403s.

**Two stale recorded reasons found and corrected rather than inherited.** `resolveOwner` refused to run without `LEAD_TASK_OWNER` on the grounds that *"an unassigned task never reaches Google Tasks at all"* — true of a per-person sync, and false the moment the board publishes to a shared sheet with its own Unassigned tab. The stop is kept, but now as a judgement (a bid nobody owns is how a bid gets missed) rather than a mechanism, with the change recorded, because §12's lesson is that a comment explaining why something cannot work is the thing least likely to be re-checked. And `leads/tasks.ts`'s rule 2 — nothing derived from the clock — survived for a *different* reason than the one written down: the diff-based push it was protecting is gone, but these strings are stored on the row and stored columns are what Pepper emails (§12, 09-26).

**⚠ `git rm` STAGES IMMEDIATELY, AND THE INDEX IS SHARED BETWEEN THE TWO SESSIONS.** The seven Google-Tasks deletions were staged early with `git rm`, and the concurrent text-message session's commit swept all seven into `7a8b883 docs: open items for the text-message sweep and the call-recording half` — its own `add -A`, its own message. Nothing was lost (the tree is correct and the build is of this commit), only misattributed, and rewriting history under a live concurrent session would have been far worse than a wrong commit message. §12 already says to stage by name; the new half is that **staging early is itself the hazard**, because the shared thing is not just the working tree but the index. Delete with plain `rm` and stage the deletion at commit time. Fifth recorded occurrence, and the first in this direction — previous ones were this session absorbing the other's work, not the other way round.

**Verification.** 23 new tests, all four arms of the truth table named individually; 250/250 across the suite. `tsc` clean, lint unchanged at 21 problems (the §9 baseline, so no new noise). `gen-types` regenerated 100 of 100 tables — and its refusal-while-dirty guard is why it was safe to run: the other session had committed `src/types/database.ts` minutes earlier, so the file was clean, and the before/after table-name diff is exactly two renames plus `task_sheet_state` and nothing else. Build exit 0 with `/api/cron/task-sheet` registered, app answers 200, old launchd agent booted out and removed, `install-agents.sh` loaded 20 including `cron-task-sheet`. The route was hit live and returned `sheets_api_disabled` with the enable URL — which also proves the middleware entry works, since the §12 tell for a missing one is `{"error":"Not authenticated"}` rather than the route's own reply. `tailnet-setup.sh` and `lmstudio-check.sh` both green.

**Left for Richard:** enable the Sheets API (one click, link in the cron response and in §13), then the 06:50-ish cron builds the workbook and shares it. After confirming it works, `scripts/retire-google-tasks.mts --apply` clears the 39 stale copies out of the two Google Tasks lists.

**Done 2026-10-11 (a text is read only if it is clearly work, and forgotten if it is not):**

Richard read the first live selection and narrowed the rule the same evening. His words, which are the specification: *"if the text clearly references a project then we should incorporate them. I am just saying that if the text isn't work related to ignore it. Was thinking that if it isn't clear that it is a work text or not and the person on the text isn't in the CRM then we could ignore it… I just don't want to clutter the CRM with private text so applying some sort of discernment would be great."*

**The first reading of that was wrong, and measuring it is what showed why.** Taken as a hard gate — only conversations with a CRM contact in them — it admits **14 of 530 conversations, 258 messages**, and excludes Eric's thread, all four Ber Wilson group chats and the Steelton thread that had just routed at 0.99. The cause is not the rule but the directory: **96 contacts on file, 12 with a phone number.** Every valuable conversation reads `0/N participants are contacts` because the numbers were never filled in — Eric's record holds …5507 and he texts from …6519. A hard gate would have switched the feature off and looked like a privacy win.

**⚠ THE BAR WAS A SCORE AND IT NEEDED TO BE A RULE, BECAUSE A SUM ADMITS FOR REASONS THAT DO NOT JUSTIFY EACH OTHER.** `knownParty +2`, `namedRecords +2`, `dealTerms>=2 +1`, `>=4 +1`, `bigMoney +1`, floor 2 — so *"2 deal terms; deal-size figure"* cleared the bar on a 125-message thread with no record named and nobody on it in the directory, which is indistinguishable from two friends buying a house. Now two independent doors and ambiguity is not one of them: the conversation **clearly names a record** (whole name, or a word rare in this corpus), **or** somebody on it is a **CRM contact AND there is a work signal**. Measured: 38 → 21 conversations, 6,830 → 6,335 messages. It keeps Eric, My Golden Soldiers, Ber Wilson Executive Team, BER WILSON BRAINTRUST, Ber Wilson RE / Development Team, Steelton, Delta, Weirton, Box Elder, WES; it withholds 17, one of them carrying **nine deal terms from a stranger**. `score` survives only to order the dry run by strength and decides nothing.

**A CRM contact alone stopped admitting too, which is the half that is easy to miss.** It used to clear the whole bar on the reasoning that a directory entry is a human filing decision. But directory membership says who somebody is, not what this conversation is about — a contact can also be a friend, and "ok / thanks" is not work. Six conversations were withheld on exactly this and the reason string now says so: *"a CRM contact, but nothing work-related in it — private"*.

**`internal` stopped being a door, so "same goes for Eric" holds literally.** It used to return `business: true, score: 99` before anything was scored. Eric now qualifies on his own merits — his conversation names `steelton`, `delta`, `dino`, `elite` and more — so there is no exception for him in the code at all. It stays a FLAG because attribution downstream needs it, and it still beats the broadcast heuristic: `automated` fires on a thread never replied to inside the window, and since his number is not on his contact record a quiet fortnight would otherwise have had his thread thrown out as marketing.

**⚠ AND A REWRITTEN TEST CAUGHT THAT THE FLAG HAD STOPPED BEING SET.** The final return still hardcoded `internal: false`, which was correct while `internal` returned early with its own object and silently wrong the moment it fell through. Every colleague's thread reported `internal: false` while its own reason string read *"internal — every other participant is on the team"*. That flag is what stops a commitment in a two-insider thread being attributed to a teammate as though they were the counterparty, and a party record being invented from a colleague.

**Stage 2 is the answer to "clutter", and it is a different question from privacy.** Whether a CONVERSATION is business can be decided before anything is read. Whether a particular DAY of it is cannot — the people who run a company by text also arrange dinner on the same thread. So a session is admitted on the conversation's merits, read once by the model, and then either kept or **forgotten**: `relevance === 'noise'` now discards `raw_markdown` the moment it is classified, inside the summarize pass rather than on the next text sweep, because the sweep runs four times a day and a backstop there would leave a personal conversation's full text searchable for up to six hours.

**⚠ NULLING THE COLUMN IS THE MECHANISM BECAUSE IT IS A CHOKE POINT.** Four separate things read `email_threads.raw_markdown` — the keyword search behind `/api/thread-links`, `commitments/extract-phase`, People Intake's profile builder in `contacts/profile-intake.ts`, and `leads/triage-phase`. Filtering each would be four places to forget and a fifth next year. The text stops existing instead. `apply-phase` already did `raw_markdown ?? ''` and `deltaFor('')` returns null, so nothing needed guarding there. **The row is the tombstone** (§12): deleting it would have the next sweep re-ingest, re-summarize and re-forget the same conversation nightly, forever. What survives is `{"relevance":"noise"}`, the marker, and the subject — metadata, not content. The model's prose summary goes with the text, because *"casual personal text exchange regarding weekend plans"* is harmless but a one-line description of a private conversation is still one, and the next one might be medical.

**Applied retroactively rather than going forward only**, since the instruction was about texts already held: **23 sessions removed** from the 9 conversations the new rule no longer admits (printed before deleting, §12), and **34 noise sessions redacted**. No `updates`, chunks or commitments cascaded — all the derived work belonged to admitted conversations. 137 → 114 sessions, of which 47 are classified so far: **34 noise and 13 work, so the per-session filter is doing roughly three quarters of the discernment.**

**Verified.** 251 tests pass (up from 227; four rewritten to encode the new rule rather than the old threshold, which is what caught the `internal` flag bug). Lint back to its pre-existing 21. Build clean, deployed, app answering 200.

**Still outstanding:** `bw-snapshot` has no Full Disk Access grant of its own — the first run inherited it from the terminal — so `com.berwilson.snapshot` cannot read anything until it is granted. And the directory gap is now the thing limiting coverage rather than the filter: 84 of 96 contacts have no phone number, and door 2 cannot fire for any of them.

**Done 2026-10-11 (text messages become correspondence, and the dry run found the filter's real defect):**

Richard asked for three things: read his texts (particularly Eric's) and make tasks and project updates the way Pepper does with mail; read Eric's texts from Eric's own devices; and ingest the phone-call recordings that land in the Notes app. This session built the first. The call half is specified and not started.

**The read half already existed and nothing used it.** `src/lib/imessage/{read,decode,classify}.ts` — 1,350 lines with tests — landed earlier the same day across three commits and deliberately stopped before writing anything: *"Nothing was written. Decide the set, then ingestion can be wired to it."* No cron route, no API route, no migration, no plist. The work here is the writer.

**The architecture finding: nothing below `fetch-phase.ts` is Gmail-specific.** `email_threads` is the pipeline's front door, and summarize → cluster → stage → route → apply → embed → commitments → predecide all read that table. Only three of its columns are NOT NULL without a default (`fingerprint`, `mailbox`, `gmail_thread_id`). So a text conversation written as `email_threads` rows inherits all eight phases, `/decide`, retrieval, the commitments ledger and Pepper's morning note with **no change to any of them**. The whole ingestion is one new cron that translates and hands over — `src/lib/imessage/to-thread.ts`. A parallel pipeline for texts would have been a second place for every one of those decisions to drift.

**⚠ A CHAT IS NOT A THREAD, AND MODELLING IT AS ONE WOULD HAVE GROWN FOREVER.** A mail thread is a bounded conversation that ends. Eric's chat is 5,492 messages over 180 days and never ends — as one row it would be re-summarized on every sweep, with `deltaFor` posting a monotonically growing update onto the record. So the unit is a SESSION: a burst separated from the next by six hours of silence. Measured across 49,183 consecutive-message gaps in 365 days — median gap 2.2 minutes, 11,835 gaps over 30 minutes, 5,476 over six hours, 3,084 over a day. On Eric's thread: 3h → 285 sessions averaging 19.3 messages; 6h → 183 sessions averaging 30.0, longest 219; 12h → 79 sessions averaging 69.5, longest 409. Six hours is one session per day, which is what a day's texting about a deal is. Twelve hours is the one that breaks something: 409 messages renders past the local model's 40,000-character cap and would be silently truncated.

**Only CLOSED sessions are written, and that is what makes it cheap.** A session whose last message is inside the gap is still being written; emitting it would re-summarize the same conversation every run at 30-60s of local model each, and LM Studio serves one request at a time, so that queue is paid by whoever is waiting on Ber AI. The cost is up to six hours of latency on a text. That is also why the 04:40 cron run is the load-bearing one: last night's texting closes around 03:00 and Pepper's note goes out at 06:50, so without a run between them every evening conversation waits an extra day to reach the morning it belongs to.

**⚠ THE DRY RUN'S WHOLE POINT, DEMONSTRATED: COUNTING NAME TOKENS SELECTED A 664-MESSAGE PERSONAL THREAD.** The first live survey chose 33 of 530 conversations, and reading it showed why one of them: *"names Stockton Power Nexus - ER Hospital & Medevac Airport Tower"* — matched on **hospital** (8 chats) and **airport** (9 chats), two of that name's six tokens and an entirely ordinary pair of words in a year of family texts. `Felix Gold Alaska Treasure Creek Inc.` did the same through **gold** and **creek** on 1,181 and 566 messages; `Dino plumbing and HVAC` through **plumbing** and **hvac** on a nine-message thread that was somebody asking for a plumber. **A six-token name offers fifteen pairs, so counting makes a LONG name easier to match by accident than a short one — the opposite of what counting implies.**

The fix is not "require a rare word", because that breaks the mirror case: `myton` (9 chats) and `rail` (4) are each too common to name a record alone, yet together they are **Myton Rail's entire name**. So a name is matched when the matched tokens either cover the WHOLE name (two tokens minimum — `Case Garage` keeps its lesson, since `case` is dropped as ordinary and `garage` alone must earn it on rarity) or include one token distinctive in this corpus. Measured here: `premier` 1 chat, `corridor` 1, `tonga` 1, `wendover` 2, `workforce` 2, `dino` 3, `elite` 3 — against `hospital` 8, `airport` 9, `gold` 10, `services` 11, `american` 14. The first list names a deal; the second is what a year of family texts says anyway. So the first 30-day cron run judged `stockton`, `strategic` and `bloom` identifying when over 180 days they are ordinary (4, 5 and 5 chats) — **the filter gets looser the less it looks at.** The ingest window is a question about scope and the calibration window a question about evidence, and they are not the same number: the sweep now reads 180 days to calibrate and writes sessions from 30.

**The two-stage filter is the part that makes a conversation-level false positive cheap.** The classifier judges the whole CONVERSATION (classify.ts's privacy decision — per-session scoring would leak the odd private evening out of a personal thread every time a word matched), and the model then judges each SESSION for relevance. Verified live: the first three sessions summarized came back `relevance: noise` — *"casual personal text exchange regarding weekend plans and family updates"* for the …8693 thread that the `williams` rare word had selected. Noise is excluded from clustering and embedding, so a conversation-level false positive costs one model call, not a wrong record.

`CRON_SECRET` rotated cleanly. The assumption that needed checking first was where the launchd crons get it: not hardcoded in 15 plists as expected, but read at invocation time — `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(grep '^CRON_SECRET=' .env.local | cut -d= -f2-)"` — so rotation is one line in `.env.local` plus a kickstart. Verified old → 401, new → 200, and a launchd-style invocation → 200.

Supabase keys deliberately NOT rotated, and the measurement is why: `JWT_SECRET`/`ANON_KEY`/`SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` are referenced 25 times across 8 containers, the anon key is baked into the built bundle (found in `.next/static/chunks/0bhwgvpkpuywn.js`, because `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is build-time), and 33 live refresh sessions across 3 users would be invalidated. Against that: Supabase is `tailnet only` on :8443, so an exfiltrated service-role key is unusable without first being on the tailnet. Highest risk, lowest payoff of the four.

⚠ **AND THEN THE GOOGLE ROTATION BROKE MAIL, BY DOING EXACTLY WHAT IT WAS DESIGNED TO DO.** The sequence was deliberate and, for any other provider, correct: capture the three old refresh tokens, have the humans re-consent (verified the script sends `access_type=offline` + `prompt=select_account consent`, so fresh tokens really are issued), validate the NEW tokens against Google — all three returned access tokens with the right scope counts, 11 for moose@, 8 for info@, 8 for tuaone@, matching the documented tiering — and only then revoke the old ones, so there was no outage window.

**`https://oauth2.googleapis.com/revoke` does not revoke a token. It revokes the GRANT.** Google keeps one authorization per client+user, so revoking any refresh token issued under it invalidates every token for that authorization — including the one minted ninety seconds earlier from the same consent screen. Three `HTTP 200` revocations, then all three mailboxes `invalid_grant`. The validation step worked perfectly and proved tokens that the next step destroyed.

What this cost and did not cost: the security objective was MET — every token that existed while Grok Bot held Full Disk Access is invalid, which is the whole point. The cost is a second round of browser consents, and mail/Drive/Calendar/Tasks being down between the two. What it should have been: **re-consent IS the rotation.** `prompt=consent` issues a new refresh token and the platform stops using the old one the moment the file is rewritten; the old token's remaining validity is the residual risk, and accepting it is cheaper than a revoke that cannot be scoped. Revoke only to end access entirely, and expect to re-consent afterwards. Added to §12 under Google Workspace.

Also this session: `tccutil reset SystemPolicyAllFiles com.anysphere.sand` — Grok Bot held Full Disk Access, granted 2026-10-09 17:18:18, and nothing else: no Accessibility, no Screen Recording, no synthetic input, and its own `messagesEnabled` was false. ⚠ Revoking FDA does NOT protect the credentials, and that is worth stating plainly: `.env.local` and `~/berwilson-data/google-oauth-tokens.json` live in ordinary directories TCC does not gate, so any process running as the user reads them with no prompt and no record. FDA only ever gated Messages, Mail and Photos.

**The first answer was about WHERE the agent sits, not which model it is.** Grokbot is a computer-use agent — it reads the screen, the mail and the texts — and Richard intended to run it **on the Mac Studio**, which is production. Every containment control in this codebase filters rows *server-side at read time* (`hiddenProjectIds`, `dropHidden`, `scrubHiddenProjects`, `readOpenCommitments`), so a screen reader sits downstream of all of them: the lock is not weak, it is in the wrong place relative to something reading pixels. Worse, the confidential step-up **inverts into a leak** — clear TOTP and the project opens for 30 minutes, so an agent capturing continuously ships the protected deal out with the lock cleared and Richard's own hand on it. The 30-minute absolute TTL bounds human exposure; it bounds nothing about a capturer. And the box holds credentials, not just data: `google-oauth-tokens.json` (refresh tokens, all three mailboxes), `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, `CRON_SECRET`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`.

**Grokbot's own plan was a genuine improvement and was adopted in shape.** MCP removes the screen entirely; its plan also independently landed three rules this repo had already paid for — policy enforced server-side never by the assistant, fail-closed defaults, and never revealing that a blocked record exists. Six corrections were made, two of them load-bearing:

- **`ask_crm` was dropped, and with it the three-tier model.** The plan had the local LLM read full records *including* `summary_only` projects, then stripped dollar figures, emails and a denylist from the output. That makes a regex over free-form LLM prose the only barrier to a cloud assistant, and it cannot work: *"the counterparty is pushing closing to the first of November"* names no project, carries no figure, and discloses a live negotiating position on Steelton. This repo had already measured this class of filter in September — share-of-prose and share-of-short-tokens each withheld >11% of the index — and the failure direction is inverted here: there a false positive cost evidence, here a false negative costs the secret. **There are two tiers, not three.** `summary_only` sounds like a middle ground and is actually full access laundered through an unverifiable filter.
- **The third visibility system was refused.** The platform already has `projects.confidential` + `step_up_sessions` and `documents.classification`; a third with an undefined interaction (what happens when `confidential=true` and `visibility='open'`?) breaks "one quantity, one definition". `confidential` already means *never leaves the box*, so it excludes categorically and a new field could only further restrict.
- **Funnel was not turned on.** `deploy/tailnet-setup.sh` asserts TWO listeners; a third is outside the only check watching for them disappearing, and §12 warns `matchesPrefix` is not method-aware — so `/api/mcp` is allowlisted in `middleware.ts` as an **exact match, not a prefix**, deliberately, so anything added underneath it later is not silently unauthenticated too.

**Done 2026-10-09 (a retirement the source undoes overnight, and 77 duplicate documents nobody could retire):**

Richard's ask: *"What is the best way to declutter projects with out of date documents? I would like Pepper to recognize when a document is a more recent version of the same document and get rid of the old ones.. what do you think?"* then *"Just do how you think is best."*

**The premise measured away, as usual.** 651 live documents, 185 pairs at ≥90% text similarity within one record. Classified: **65** were the same contract template sent to DIFFERENT counterparties (`BW MNDA Sean Reyes`, `Tyler`, `DA Davidson`, `Firm Power` — each 11,502 characters, scoring **1.000** against each other), 37 carried an `(email subject)` suffix, 18 Drive `(n)` decoration, 6 `Copy of`, 5 image-OCR noise, 54 genuine judgement calls. So the largest near-duplicate class in the corpus is the one where merging destroys a distinct legal instrument, and it is textually indistinguishable from a real version chain. **Similarity can say two documents are nearly the same; it can never say one REPLACES the other.** The version-chain queue Richard asked for was not built, and should not be built on similarity.

What the clutter actually was: **one missing column.** Only the email-attachment importer wrote `content_sha256` — 103 of 666 rows had a hash — so its content dedupe could not see a single Drive-imported document. It collided on the NAME instead, `disambiguateName` appended the thread subject, and a second row landed. That is the signature on 37 of the 185 pairs, and the hypothesis was confirmed by the fingerprint: in every suffixed pair the suffixed copy is the one carrying a hash. Two Drive files holding the same bytes (the GridEdge MNDA filed under both `Signed MNDA's` and `NDA NC`) are two different `drive_file_id`s, so neither Drive importer could see that collision either.

**And the retirement could not stick.** `scripts/dedupe-documents.mts` already existed, already found 53 duplicate groups, and **refused to act on 48 of them** — correctly: both importers treat a superseded row whose file is still in its folder as `returning` and call `restoreDocument()` on it, so superseding a Drive-sourced copy is reversed by the next nightly run. Measured: of 15 superseded rows, the 10 that survived were files that had genuinely left Drive and the other 5 had no `drive_file_id` at all. **No Drive-sourced document had ever been durably retired — which means the Retire button on the Documents tab was a no-op for most documents, not just for the deduper.** The 2026-09-30 migration comment describes this exact bug for `excluded_at` and fixed it only for "not knowledge"; plain "retired" was left behind.

The fix is one distinction: **a supersession the SOURCE made is the source's to undo; one a HUMAN made is not.** `superseded_by_hand` is held out of both importers' `known` map and checked BEFORE the restore branch (after it, `returning` has already un-retired the row and the check protects nothing — the ordering the exclusion check was written to avoid). `duplicate_of` names the copy that was kept, so the screen says which and "not a duplicate" is one click. The vanish path deliberately sets neither, because a file dragged back out of Archive should return.

Built: `src/lib/documents/dedupe.ts` (one hash definition, scope-loaded hash map, `findDuplicate` with an `ignoreId` so an edited file does not match the version it replaces); both Drive importers write the hash on insert AND update and retire a duplicate **at the door** — inserted so its `drive_file_id` blocks tomorrow's re-import, then superseded at once, never reaching the index; `scripts/backfill-document-hashes.mts` (fill-only, both tables, counts the reason beside the number).

**Results.** Hash coverage 103/666 → **708/708 and 101/101**. 42 byte-identical groups in `documents` and 29 in `opportunity_documents` — **77 duplicates retired, ~500 chunks dropped**, second run reports 0. `documents` 666 → 708 over the session because drive-watch imported 42 new files meanwhile; nothing was restored.

⚠ **IDENTICAL BYTES ARE NOT THE SAME DOCUMENT WHEN THE NAME IS THE ONLY THING CARRYING THE DISTINCTION.** The four `BW MNDA <counterparty>` files are byte-identical copies of the blank template, one prepared per counterparty, none filled in yet. Retiring three loses nothing from retrieval and destroys the only record that an NDA was drafted for three of those parties. A group is acted on only when the names AGREE once machine decoration is stripped; the guard held back exactly that one group out of 42, and nothing else. The mirror of the existing rule that a name is not evidence of sameness — here the name is the ONLY evidence of difference.

⚠ **The bug demonstrated itself on this session's own data, inside the hour.** After the first apply the second run was clean. Twenty minutes later it reported 5 groups again: the hourly `cron-drive-watch` (:20, hitting `api/cron/drive-sync`) had run against the still-deployed OLD build and un-retired 4 retirements — leaving them in a state only the old restore can produce, `superseded_by_hand` set with `superseded_at` NULL. `next start` loads the build at boot; the fix existed in the working tree and not in production. 13 rows had drifted into that state by the time the new build was live.

⚠ **And that exposed a latent bug in the fix itself:** both guards read the lock WITHOUT checking the timestamp, so a live row carrying a stale lock would be held out of `known` forever and never updated again. Both now require both columns, and the migration clears the rows that drifted.

⚠ **31% of `opportunity_documents` was redundant copies** (29 groups, 31 of 101 rows) — a higher share than `documents` carried. A dedupe pass covering one of two parallel tables leaves the half it misses reading as clean. `supersedeDocument` took a table target rather than a fork, because the two tables keep their chunks under different keys (`document_id` vs `opportunity_document_id`) — a supersede written for one drops NO chunks for the other, leaving the row reading as retired while every passage keeps being cited.

Three measurements that changed a decision mid-build: the `keep` preference originally tie-broke on name LENGTH, which rewarded exactly the noise it was meant to drop (`Copy of Tensor MNDA` kept over `Tensor MNDA`, `R0183 (1).pdf` over `R0183.pdf`) — replaced by a decoration score that treats a trailing parenthetical of digits and dashes as an identifier, not decoration, so `Title Commitment - AS (02-0138-0000).pdf` keeps its parcel number. Extracted-text LENGTH was dropped as a tiebreak after measuring it: only 3 of 42 groups differ at all and by 0.1–0.4%, which is extraction jitter on identical bytes, not a better read — only emptiness is a real signal. And `nameStem` needed a fixpoint loop, because decoration NESTS: one Elite Solutions file carried an email-subject parenthetical after an export timestamp, so a single pass stripped the parenthetical, left the timestamp stranded at the end, and held back a pair that was plainly the same file.

Also: retired documents moved out of the Documents tab's reading list into a collapsed "Show N retired (N duplicates)" disclosure. They had rendered inline at 60% opacity, which made decluttering self-defeating — retiring the 46 duplicates would have put 10 dimmed rows among Myton Rail's 21 real ones and 14 among DUBHES's 80. A retirement has to REMOVE the row from the list to be worth making, while staying one click away. The reason moved out of a `title` tooltip into the row, because a tooltip does not exist on a phone and "duplicate of X" is the whole information.

The gen-types guard worked as designed: it refused to overwrite `src/types/database.ts` while it held an uncommitted diff, and the diff was verified as this session's own two columns before `--force`.

DEPLOYED + MIGRATED + PUSHED.

**Done 2026-10-09 (the queue gets a keyboard, and a loading boundary takes the record down):**

Richard's ask: *"Is there anything you would do to enhance the UI or UX?"* then *"Do them all. Do what you think is best while keeping the system scalable and efficient."* Seven items were proposed after reading the surfaces; all seven were done, plus two defects found by opening the result in a browser — one of them a production outage caused by the session itself.

---

### What the survey actually found

The craft level here is high and the obvious wins were already taken: ⌘K already searches every record type with area chips, toasts and `ConfirmDialog` are everywhere, `focus-visible` landed on 10-08, empty states exist, 44px touch targets are honoured. So nothing proposed was "add a design system". What was left were places where the UI does not match where the work happens:

| | Found by |
|---|---|
| `/decide` had no keyboard at all — `toggle(key)`, one click per row, no range select, and the batch bar in normal flow | reading `DecideClient.tsx:448` against a queue of 279 |
| ⌘K with an empty query returned ONE row (`if (!t) return []`) | reading `CommandPalette.tsx:85` |
| the Ask Ber AI dock matched `/projects/<uuid>` and nothing else | `AskBerAIDock.tsx:22` |
| `/contacts` is a 3-up card grid with an 80px portrait — six records a screen of 83, 80 of which have no photograph | `ContactsClient.tsx:279` |
| the whole `opportunities/[id]` tab family had no `loading.tsx` while `projects/[id]` carries thirteen | `find src/app -name loading.tsx` |
| 25 `notFound()` calls and **zero** `not-found.tsx` | `grep -c` |
| no `beforeunload` anywhere in the repo, against the three longest forms in it | `grep -rn beforeunload src` → nothing |

### The queue's keyboard

`j`/`k` (and the arrows) move a cursor, `x` ticks, `shift`+click takes a range, `a` accepts **through the existing confirmation** — a mistyped key must not create a project — `Enter` opens, `esc` clears both the selection and the cursor. The handler ignores modifier combinations so ⌘K/⌘J still work, ignores keys typed into a field, and is inactive while a batch is running or a dialog is open: a key that queues another write behind seventy in flight is worse than no shortcut.

Two things were taken from existing precedent rather than invented. The cursor is clamped at READ time (`Math.min(cursor, visible.length - 1)`) exactly as the command palette clamps its active index — the list shrinks under the cursor as rows are accepted, and an index past the end must neither throw nor silently jump to the top of a queue the reader was halfway down. And the shift-range only ADDS: a shift-click that could silently clear thirty gathered rows is not worth the symmetry.

The batch bar is now `sticky top-0` (the same idiom as `ProjectsClient.tsx:418`). Measured on the live queue: Accept had scrolled off screen by row twelve of 279.

⚠ **The checkbox handler had to move from `onChange` to `onClick`.** Only the click event carries `shiftKey`. A keyboard Space on a checkbox dispatches a click too, so both routes land in one handler; `onChange` stays as a no-op for React's controlled-input contract.

### ⌘K opens on what you last had open

`src/lib/recents.ts` keeps the last twelve records per browser in `localStorage`, written by `<TrackVisit>` — a null-rendering client component mounted by the page that knows the record's NAME. That placement is the whole design: the app shell sees a URL and a page title, and "Projects" is not the name of the deal the reader wants to get back to. Six mount sites (project, opportunity, contact, vendor, steel deal, investor); adding a seventh is one line with no registry to keep in step. The label is rewritten on every visit, so a renamed deal shows its current name.

Read as the palette's initial state rather than in an effect, because the palette is mounted fresh on every open — there is no stale list to refresh, and no new `set-state-in-effect` lint error.

### ⌘J finally knows an opportunity

The dock's scope was one inline regex, so standing on an opportunity — the record type carrying most of the live pipeline since 09-23 — opened the agent portfolio-wide and the reader had to name the deal in the question. The scope is now a TABLE (`SCOPE_ROUTES`), and `opportunityId` runs the whole way down: dock → `AgentChat` → `POST /api/ai/agent` → `AgentContext` → its own preamble.

A sibling preamble, not one generalised function: a project asks "can we deliver it and get paid", an opportunity asks "should we do this at all", so the fields are the counterparty, the thesis and the next step — and `stage` does not exist on the record at all. Collapsing them would have produced a preamble half full of "Not specified", which §12 already names as a lie the model repeats with confidence.

`AgentChat` was spelling its scope out in THREE places (the history load, the dropped-stream recovery lookup, the POST body), so a second record type meant finding all three or scoping two of them differently. One `scopeQuery` memo now, and `tsc` names every reader when a third kind is added.

Migration `20261009000002`: `agent_conversations.opportunity_id`, nullable FK with `on delete cascade` beside `project_id`, plus `agent_conversations_one_record` — a CHECK that at most one is set — and a partial index. The route refuses both-at-once with a 400 rather than letting the CHECK answer 500, since §12 is explicit that a 500 reads as the reader's own mistake. Verified in psql: both pointers refused, opportunity-only accepted, test rows removed. Verified live: asking "Summarize where this deal stands" from the Zenthium record wrote `project_id` NULL, `opportunity_id` 84c5f711.

### The directory's default is now a row

`list` (64px, avatar + name + title·company + mailbox + tags + project count) against `cards`, remembered per browser. The default is a measurement, not a taste: 80 of 83 contacts have no photograph, so the photo-forward grid was spending three-quarters of its area on an initial in a circle. The cards stay for the day the directory has faces in it — the open item about contact photos is still open.

One delete path serves both renderings (`useContactDelete`), because a second density is not a reason for a second delete path.

### Loading boundaries, and the outage

`projects/[id]` carries thirteen per-tab `loading.tsx` files and the opportunity family carried one. The reason is not redundancy: **a loading boundary belongs to its own segment**, so `opportunities/[id]/loading.tsx` fires on the first load of the record and never again, however many tabs are clicked. Eleven files added, four shared shapes behind them (`src/components/shared/tab-skeletons.tsx`) so a new tab names a shape in one line.

⚠⚠ **And a twelfth file took production down.** `opportunities/[id]/(detail)/loading.tsx` — a boundary at the ROOT of the route group, beside that group's own `page.tsx` — was added to cover the walk back to Overview. It typechecked, `npm run build` exited **0**, every route was listed in the build output, and then every request to `/opportunities/[id]` answered:

```
Invariant: The client reference manifest for route "/opportunities/[id]" does not exist.
```

The manifest is emitted at the GROUPED path (`.next/server/app/opportunities/[id]/(detail)/page_client-reference-manifest.js`) and the runtime looks for it de-grouped. Found by opening the page in a browser four minutes after deploying — not by any check in the pipeline. Removed, rebuilt, verified; the eleven boundaries inside the group's SUBSEGMENTS are unaffected and were each confirmed live. The reason is written at the top of `tab-skeletons.tsx`, where the next person to add one will be reading, and as a §12 rule.

**The lesson is not about Next.js.** A build that exits 0 having listed the route is not evidence the route answers. The deploy runbook asserts the tailnet listeners, the env, and LM Studio — and then checks that `/login` returns 200, which is one route of ninety-seven.

### The two small ones

`src/app/not-found.tsx`: 25 `notFound()` calls were landing on Next's built-in page — a line of text outside the app shell, no sidebar, no way back but the browser's own button. The copy covers both reasons a record 404s here, because the access guards answer `notFound()` deliberately: a record a viewer may not see must not be distinguishable from one that does not exist, so the page may never claim it was deleted.

`UnsavedGuard`: `beforeunload` for the browser, and a CAPTURE-phase click listener on `document` for in-app `Link` clicks, which `beforeunload` never sees because the page never unloads and App Router exposes no navigation event to block. Deliberately NOT a localStorage draft: restoring one means writing values back into controls, and half the fields in these forms are custom components holding React state (`DatePicker`, `TagInput`) that a DOM write would not reach — the restore would silently drop exactly the fields a reader is least likely to re-check. Verified live on `/projects/new`: typed, clicked Tasks, got the dialog; "Keep editing" stayed; "Discard and leave" navigated; an untouched form navigates with no dialog.

### Found while verifying

⚠ **`/decide` was rendering a chip reading "Unfiled document NaN".** The counter map was seeded `{ all, lead: 0, intake: 0, review: 0 }` while `DecideKind` has five members, so `c['document']` was `undefined` and `undefined++` is `NaN` — and the economics chip showed no count at all. Pre-existing, visible on the live queue, and invisible to `tsc` because the map is `Record<string, number>`. Seeded from `KIND_META`'s own keys now. After: 81 + 122 + 38 + 38 + 0 = 279, which is the total shown.

⚠ **The untyped cast on `/contacts` was a workaround whose reason had expired.** `const db = supabase as unknown as SupabaseClient`, commented *"bypass generated types — parties.status / entities.category added via migration"*. Both columns have been typed since `gen-types` was repaired on 10-08. Deleted; the page typechecks against the generated client. This is the second instance of the 10-08 rule (a workaround's recorded reason must be re-tested before it is inherited) in two days.

### Shared-repo mechanics

The other session was mid-feature in this working tree throughout. `src/types/database.ts` was regenerated with `--force` AFTER applying this session's migration, and the regenerated file was diffed against a copy of theirs first: **the only difference was this session's column**, which proves their file was pure generator output and that the regeneration was a strict superset. Staged as a filtered patch of two hunks out of five, with the three dropped hunks named (`commitment_action_tokens`, `commitments`, `pepper_note_items`) and the staged diff grepped for their keywords (0 hits). Both sessions messaged each other before building, since the runbook builds the working tree and a kickstart restarts both sessions' code.

- `tsc --noEmit`: clean at every step. Three builds, all exit 0 — including the one that took the opportunity record down.
- Routes with a `loading.tsx`: 50 → 61 of 97 pages. With an `error.tsx`: 51 → 52.
