**Done 2026-10-06 (an SPV becomes a record on the project, with the people in it):**

Richard's ask: *"On each of our development projects we have an SPV around Land, SPV around Energy and SPV around Data Center. Each will have different participants, equity splits, capital raise etc… Can you modify so that I can easily add SPVs to each project? How would you organize these massive projects?"*

Half of it already existed and the half he actually wanted did not. `economics_spvs` already held many vehicles per deal with `purpose in (land, energy, data_center, housing, other)`, `DEFAULT_SPV_PURPOSES` was already exactly his trio, and the "Set up Land, Energy and Data Center" button had shipped the day before. What the table held was **eight columns and one ownership number** — `bw_ownership_pct` — with everything not Ber Wilson's as unnamed residue. No participant list, no way to total splits to 100%, no capital figure, and **no edit path at all**: changing a split meant deleting the vehicle and re-adding it, and `economics_lines.spv_id` is `on delete set null`, so that silently reparented every revenue line to Ber Wilson Corporation at 100%.

⚠ **THE PARENT WAS WRONG, AND THAT IS WHAT DECIDED THE SHAPE.** `economics_spvs.economics_id` was `not null references deal_economics(id) on delete cascade`. So a vehicle could not exist until an economics model had been built, and deleting that model destroyed every vehicle with it — including, once this feature landed, its cap table and its committed capital. An SPV is a **structural** fact, true long before anyone computes a dollar: the land goes in one LLC and the energy in another. It now hangs off the project or the opportunity directly (shared-children convention), and `deal_economics` reads it.

⚠ **AN SPV WAS NAMED THREE UNCONNECTED WAYS, WITH ZERO FOREIGN KEYS BETWEEN THEM.** `economics_spvs` (0 rows); `org_nodes` with `kind='spv'` — **15 rows**, the real corporate chart at `/company/structure`, holding *Myton Energy SPV*, *Myton Rail SPV*, *Myton Data Center*, *Myton Residential/Commercial SPV* and *Stockton 150MW SPV*, **none of them linked to any project**; and `entities` via `investments.spv_entity_id`, whose picker offered **the entire unfiltered vendor directory** (5 rows, all `category='vendor'`, not one an SPV) with no validation that the entity was an SPV, belonged to the project, or existed. The 2026-07-10 investors migration states *"SPVs are `entities` rows"*; the 2026-10-05 economics route states the opposite and refuses to create one. Both were right about their own half.

**Richard's four decisions, asked before anything was built.** The site stays **one project** — one map pin, one parcel schedule, one Drive folder, one cast, one negotiation — with the vehicles as children of it, rather than one project per SPV under a parent (`parent_project_id` is used on **0 of 14** projects, and an SPV is a financing and liability structure, not a scope of work: one EPC contract can be earned across two of them). **Capital raise is the participant ledger**, not new raise plumbing. **An optional `org_node_id`** linking a deal's vehicle to the chart. **Its own count-gated Vehicles tab.**

**The shape: one ledger answers all three of his things, because they are one set of facts.** `project_spv_participants` carries, per row, the holder (`holder_name` always, plus a nullable link to `parties` / `entities` / `investors`), the role, the interest class, `equity_pct`, `capital_committed`, `capital_funded` and `preferred_return_pct` — so participants, equity splits and capital raise are the same rows and cannot drift. The vehicle carries a raise **target**, deliberately not a rollup of the rows beneath it. `investor_id` is the seam to `raises`/tranches, left unbuilt.

⚠ **WHICH ROW IS OURS IS A FLAG, NEVER A NAME MATCH** — `is_ber_wilson`, with `create unique index … where is_ber_wilson` allowing at most one per vehicle. "Ber Wilson" appears in the name of half the entities in this business, and matching on a name is how `bestMatch` once resolved the reader himself as a counterparty.

**The derivation, and why the engine needed no change.** `ownershipWeight()` in `capture.ts` reads one number per vehicle, so `resolveBwShare` supplies it: the ledger's flagged row when there are participants, the typed `bw_ownership_pct` when there are none, and it reports **which of the two it read** so the screen can say so. `computeEntityRollups`, `computeCaptureTiers` and the `Spv` interface are untouched. Measured live: three participants at 40/35/25 on a vehicle earning a $10M one-time fee → **$10M generated, $10M Ber Wilson gross, $4M net.**

⚠ **A LEDGER WITH NO BER WILSON ROW RETURNS NULL, NOT THE RESIDUE.** Inferring our share as 100 minus the others assumes the ledger is complete, and a half-entered cap table is the normal state of a live negotiation — so the inference would report a confident figure precisely when nobody has decided. Undetermined is held out of the net total; a guess is counted.

⚠ **A PRE-EXISTING BUG IN THE 10-05 ECONOMICS FEATURE, FOUND BY EXERCISING THE NEW ROUTES OVER REAL HTTP AND FIXED AT THE ROOT.** `normalizeCollectionPayload` set every whitelisted field it did not find in the body to an **explicit NULL** on a create — and an explicit NULL does not fall back to a column's DEFAULT, it violates its NOT NULL. So `POST /api/economics/<id>/sources` answered *null value in column "status" … violates not-null constraint* and `POST …/buckets` the same for `priority`. **Neither "Add a capacity source" nor "Add an allocation bucket" had ever worked**, on a tab that shipped the day before; nothing reported it because the failure is a 400 a reader reads as their own mistake. The fix is one line — a field absent from the body is now omitted, so the default applies — and it is **not** §12's multi-row rule reversed: that rule is about one INSERT carrying several rows, where Postgres demands a uniform column list, and `lineInsert` and the standard-vehicle bootstrap both still spell every column out. What is wrong is doing it from a single request body, where *absent* means *the caller did not say*. A field explicitly sent as `''` still writes null, because that is a reader clearing it.

⚠ **THE BOOTSTRAP NAMED A COMPANY WITH A COLUMN HEADING.** `SPV_PURPOSE_LABELS.data_center` is `'Data center'`, correct over a table column and wrong inside a legal entity's name: the first live run produced **"Myton Data center LLC"**, which then reads as a typo on every screen and signature block it reaches afterwards. `SPV_PURPOSE_NAMES` is the title-case twin, used only where the string becomes a name.

⚠ **AND IT DE-DUPED ON PURPOSE, WHICH MADE "COULD HAVE MORE" UNREACHABLE.** The route it replaces skipped any purpose already present, so a **second** energy vehicle could never be created through it — against an ask whose own words were *"(Could have more)"*. It de-dupes on **label** now, which is what the constraint actually says. Verified live: pressed twice reports `created: 0, skipped: 3`, and *Myton Energy II LLC* is reachable.

**What is refused, and in what words.** A revenue line naming another deal's vehicle: *"That vehicle does not belong to this deal."* The guard is in `src/lib/spvs/access.ts` rather than in either route, because **both** the line create and the line patch can set `spv_id` and a guard half the writers call is the half that gets forgotten. Deleting a vehicle that earns revenue: *"1 revenue line is earned in this vehicle. Move it first, or the revenue would silently become wholly ours."* A participant patched through the wrong vehicle: `Not found`, because every participant write filters on `spv_id` as well as the row id.

**Also:** `byEntity` — the per-vehicle gross and net the engine has computed since 10-05 and **no screen had ever rendered** — now appears on the vehicle card and in the Economics tab's summary. `org_node_name` is snapshotted beside the FK (the chart is a board people drag boxes around on, and the FK is `on delete set null`) and is **absent from the whitelist**, resolved server-side, because a client that could set it could make a vehicle claim to be an entity it is not. Both new tables carry the audit trigger and are in `_audited_in_full`, so moving a partner from 35% to 25% logs `{"equity_pct": {"old": 25, "new": 10}}` against a named person; the function was derived from `pg_get_functiondef` and patched programmatically under four assertions, never retyped.

**Verification.** **135 unit tests** (97 existing + 38 new, 20 of them on the derivation rule alone) and a new `scripts/verify-spvs.mts` with **25 live checks** against the real database: the constraints refuse what they exist to refuse, the ledger reaches the engine as one weight, the audit row names the field and the person, and a bootstrap pressed twice reports nothing. ⚠ Its first run **passed 17 checks and hid an exception** — a `finally` block calling `process.exit` swallows the throw it is unwinding, so a crash halfway down the file looked exactly like the checks below it silently not running. It catches and names the throw now. Two of the three original failures were the *test* reading the wrong columns: `activity_log.action` is `TG_OP`, so it is `'UPDATE'` and not `'updated'`, and the diff lands in `field_changes` rather than in `metadata` — getting either wrong reads as "the trigger is not firing" when it is firing perfectly.

The whole flow was then exercised over real HTTP as an authenticated admin, and every record it created was removed afterwards along with its 57 audit rows.

**Deliberately not built:** no new raise plumbing (`raises`/`investments` keep `target_kind = company | project`); no documents, tasks or milestones on a vehicle; no automatic org-node creation; no promotion into `ownership_interests`, which stays the executed corporate record that the `org_node_id` link makes reachable later.

**Done 2026-10-05 (a deal economics calculator: how big is this, and how much of it is ours):**

Richard's brief, written with Claude elsewhere, asked for a deal economics engine on every deal record plus a scratchpad for running numbers on a call. The premise checked out in one query and was worse than described. `projects.estimated_value` is a single unlabelled `numeric` holding **$57.65B across 9 records**: Myton Rail at **$48,000,000,000** beside the Alaska Strategic Materials JV at **$1,500,000**, plainly not the same quantity. Six of fourteen projects were blank, and the blank ones include **Stockton Power Nexus, for which the platform holds an 88,498-character proposal stating its $152.5M**. `financing_structures` held **0 rows** across all fourteen (built 2026-06, never used — and it is sources of funds, not uses). `entity_projects.equity_pct` existed and was populated on **0** links. No total built on that column could be defended, and nothing on screen said which quantity it was.

**Richard's four decisions, asked before anything was built:** clear `estimated_value` entirely and recompute; show revenue to Ber Wilson *distinctly* from revenue generated, because partners consume much of the gross; give each project the option of Land / Energy / Data Center SPVs, with splits not yet known; one live model per deal plus saved versions; and the AI path in this build rather than after it. He also supplied a shape the brief had no home for: **Elite Solutions / Avant builds the data center internals at $3B to $4B per 200MW and is paid 1.5% each year, split 50/50.**

⚠ **ALL ELEVEN OF THE BRIEF'S ACCEPTANCE TESTS ARE ARITHMETICALLY CORRECT**, checked by hand before any code. One ambiguity had to be pinned down: in reverse mode "implied average MW" is `MWh / 8760` with **no load factor applied**, which is the only reading under which the four Stockton lines total 115.5 MW and 77.0% utilization against 150 firm. Applying a load factor as well would double-count it.

⚠ **THE REPO HAD NO TEST RUNNER, NO TEST FILE AND NO TEST SCRIPT**, and the brief asks for automated tests. Verified working with **zero new dependencies**: `node --import ./deploy/register.mjs --test "src/**/*.test.ts"` runs TypeScript with `@/` aliases through the alias loader already sitting in `deploy/` for the verification scripts. That is now `npm test`. **97 tests.**

**The engine, in `src/lib/economics/`, pure and sibling-only.** Nine modules behind one entry point, `computeDealEconomics`. Thirteen line types: the brief's eight plus five for the business as it is — environmental attributes riding on an energy line's volume and drawing **zero** MW (without which booking RECs needs a second claim on the same megawatts and the ledger correctly rejects it); a recurring percentage of a **declared** base, which is the Elite/Avant shape; per-unit one-time covering homes, lots, tons and square feet with one type instead of three; tax credits as money that is **not revenue**; and an O&M agreement. Three capture tiers — revenue generated, Ber Wilson gross, Ber Wilson net of SPV ownership — with an unset split reported as **undetermined** and never as 100%.

⚠ **FOUR DEFECTS IN THE ENGINE, EVERY ONE FOUND BY RUNNING IT AND EVERY ONE THE ENGINE BREAKING ITS OWN RULES.**

1. **A stated deal total was compared against contract value**, mixing an annual figure with a term total. Stockton's $152.5M is annual; the comparison reported the entire deal as unattributed. `statedTotal` now carries its money **shape** and a CHECK enforces that both are set or neither. That is what makes the reconciliation land on **$31,600,040** as the brief specifies.
2. **A rollup summed to 0 where nothing had contributed**, so a model whose four lines had no term printed "$0 contract value" beside a real $120.9M annual figure. Every `DealSize` figure is nullable now and `tsc` named all seven call sites.
3. **A drawing line with no bucket blocked**, which made the scratchpad shape — MW and one price, no ledger — permanently invalid. The ledger is enforced when a deal *has* one; a model with no buckets is a back-of-envelope calc, and a warning says the ledger is absent rather than pretending one was violated.
4. **An O&M line allocated the capacity it was priced on**, double-booking the plant against itself: a full campus model showed **290 MW allocated against 225 MW firm**. Maintaining a 125 MW plant takes 125 MW off nothing.

And **capture as a share of total project value was returning 172%** — a fifteen-year contract total over a one-time build figure, which is not a share of anything. Split into a like-for-like share of gross and a one-time fee-on-build ratio; both read 12% on the brief's EPC case.

⚠ **A CARVE-OUT IS NOT ADDITIONAL REVENUE, AND THE FLAG IS A FIELD BECAUSE BOTH ANSWERS ARE REAL.** Our $18M margin on a $150M build is already inside the $150M, so gross stays $150M and never becomes $168M. A commission the owner pays Elite on top of the internals package *is* incremental. One is true of margins, the other of commissions, so the screen asks. The same reasoning made the fee **base** a field: 1.5% of a $3.5B capital figure and 1.5% of its annual revenue differ by two orders of magnitude.

**Eleven tables, applied as `postgres`** so they carry API grants (checked in `role_table_grants` before reading any code). Shared children throughout with `unique nulls not distinct` on the parent pair. `line_type` is a CHECK and **not** a registry, which is the opposite call to `lead_categories` and for a stated reason: each type is a formula in `lines.ts`, so adding one is necessarily a code change. Benchmarks and templates, which do grow with the business, are registries.

**The audit function was patched by deriving it from `pg_get_functiondef` and editing programmatically**, never retyped — 148 lines of per-table branches where a transcription slip corrupts the whole trail. Guarded by assertions that the array grew and `$function$` still appears twice, with `pg_proc` checked afterwards to hold exactly one `log_activity`. Nine narrow scalar tables get the trigger; `economics_versions` (wide jsonb) and `economics_input_proposals` (machine churn, human half on the row) stay off it for the reasons `commitments` does. Verified live: changing a discount rate records `{"old":9,"new":11.5}` against a named actor rather than "system".

⚠ **A MULTI-ROW INSERT CAUGHT US AGAIN (§12, 09-15).** `economics_lines` has four NOT NULL booleans with defaults, and a hand-written array where only some rows mentioned `is_ber_wilson_revenue` failed the whole statement. That is the *good* case; the bad one is a nullable column silently nulled on half the rows. `lineInsert()` now gives every writer a uniform column set and the routes inherit it. Found by the round-trip script, not by reading.

**`estimated_value` is no longer read anywhere.** Eight sites go through `pipelineValue()`, which returns the figure **and the name of the quantity**, preferring a computed capture and falling back to a hand-entered estimate without ever overwriting it. A total that mixes the two says so: "4 modelled, 3 estimated by hand". `formatPercent` added, because the repo had none and every call site rounded its own way. `/activity`'s private copy of `ACTIVITY_TABLE_LABELS` is gone rather than extended — the two had already drifted in both directions.

**The scratchpad computes in the browser, with the same engine.** `src/lib/economics` imports only its own siblings (verified), so the identical code runs client-side with no round trip and no second, looser formula. The price unit picks the formula and the screen says which one ran. State lives in the query string via `history.replaceState`, so a figure quoted to a prospect is a link that reproduces it exactly.

**The benchmark library is rows, not constants** — `STEEL_PRICE_FLOOR_PER_SQFT = 30` is the counter-example. Picking one fills the input **and** records which benchmark, resolved server-side from the key; without that second half the provenance ladder is decoration. A benchmark is offered **only where its unit matches the field**, because a $/kW-month rate filling a $/kWh price is a 1,000-fold error that reads as plausible. Eight seeds, every one `needs_review = true`, and the page leads with that count: they are plausible public ranges entered so the mechanism works on day one, and the source field says exactly that.

⚠ **THE EXTRACTION'S QUOTE RULE WAS WRONG TWICE, AND ONLY THE CORPUS SHOWED IT.** A figure is discarded unless a reader can check it, which means it needs the sentence it came from. A length-only floor of 8 characters let `"see above"` through at 9. A word-count floor of five then **rejected every figure a real pass actually produced**: run against `A2_GridEdge DC Customer Engagement Process — 20MW System 4.0`, the local model returned `"20MW System"`, `"PUE guarantee (1.18)"`, `"5-10-year initial term"` and `"$50-100K assessment fee"` — four correct figures, two to four words each, verbatim and perfectly checkable. **What separates them from a pointer is whether the quote contains the figure**, which is checkable rather than guessable: digits on both sides, with a two-digit minimum so `"see item 1"` cannot vouch for 145. A five-word clause remains the fallback, because `"one million two hundred fifty thousand dollars"` carries no digits at all. This is the 09-27 noise-filter lesson exactly — every clever version costs evidence.

**That live run is also the proof the AI path works, and works honestly.** 4,131 tokens in, 6,255 out, 130s on `qwen3.6-35b-a3b`. It handled both ranges correctly (proposing the low end and saying it is a range), flagged two figures as **GridEdge DC LLC's revenue rather than Ber Wilson's**, and volunteered that the document "is a vendor pitch deck … It contains no Ber Wilson deal economics, lease rates, energy pricing, cap/discount rates, or executed terms." A careful refusal is a correct answer.

**Proposals reach `/decide` as one row per DEAL, not per figure.** Forty figures out of one proposal document are one sitting, and a global queue row reading "accept 145 $/kW-month" has no model beside it, which is precisely where that decision cannot be made. The row points at the tab and carries no Accept button; `DISMISS` became `Partial<Record<DecideKind, …>>` and a kind with no dismiss path renders no button rather than one that fails.

**Two departures from the plan, both because the code disagreed.** "Create the three SPVs" creates **no `entities` row**: that table's category is `vendor | partner | contractor` and it drives the Vendors & Contractors directory, so a row for an unformed SPV would list "Helper Land LLC" as a company we buy from, and would assert a legal entity exists when on a pursuit nothing has been formed. `economics_spvs.entity_id` stays null until there is something real to point at. And **an invalid model publishes nothing to the pipeline** — 160 MW against 150 MW firm has no defensible deal size, so the record keeps what it had while the model still records that it is invalid, so the tab can say why.

**Verified.** 97 tests. A 26-check round trip against the live Studio stack covering all thirteen line types, the `numeric[]` ramp, an invalid model publishing nothing while still recording its invalidity, version snapshots and the audit diff — every record it creates removed in a `finally` block, and it prints the psql one-liner for the audit rows it cannot remove itself (114 from three runs were cleared by hand; they described a project that never existed as a business record). A worked-example script prints every derived figure for the Stockton reconciliation and a full campus so the arithmetic can be argued with. All routes 401 at the middleware unauthenticated and both pages 307 to login. `tsc` clean, `npm run build` clean (exit status captured **unpiped**), **18 lint problems against the documented 19 and none in the new code.**

**`estimated_value` backed up and read back before clearing** — 9 rows, $57.65B, to a filename carrying seconds so a same-minute retry cannot overwrite the good copy. Dry run by default.

**Done 2026-10-05 (a debug pass: a bracket in a name hid the record, a corpse read as a worker, and the off-box backup had been failing for four days):**

Open brief — *"review and debug the platform looking to fix, repair or remove any broken code"*. Started from the cheap signals and let the measurements pick the targets. `tsc --noEmit` was clean. `eslint` reported **27 problems (20 errors, 7 warnings)** against the 20 §9 documents. All 13 cron routes were named in `middleware.ts` (the 09-24 class), all 16 launchd agents loaded with last exit 0, `lms ps` matched the documented 131,072/parallel-1 with no `:2` duplicate, and an audit of every `process.env.X` **plus** the string-keyed `envInt('NAME', …)` form found nothing set in `.env.local` that code does not read — 53 read against 27 set. **The first pass of that audit was wrong and worth recording:** grepping only `process.env\.` reported `AGENT_CONTEXT_BUDGET_CHARS` as read by nothing, which would have been the `SUPABASE_DB_URL` class of defect on the one knob §12 cares most about. It is read at `agent.ts:433` through a helper that takes the name as a string. An env audit that greps one access form reports the other form as dead.

⚠ **A BRACKET IN A RECORD'S NAME MADE THE RECORD UNFINDABLE, AND THE QUERY REPORTED NO ERROR.** `query_opportunity` built its `.or()` by hand — `.replace(/[%,]/g, '')` — which strips the separator and leaves `(` and `)`, and those are logic-tree *grouping*. Measured against live PostgREST: `name.ilike.%IAN (EMP)%` returns **`[]` with no error** against the live opportunity actually called **"IAN (EMP) Technology aquisition"**, while the quoted `name.ilike."%IAN (EMP)%"` matches. So Ber AI, asked about that deal by name, concluded it was not on file. `GridEdge` worked, which is why this never surfaced: the defect needs a punctuated name.

⚠ **AND `sanitizeFilterTerm` WAS OVER-STRIPPING, WHICH COST MATCHES RATHER THAN WIDENING THEM.** Its docstring asserted that a quoted value "still cannot carry safely" quotes, parentheses and backslash. Measured, one character at a time, against live PostgREST: a **double-quoted** value carries `( ) , . ' / &` as plain text — the comma case is decisive, since `name.ilike."%Gold mine%,x.y.z"` parses and the same filter unquoted answers `PGRST100 failed to parse logic tree`. **Quoting is the defence; stripping is not.** Only three characters genuinely cannot survive: `"` ends the quote, `\` escapes, and `*` is PostgREST's own wildcard. Stripping `(` `)` `.` turned a phrase into one the record does not contain: three live `parties` rows — **`Arthur P. Valencia`**, **`Paul Hunsaker (Vancon Inc.)`** and **`PrivateLenders.com`** — could not be found by their own exact names, verified failing before and matching after through the real helper. Word splitting moved to its own `filterWords`, because the two jobs want opposite things: a phrase filter needs the punctuation, while the any-word fallback and the `hits` ranking need it gone or `hay.includes('commitment,')` is false for text that says "commitment".

⚠ **A DOCUMENT STRANDED MID-PASS FOR THIRTEEN DAYS READ AS A PASS THAT WAS RUNNING.** Two halves. `embedOpportunityDocument` inserted chunks and left `embedding_status` to whichever caller remembered — §12 said "settle it yourself on the opportunity side", and **three of the four callers did**. `api/admin/backfill-embeddings` did not, which left `Email research — englertmining@gmail.com` at **4 chunks, 7,125 characters, 4 × 1024-dim embeddings and a status of `pending`**: indexed, searchable, and rendered "Indexing…" forever by a UI waiting on a row nothing would return to. The contract moved into the function, mirroring `embedDocument`; a failed chunk delete now goes back to `pending`, not `error`, because the next pass should retry it.

The health check hid the other half, and **the comment directly above the rule already named the victim** — *"one had been stranded mid-pass since 09-22"*. `probeDocumentIndexing` excused up to two `processing` rows as "a pass running now", reasoning that the importers work sequentially, and that rule excused **that very row, every night for thirteen days**, while `GridEdge DC Use of Funds 0526626.pdf` sat at 0 chunks and 0 characters with nothing on earth due to retry it. **Excusing by count alone cannot tell a worker from a corpse.** Neither table has an `updated_at` (checked), so `uploaded_at` is the only clock — a *floor* on the row's age, which errs toward calling a stranded row young and never toward calling a live one old. Verified live: the card now reads **"30 documents never finished indexing (29 pending, 1 processing) … the oldest mid-pass row has been stranded 13 days, so no pass is coming back for it"** where it used to say 29 and mention nothing. Both rows corrected in place — the englert row to `complete` (guarded on it actually having chunks), the GridEdge row to `pending` so a retry can reach it. `opportunity_documents` now reads **46 complete / 28 pending / 20 skipped with every complete row holding chunks and every pending row holding none** — consistent for the first time.

**The focus-ring tail: 230 utility occurrences across 62 files.** §12's rule is that `focus:ring` fires on a *mouse click* too. The 09-26 pass fixed 248 sites and the shared sources have been right since — `field.tsx`, `field-classes.ts` and `button.tsx` all use `focus-visible:`, and their only `focus:ring` hits are the prose explaining the rule, so both files were excluded from the rewrite. The 62 files left are the ones that never migrated off their own local class strings. Kept deliberately as a *trigger* fix and not a restyle: each site keeps the ring size it was given, so `ring-2` stays `ring-2` rather than converging on the canonical `ring-3` — converging them means moving these files onto `field-classes.ts`, which is the documented migration and a different job. **Done 2026-09-30 (a project can be protected: containment, and a TOTP step-up to open it; DEPLOYED + MIGRATED):**
- **Richard's ask: "If I have a project that is Military. I want an additional password to protect it. (I only want it on certain projects to provide an extra layer of security.) What would meet the requirements."** Then, on being told the local stack could serve real MFA: *"We aren't really using Supabase for anything, it is a local database, so can we still get the text mfa? That would be cool. Do what you recommend given our situation."*
- **THE PASSWORD WAS NEVER THE HARD HALF, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAID SO BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN.** `grep -l "from('projects')" src/` returned **61 files**. `match_chunks` could only ever INCLUDE (`filter_project_ids` *widens* a search), so every unscoped portfolio question — which is most of what Ber AI is asked — already retrieved the project with no way to say no. And five outbound channels summarise projects into things that LEAVE the box: the weekly brief, Pepper's 06:50 note, the per-member task digest, document-arrival notifications, and the Google Tasks push onto a phone. A password on a web page answers none of that.
- **So it was built as TWO things, and the split is the whole design.** `projects.confidential` is **containment**: absolute, applies to both admins, and *cannot be unlocked away* — because an email that has been sent cannot be locked afterwards. `step_up_sessions` is **access**: a 30-minute, per-user, per-project record that a TOTP challenge was cleared.
- **⚠ "TEXT MFA" IS THE ONE FACTOR TYPE THIS BOX CANNOT HAVE, AND THE LOCAL STACK ALREADY HAD THE BETTER ONE.** `auth.mfa_factors` / `mfa_challenges` / `mfa_amr_claims` are all live on gotrue `v2.189.0`, and `select unnest(enum_range(null::auth.factor_type))` returns **`totp`, `webauthn`, `phone`**. `phone` means SMS: `/auth/v1/settings` reports `sms_provider: ""`, so it would need Twilio, and a texted code sends a phone number and a one-time secret off the machine — against the whole point of the 2026-07-07 local cutover. **TOTP is HMAC over a shared secret and the clock: no network, no provider, nothing leaves.** On a tailnet-only platform that is not a compromise, it is the correct answer. (`webauthn`/Touch ID is in the enum and `passkeys_enabled: false` in settings — a later option, same plumbing.)
- **A per-project password was rejected on its merits, not just because TOTP is available.** A shared secret gets written down, never rotates, and is the same for whoever asks; a 6-digit code is per-person, lives 30 seconds, and cannot be usefully told to anyone.
- **⚠ ADDING AN ARGUMENT TO A POSTGRES FUNCTION OVERLOADS IT — IT DOES NOT REPLACE IT — AND THE FAILURE IS FAIL-OPEN.** `create or replace function match_chunks(…, filter_exclude_project_ids uuid[] default '{}')` creates a **ninth-argument** function and leaves the eight-argument one standing. Both then match an 8-named-argument PostgREST call, PostgREST answers *"function is not unique"* rather than picking one, and the retry path in `match-chunks.ts` falls back to the **legacy signature that has no exclusion at all**. The migration drops the old signature explicitly first; `select count(*) from pg_proc where proname='match_chunks'` returns **1**.
- **THE EXCLUSION HAD TO BE IN SQL, NOT IN THE CALLER.** The RPC's `LIMIT` is applied before anything the caller could filter, so twenty protected passages at the top of a ranking would hand back an **empty answer** instead of the next twenty real ones — and an empty result reads as *"there is no correspondence on this"*, which §12 already names as the one wrong answer. A TS post-filter sits behind the SQL anyway, so the guarantee does not depend on the migration being applied.
- **THE FILTER IS A DEFAULT AT THE CHOKE POINT, NOT A PARAMETER CALLERS REMEMBER.** All five retrieval call sites go through `matchChunks`, so the exclusion lives there and callers opt **in** with `unlockedProjectIds`. Forgetting to opt in costs a few results; forgetting to opt out would cost the secret. The project's own brief passes its own id, because otherwise the brief for a protected project comes back with no evidence — which reads as an empty file rather than a refusal.
- **⚠ A NEXT LAYOUT IS NOT A DATA BOUNDARY.** The obvious place for the gate was `projects/[id]/layout.tsx`, and it is wrong: layout and page render in **parallel**, so a layout that decides to show an unlock prompt has not stopped the page beneath it fetching the project. The gate is a middleware **rewrite**, which replaces the whole tree before any of it runs and keeps the URL — the address bar still reads `/projects/<id>`.
- **⚠ AND THE UNLOCK PAGE HAD TO BE A SIBLING OF `[id]`, NOT A CHILD.** `projects/[id]/layout.tsx` selects name, client, sector, stage, location and coordinates and then runs **ten head-count queries** before rendering its tab bar. A `locked` page nested under it would have printed most of what the lock exists to withhold — and spent ten queries doing it. It lives at `/projects/locked`, which `projectIdFromPath` returns null for because `locked` is not a uuid (shape, not a word list, so a route added next year cannot become a project id).
- **⚠ A `Set` THAT LIES ABOUT ITS OWN `size` IS A TRAP, AND THE FIRST DRAFT SHIPPED ONE.** The fail-closed answer for "the confidential set could not be read" was a `Set` subclass whose `has()` always returned true — with `size === 0`. Every caller that reasonably writes `if (hidden.size)` as a shortcut for "nothing to hide" would have been handed a disclosure by a helper designed to prevent one. Replaced with a real enumeration of every project id.
- **CONTAINMENT, surface by surface.** Projects list (protected projects lift into their own **name-only** block, so an admin can still find and unlock one), dashboard (every figure is a sum, so they leave all of them — and the page **says how many are missing**, because an unlabelled count is not a coverage signal), timeline, map (pins *and* parcel boundaries — a location is the one attribute a military site should least publish to a screen), task board, command palette (⌘K searches names across nine areas and was the shortest path to a protected project from anywhere), `computeAttention` (one edit covering `/api/attention`, Ber AI's `get_attention_items` **and** Pepper's email), `fetchTasksForDigest`, `fetchOpenTasks` when unscoped, the weekly brief, `notifyArrivals`, `reconcileDrivePublishing`, the Google Tasks push, and correspondence search via `thread_links`.
- **A TASK'S TITLE IS WHY DROPPING THE TAG IS NOT ENOUGH.** "Send Hill AFB the bonding letter" names the deal in the one column every digest prints. The row goes, not the tag.
- **BER AI NEVER SEES A PROTECTED PROJECT AT ALL — EVEN WHEN THE READER HAS STEPPED UP.** Stricter than the rest of the platform, on purpose: a turn is streamed into a transcript and **persisted to `agent_conversations`/`agent_messages`**, where surfaces that know nothing about the lock will read it; the dock is on every page under ⌘J; and the model paraphrases, so there is no way to un-say a figure once it is in the thread. With 42 tools and a dozen separate `projects` reads in a dozen result shapes, filtering each by hand was twelve chances to miss one — so `executeToolCall` was split, and the result is **scrubbed recursively** on any key that is `id`, `project_id` or `*_project_id`. **The count of what was withheld is handed to the model**, because an agent answering "Ber Wilson has 13 projects" from a list silently trimmed from 14 is confidently wrong, which is worse than one that says some are protected.
- **`canAccessRecord` ANSWERS IT TOO, WHICH IS WORTH MORE THAN SEVEN EDITS.** Milestones, diligence, financing, players, entity links, milestone-by-id and profile intake all already ask that one function. Adding the check there covers all seven *and* the eighth route somebody adds next year, which would otherwise miss it by default.
- **⚠ THE MIDDLEWARE CAN ONLY SEE AN ID IN THE PATH.** `/api/ai/brief`, `/api/ai/draft`, `/api/documents/[id]` (the **bytes**, via a signed URL), `/api/updates/save` (which also *embeds* into `chunks`), `/api/compliance-items`, `/api/dependencies` and the signed-upload-url route all take a project id in a **body or query** and were invisible to the gate. `requireProjectAccess()` closes each one and returns the helpful refusal (`needsStepUp`, `needsEnrollment`) where the role gate would only say "Not authorized".
- **A DEPENDENCY NAMES BOTH ENDS, so either end being protected removes the row** — the record *is* the relationship, and half of one is not a dependency.
- **SESSIONS ARE A TABLE, NOT A SIGNED COOKIE.** A cookie cannot be revoked and cannot be audited. `delete from step_up_sessions` closes every open session on the platform; "Lock everything" in Settings → Security is one call; and **refusals are logged beside grants**, because three refused codes against a military project at 02:00 is the single most useful thing this feature can ever say, and it only exists if the failures are written down. Expiry is **absolute, never sliding** — a sliding window means a tab left open on a desk stays unlocked all day, which is the threat.
- **TURNING PROTECTION ON AND OFF ARE DIFFERENT ACTS (§12, 09-30).** ON needs only an admin — hesitating over a code is how a project stays unprotected — and closes every open step-up so the state afterwards is unambiguous. OFF needs a **live step-up**, because declassifying is the dangerous direction and an unattended session is exactly what this answers.
- **AND SWITCHING IT ON NAMES WHAT PROTECTION CANNOT REACH.** The response carries caveats built from the record itself: a shared Drive folder stays shared with whoever already has it, and `n` stored briefs may already have been emailed. Protection starts now, not backwards. `reconcileDrivePublishing` treats a protected project exactly like a dormant one — nothing new goes out — but it does not retract what went out before, and the screen says so rather than implying otherwise.
- **VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE DATABASE, 29 CHECKS, NO MOCKS** (`scripts/verify-confidential.mts`, `scripts/verify-confidential-lib.mts`). Retrieval on the heaviest project in the corpus (West Wendover, 622 chunks): **60 passages without the exclusion, 0 with it**. `match_chunks` still answers with only its required argument. Step-up written, found live, not found once expired, revoked. The cron-vs-user asymmetry both ways: a stepped-up user does not see it hidden **and the cron still does**. Path parsing including `/projects/new` and `/projects/locked`. The scrubber removing a list entry by its own id, nulling a nested object, and counting both. Every fixture removed and the subject project restored to its original flag, re-read to confirm.
- **No new env vars.** Nothing to set, nothing to forget — which was a deliberate goal after `DINO_LEAD_EMAIL` sat unset for its entire life and 400'd every press.
- **Lint unchanged at 20 problems**, the documented baseline. The one new load-on-mount effect was avoided rather than added to §9's twelve: Settings → Security reads its factor list on the **server** and refreshes through the router.
- **⚠ TWO SESSIONS, AND MIGRATION NUMBERS COLLIDE THE SAME WAY FILES DO.** §12 already says to stage by name in this repo; the governance session was running concurrently and we **both** picked `20260930000004`, then **both** renumbered to `20260930000008`. Mine is `20260930000012`. `src/types/database.ts` was being edited by both of us at once, so only my three `confidential` hunks were staged — `git diff -U0`, filter the hunks, `git apply --cached --unidiff-zero`.
- **⚠ WHAT THIS IS NOT.** It is not a compliance control: §8 stands, no CUI until GovCloud, and a 6-digit code is not CMMC L2. It does not reach Drive, Gmail or Google Tasks copies that already exist. It does not cover mail about a protected deal that **nobody has filed** on it — nothing in the database says which deal unfiled mail is about, so filing it is what protects it. And `proposal-matching` deliberately still matches against protected projects: suppressing that would create duplicate records, and it only ever shows a name to an admin who could step up anyway.

**Done 2026-09-30 (a departure becomes a record instead of a deletion; the corporate, personnel and compliance registers; DEPLOYED + MIGRATED):**
- **Richard's ask: "on the ber wilson area where we track the board meetings etc... I also want to track when we delete personnel. (with notes as to why we parted ways etc... What other note types and audit trail might I need to meet all of the compliance demands for corporate governance?"**
- **⚠ THE PLATFORM WAS TAKING "DELETE PERSONNEL" LITERALLY, IN TWO PLACES, WITH NO AUDIT BEHIND EITHER.** `api/org/people/[id]` DELETE was a hard delete on `org_people`, whose status set was **only `active | open`** (`orgPersonStatus()` coerced anything else to `active`, so even a hand-written `'departed'` round-tripped as active) — a person left, the box vanished, and no date, reason or trace survived. `api/admin/users/[id]` DELETE was a hard delete on `team_members` that also deleted the auth login and **CASCADED `access_grants`**, so the record of *what a departed employee could reach* died with them. For a federal contractor that is the single question most often asked about one.
- **⚠ AND THE TWO REGISTERS A GOVERNANCE QUESTION IS ASKED OF WERE THE LEAST-AUDITED TABLES IN THE APP.** `log_activity()` triggers existed on eleven tables — projects, tasks, documents, milestones, dd_items, compliance_items, financing_structures, updates, review_queue, dev_notes, lead_categories — and on **none** of `team_members`, `org_people`, `org_nodes`, `meetings`, `access_grants`, `company_profile`, `certifications`. A project's value changing was logged; a director's signature authority changing was not. Exactly backwards.
- **The answer is §12's own rule — THE ROW IS THE TOMBSTONE — applied to people instead of Drive documents.** Four migrations (`20260930000008`–`20260930000011`), twelve new tables, three new admin-only pages, one shared renderer.

**THE PERSONNEL REGISTER (`/company/people`)**
- **`personnel` is a FIFTH people table and that is deliberate, against §9's warning.** The three that exist answer different questions and none answers this one: `parties` is a contact (global, shared, deliberately not private); `org_people` is a **box on the chart** — it carries vacant seats with `name IS NULL`, which is the proof it is not a person; `team_members` is a **login** and a task assignee. An employment relationship is none of those: someone can be employed with no login and no box, and the same human can hold two engagements years apart. It also keeps the employment-law-sensitive narrative in **exactly one** admin-only place rather than smeared across three — which matters because §8 is explicit that RLS is defence in depth here and the middleware IS the boundary.
- **The division of labour is drawn so nothing is stored twice:** `team_members.deactivated_at` = when platform **access** ended (a system fact); `personnel.separated_on` = when **employment** ended (an HR fact); `personnel_notes` = **why**. §12's "two sources for one figure get two columns, not a winner" is about *disagreeing* sources — these are two different figures, and the gap between them is itself the interesting number on an offboarding review.
- **`status` is a GENERATED column** (`separated_on is null ? 'active' : 'departed'`), so a row cannot be active with a separation date on it. One quantity, one definition, in the schema.
- **⚠ RECORDING A DEPARTURE IS A PASS, NOT A COLUMN WRITE** (`src/lib/governance/separation.ts`). It seeds a 25-step offboarding checklist, **closes every open signature-authority row**, revokes the platform login while **snapshotting the grants it could reach**, marks the chart departed — and reports which of those it did, by name and count. **The second of those is the one that matters and the one that would have been forgotten:** an officer's signing authority outliving their employment is a live exposure on a construction job and nothing else in the system would ever close it.
- **EVERY STEP FILLS A BLANK AND NONE OVERWRITES A VALUE** (§12, 09-30). `effective_to` is written only `is('effective_to', null)`, so an appointment someone already closed for a different reason keeps that reason; `deactivated_at` only where null, so a re-run cannot move the date access actually ended; the checklist is seeded only when the person has **no** steps, so a re-run cannot wipe ticked boxes. Nothing is renamed and no judgement is revised.
- **⚠ THE PASS LIVES IN `lib` AND NOT IN THE ROUTE HANDLER, AND THAT IS WHY THE BUG WAS FOUND.** §12: a shared lib no script can load is a shared lib nothing can verify. `scripts/verify-separation.mts` runs 18 checks against the live database — and check 16 **failed on the first run**: the org-chart step wrote unconditionally, so a second pass reported *"org chart marked departed"* having done nothing. Idempotent in **effect** is not the same as honest about it, and the entire value of the `applied` list is that the reader can believe it. Now it reads the box first. Written inside a route handler this would have shipped.
- **The checks that are worth having, all passing:** status derived not written · checklist seeded 25/25 with "Signature authority ended" present and required · open signing authority closed at the separation date with reason `separation` · **an already-closed appointment keeps its own `2023-06-30 / role_changed`** · access revoked with a date and a named actor · **1 project grant snapshotted before any cascade** · chart departed, not deleted, carrying the date · a second run moves no date, duplicates no step, reports no work · a held record refuses deletion **in words** · the audit log diffed the separation as `status, separated_on, separation_type`. Every fixture removed in a `finally` block; verified afterwards that `personnel`, `org_roles`, `personnel_offboarding` are all back to 0 rows and `access_grants` has no orphan.
- **`legal_hold` / `retention_until` are enforced by a BEFORE DELETE TRIGGER, not a comment.** The RAISE names the hold and its reason — *"Personnel record X is under legal hold (EEOC charge pending) and cannot be deleted. Clear the hold first."* — and the route passes that sentence straight through rather than turning it into a code. `legal_hold = true` without a reason is itself refused by a CHECK: a hold nobody can explain cannot be lifted with confidence either.
- **Note kinds are a REGISTRY with an FK, not a CHECK** — straight from the `lead_categories` lesson a few hours earlier. Twelve seeded (separation, performance, disciplinary, commendation, incident, compensation, classification, onboarding, licence, grievance, leave, general), `on update cascade` so a rename carries its notes, **no delete rule** so a kind with notes cannot be deleted at all — which is what `active` is for. **⚠ And the tone is a NAME against `TONE_BADGE`, never a class string:** the seed was first written with `red` and `green`, which are not in that palette — caught before deploy, and a stored Tailwind class would have rendered unstyled with no error anywhere.
- **Offboarding steps store their own `label` as TEXT, not an FK to the template** — the opposite call from note kinds, deliberately. A note *kind* is a classification you filter and report on; a *step* is a line item whose wording is part of the record, so changing the template next year must not retitle what was actually done. 25 steps across access / property / payroll / authority / external, and **required steps are counted separately** because a departure with the easy optional steps done and "signature authority ended" still open is not finished, and one percentage over everything would hide exactly that.
- **`rehire_eligible` is tri-state on purpose.** NULL means nobody has decided, which is a different answer from "no" and is the one a reference request turns on.

**THE CORPORATE RECORD (`/company/governance`)**
- **`resolutions`.** `/company/board` was already a real minute book — `meetings` carries chair, secretary, attendees, a `decisions` array and a draft→approved chain. What it could not hold is an action taken by **unanimous written consent**, which has no meeting and therefore had nowhere to live; and a `decisions` array of sentences cannot be cited by number, bound to an entity, signed or superseded. **`check (kind <> 'written_consent' or meeting_id is null)` makes the modelling point structural** rather than a convention. `unique nulls not distinct (org_node_id, reference)` because group-level resolutions have a NULL entity and a plain unique over a NULL column **enforces nothing** (§12, 09-28).
- **`org_roles` — and the question it exists for is "who held signature authority on 14 March 2024".** `org_people` carried **no dates at all**: it is a picture of today, which is precisely what a corporate record is not. Effective-dated, with `can_sign_contracts` / `signing_limit` / `bank_signatory` / `can_bind_surety`. **NULL `signing_limit` with signing authority means UNLIMITED — a real state and a different one from zero** — so the UI prints the word "Unlimited" in alarm tone rather than a blank, and a "Can sign today" strip above the register lists every current signer with their ceiling.
- **`ownership_interests` — the cap table, with the transfer chain** (`acquired_from_id`, `consideration`, `authorizing_resolution_id`). `investors`/`investments` track the **raise**; this is the ownership that results, and `ORG_ENTITY_TYPES` already splits Series (internal capital) from Standalone (outside capital), which is the line a cap table has to respect. **⚠ `org_node_id` is `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, alone among the FKs in these four migrations** — `org_nodes.parent_id` cascades, so without it deleting a division would silently take its SPVs' cap tables with it. Verified: the delete is refused. The "Held today" strip sums **only live rows** (a historical ledger summed would read as 300% owned) and flags an entity whose live interests do not total 100%.
- **`meetings.minutes_approved_at_meeting_id`** — `approved_by` was free text and nothing recorded *where* the approval happened. For an auditor the point of minute approval is the chain: the minutes of meeting N were approved at meeting N+1.

**THE COMPLIANCE REGISTER (`/company/compliance`)**
- **`entity_obligations` — the filing calendar.** `certifications` covers DBE/MBE-class certs with expiry but at **company** level and as a capability statement; `compliance_items` is project-scoped. Nothing held what attaches to an **entity**: annual reports, registered agent renewals, foreign qualifications, contractor licences, BOI filings. **⚠ The coarse `category` is CHECKed and the specific `kind` is FREE TEXT** — the category is fixed by law and finance, the kind grows every time the company registers in a new state or picks up a licence class, and §12 forbids a CHECK on a set that grows with the business. Free text plus `enumLabel()` is the honest middle: no constraint to forget, no registry table for a label nobody filters on. `dueTone()` bands the colour — lapsed or inside a fortnight is alarm, 60 days is information — because **when every row is red, red has stopped signifying**.
- **`conflict_disclosures`, and the important column is `has_conflicts boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false`.** A "nothing to disclose" return **IS** the record: false means someone was asked and said no, and the absence of a row means nobody was asked. A register that only holds disclosed conflicts cannot tell those apart — the same shape as §12's rule that a fallback is a conclusion and can only be drawn from a check that ran. So the screen computes **who has not returned a disclosure this cycle** and names them. Not generic hygiene here: the group contracts through related SPVs and Dino is an acquired operating company billing Ber Wilson.
- **`related_party_transactions`.** `dino_revenue` already tracks the internal/external split for commercial reasons; an auditor or a lender asks for the same money as a **disclosure**, which is a different question needing the **arm's-length basis** and the **approving resolution** beside it. An amount on its own answers nothing, so a missing basis renders as *"not stated"* in amber rather than a dash.
- **`policies` + `policy_acknowledgements`, with `version` NOT NULL.** An acknowledgement of "the handbook" with no version is worth nothing: the question is always whether this person agreed to the clause now in dispute. Retiring a version keeps its acknowledgements. Coverage is shown against **active headcount**, the only denominator that means anything.

**THE AUDIT TRAIL**
- **`log_activity()` learns a generic column-by-column diff**, built with a `jsonb_each` FULL JOIN over `to_jsonb(old)`/`to_jsonb(new)` skipping `created_at`/`updated_at`. Its existing branches name one or two interesting columns per table, which is right for a project (nobody audits a description edit) and wrong for a governance record, where **which field moved is the entire question** — a signing limit raised to unlimited, a separation type changed from resigned to terminated, a resolution's signature status walked back. **⚠ Gated to a LIST of twenty tables rather than made the default**, because `documents` and `updates` carry extracted text in the hundreds of kilobytes and a generic diff over those would write both copies into `activity_log` on every edit.
- **The function was derived from `pg_get_functiondef` and patched programmatically, not retyped.** A 148-line plpgsql function transcribed by hand is a transcription bug waiting to happen. (`pg_get_functiondef` emits no trailing semicolon, which is why the first apply died with `syntax error at or near "do"` 190 lines later.)
- **Triggers on all twenty tables**, built by loop rather than written out twenty times — a hand-written list is where a table gets missed, and a missed table here is a silent gap in the one record that exists to not have gaps. **What this buys on DELETE:** the function already writes `to_jsonb(old)` into `activity_log.metadata`, and `activity_log` has **no UPDATE or DELETE policy**, so from here a hard-deleted governance row **survives its own deletion in an append-only log**. Verified — the tombstone came back carrying `full_name` and `separation_type`. That is the net underneath the delete guards, not a replacement for them.
- **The org and admin-user routes moved to `actorAdminClient()`.** They used bare `createAdminClient()`, and `team_members`/`org_people`/`org_nodes` are now tracked — so every write a human made would have been logged as **"system"** (§12). 20 new `ACTIVITY_TABLE_LABELS` entries too, or `/activity` would print "Org People" and "Personnel Note Kinds" at a reader.
- **`api/org/people/[id]` DELETE is now retire-then-remove.** First press on a named, active person marks them departed and keeps them in the record; a second press removes the box, which is the right act for a seat that genuinely no longer exists; a vacant seat removes immediately, since there is no person behind it. **`api/admin/users/[id]` DELETE now 409s with `requiresPurge` for anyone who ever held a login**, naming deactivation and `/company/people` instead — `?purge=1` is the deliberate override for a row created in error, and it snapshots the grants into the log on the way out.

**THE SHARED RENDERER**
- **Six registers, one `RegisterSection` driven by a column list and a field list, and ONE dynamic API route pair** (`/api/governance/[register]`). §12 has two separate rules pointing here: never fork a shared pass per table, and a shared renderer wired to one surface is worse than none. **⚠ The register name resolves through a fixed map and the field list is a SECURITY BOUNDARY** — nothing un-whitelisted reaches PostgREST, and `id`, `created_at`, `author` and the generated `status` are deliberately absent, so a crafted body cannot restamp an HR note's author or forge a status. `author` on a note and `completed_at`/`completed_by` on a checklist step are stamped **server-side from the viewer**: a note whose author the reader can set is not evidence of anything, and a checklist whose completion time the browser supplies is not evidence of the thing it exists to evidence.
- **`explainDbError()` turns a constraint name into a sentence that names the fix** — *"A written consent is an action taken WITHOUT a meeting, so it cannot cite one"*, *"That note kind still has notes filed under it… mark it inactive instead — the history keeps its label"*.
- **UX rules followed rather than rediscovered:** `focus-visible:` never `focus:` · 44px targets grown with `-inset-3` overlays · no hover-only controls below `sm` · every stored value through `enumLabel()` · named absences (*"not recorded"*, *"unnumbered"*, *"no date set"*) instead of a bare em dash at a value's own weight · the six-tab company row scrolls rather than wrapping to a second line that reads as a different control.

**MIGRATION COLLISION, CAUGHT BEFORE COMMIT**
- **⚠ A SECOND CLAUDE SESSION WAS BUILDING CONFIDENTIAL PROJECTS IN THIS SAME REPO AND HAD ALREADY TAKEN `20260930000004`.** Mine were renumbered to `000008`–`000011`. Worse, `src/types/database.ts` held **both** sessions' hand-edits — my 7 columns and their `projects.confidential` — so `git add` of that file would have committed half of their in-flight feature. Staged via a **filtered patch**: dump `git diff`, drop the three hunks mentioning `confidential`, `git apply --cached`. Asserted exactly 3 hunks dropped, then grepped the staged diff for `step_up|confidential` and confirmed all six remaining hits were my own `personnel_notes.confidential`. §12's "stage files BY NAME, never `git add -A`" now has a fourth recorded occurrence — and a new wrinkle: **by name is not enough when a single file holds both sessions' work.**
- **Deploy:** build RC captured from an **unpiped** `npm run build` (259 routes, rc=0) before any kickstart — §12, a pipe took production down once. `/company/people|governance|compliance` → 307 to `/login`; `/api/governance/*` → 401. `tailnet-setup.sh` clean on all three endpoints; `lmstudio-check.sh` clean at 131072 / parallel 1 / both models (swap at 20.5GB and 306MB free, which is the box's documented standing state, not this change).
- **Said plainly to Richard and worth repeating here:** this is the register, not the advice. What must be minuted, and how long records must be kept, depends on the entity types, whether investors hold information rights, and Utah employment law — that is a conversation with counsel. And putting termination narratives in a platform where app traffic is service-role and the middleware is the whole boundary (§8) is fine at two admins and is **exactly the trigger §8 already names** for moving pages to the RLS-respecting server client the moment a bookkeeper or PM gets a login.
- **Not built, deliberately:** read logging (who *opened* a personnel file). It is the genuine gap between this and an HRIS, it is a real build, and at two users it is not yet worth it (§11).

**Done 2026-09-30 (the national rail network on /map, and a flag that is not a yes/no; DEPLOYED):**
- **Richard's ask: "the stractnet rail is available to download in many formats … will you pick the best one that allows you to embed it on our Maps section? As we take on projects we will highlight certain parts of the rail. For now we just want the entire stractnet rail on there. Do it how you think is best."** Handed the BTS portal link, the 2023 DoD STRACNET wall map (34×44 PDF) and a 48MB NTAD File Geodatabase download.
- **The format question answered itself once the size was measured: 302,771 line features, 63MB of raw geometry.** The portal offers Shapefile/GeoJSON/CSV/KML/GDB; every one of them is a whole-file download the browser would fetch on every page load and simplify by nobody. The map already reads **PMTiles by byte range** for its basemap, so the rail goes in the same shape — only the lines in view, at the detail that zoom deserves, over the reader that already exists. It is also the only option that scales to *"highlight the corridor this project runs on"*: every feature keeps its **FRAARCID**, the FRA's permanent arc id, so a future highlight is a filter and not a re-import.
- **⚠ `STRACNET` IS NOT A Y/N FLAG, AND A `='Y'` FILTER BUILDS AN EMPTY LAYER THAT NOTHING REPORTS.** The column holds **`S` — 19,190 segments, 32,486 miles** and **`C` — 3,928 segments, 6,105 miles**, with NULL on the other 279,653. That is the published shape of the thing and the title of the sheet Richard sent: *Strategic Rail Corridor Network **& Defense Connector Lines***. Written from memory the filter would have produced a layer with zero features, a toggle that does nothing, and no error anywhere. The two classes are now drawn as two kinds of member of one network — connectors dashed, as they are on DoD's own sheet.
- **THE GEODATABASE NAMES ITS OWN CODES, AND `ogrinfo -fielddomain` IS HOW YOU ASK.** `net`, `stracnet`, `passngr` and `country` are all coded-value domains carried inside the `.gdb`. So `M: Main sub network`, `I: Major Industrial Lead`, `O: Other track (minor industrial leads)`, `S: Passing sidings over 4000 feet long`, `Y: Yard Tracks`, `X: Out of service line`, `A: Abandoned rail line`, `R: Abandoned line that has been physicaly removed`, `T: Trail on former rail right-of-way`, `Z: Transit-only rail line or museum/tourist operation` are **verbatim, not guessed** — which matters because §7 forbids printing a stored code at a reader and I was one keystroke from inventing labels for `T` and `R`.
- **⚠ THE DATA CARRIES ITS OWN NULL MARKERS AND THEY LOOK LIKE VALUES.** `BRANCH` holds the literal **`#N\A` 42,448 times**; `RROWNER1` uses **`XXXX`** (unknown, 5,380 route-miles) and **`PVTX`** (private) where there is no reporting mark. Caught by reading three sample rows out of the transform rather than trusting it — the first Utah sample printed `"branch": "#N\A"`, which would have rendered in the popup as if it were the name of a line. The first build shipped with that bug and was rebuilt.
- **AND THE REPORTING MARKS ARE NOT THE ONES IN MY HEAD.** Built the owner dictionary by querying the corpus for route-miles rather than recalling Class I railroads: the marks here are **UP, BNSF, CN, CPKC, CSXT, NS** — `CP`, `CPRS`, `SOO` and `KCS` do not appear at all, having merged into CPKC, and `MRL`/`PAR`/`PAS` are likewise gone. A stale dictionary is the §12 "prompt example is a lie the model repeats with confidence" failure one layer down: it would have confidently labelled nothing.
- **WHAT IS MISSING AT A GIVEN ZOOM IS A DECISION, NOT A CASUALTY.** `scripts/rail-tile-hints.mjs` sets a **per-feature minzoom by what the line IS** — STRACNET and connectors at z2, the main sub-network at z4, sidings/industrial leads/yard tracks at z9, out-of-service and rail-trail at z10 — instead of letting `--drop-densest-as-needed` do it. Density is blind to kind: it would thin a strategic corridor through a busy terminal district while keeping the yard tracks beside it, which is precisely backwards for a layer whose whole point is that the strategic network is complete at every zoom. `--drop-smallest-as-needed` stays only as the byte-cap backstop, and it sheds the **shortest** segments first, so a long corridor survives losing a stub.
- **Measured, then tuned once.** First build put the main sub-network at z6 — which made the "All rail" toggle do **nothing** below z6, a control that silently no-ops being the exact failure this log keeps recording. Moved to z4; worst-case tile (z4 CONUS) went 99KB → 329KB gzipped for 19,904 features, archive 61MB → 66MB. That is one tile, cached a day, only while the camera is continental. Accepted.
- **Verified in four ways short of a browser, because the Chrome extension would not connect.** (1) The **route's own module path**: `getArchive` + `parseTileCoords` + `serveTile` run against the real archive — tiles 200 as `application/x-protobuf` at z2/4/6/9/12, mid-Pacific 204 (no coverage is not an error), and all four coordinate guards refuse. (2) **Decoded the MVT**: z6 Utah holds 712 features, 328 STRACNET, owners UP:582 / SBG:36 / TRAX:23 / UTAH:19, and a sample carries `{owner: UP, rights: AMTK, subdiv: PROVO, passenger: A, tracks: 2, strac: S}`. (3) **Style assertions in both flavors**: the three rail layers splice at indexes 45–47 — above the basemap's `roads_rail` (44), below `boundaries_country` (48) and below the first label (60) — so place names stay readable over rail and MapView's project overlays still append on top. (4) **Rendered the linework to SVG and compared it to Richard's poster**: the Pacific Northwest loop, the Overland Route, the Sunset Route along the border and the Chicago convergence all match.
- **⚠ The basemap already draws its own OSM rail hairline, and two surveys of the same track draw as a doubled line a few metres apart.** `roads_rail` is hidden while the NARN layer is on and restored when it is off — so turning rail off leaves the map exactly as it was before this session.
- **The archive reader was extracted rather than forked.** `src/lib/map/pmtiles.ts` now holds the file-handle source, the mtime/size reopen cache, the coordinate guard and the tile response; both the basemap route and the new rail route call it. §12 has the forked-pass rule in it twice already. **⚠ And it had to stop using TypeScript parameter properties**: node's strip-only type stripping — which is how every script in this repo runs TS — refuses them outright, so the shared lib could not be loaded by the repo's own script runner, which is to say it could not be verified. Plain fields.
- **What is deliberately NOT built: the highlight itself.** Richard said *"as we take on projects we will highlight certain parts"* and *"for now we just want the entire stracnet rail on there"* — so the tiles carry FRAARCID, owner and subdivision, and no speculative layer with an empty filter was added (§11). Clicking a line instead answers the question that is live today: who owns this track, what subdivision is it, is it main line or siding, does Amtrak have rights over it.
- **Tooling note:** `brew install gdal tippecanoe` is a ~200-formula dependency tree and took about 25 minutes of downloads on this box; `pmtiles` was already present from the basemap setup. Run with the chat model unloaded — swap was at 19.1 of 20.5GB before `lms unload --all` — and `deploy/lmstudio-check.sh --fix` restored it afterwards.
- **Shipped:** `scripts/setup-rail-data.sh` (re-runnable; takes the newest NTAD zip in ~/Downloads by default, moves the archive into place atomically so a half-written file is never served), `scripts/rail-tile-hints.mjs`, `/api/map/rail/{z}/{x}/{y}`, `src/lib/map/pmtiles.ts`, `src/lib/map/rail.ts`, rail layers in `style.ts`, the Off/STRACNET/All toolbar control remembered per browser, legend entries, and a card-themed popup. Archive: **66MB, 84,950 tiles, z2–12**, at `~/berwilson-data/maps/rail.pmtiles` — outside the app dir, like the basemap, so a deploy never deletes it.
